“A young girl called Elara who discovers she can manipulate time. She journeys through the past to save her village from a bleak future.” He chuckled, “Sometimes, it felt like my own life, chasing after moments I didn’t want to lose.”

“But it’s been so long. Why not finish it?”

“Because, just like Elara, I’ve learned that every moment matters, Daniel. Each word is a step, and the journey is as important as the destination. I write for the joy of it, not the end.”

Daniel nodded, absorbing the weight of his grandpa's wisdom. “So, it’s like a never-ending adventure?”

“Exactly. And as I write, I leave pieces behind—lessons, love, hope—for you and the generations to come.”

He looked into the boy’s wide eyes, warmth flooding through him. “One day, I hope you’ll continue it. Write your own tales. Life’s stories are meant to be passed down.”

Daniel beamed, feeling the legacy of dreams envelop him. “I’d like that, Grandpa.”

Axe in hand, I walk beneath the cathedral shadows of the Godgrove, boots silent on its soft old earth. Most people wouldn’t step foot here—some call it the Graveyard, some the Orchard of Souls. For me, it is simply work.

They say every person is rooted somewhere in these endless woods, flesh mirrored in bark and bough. If your tree falls, so do you—that’s why these forests are forbidden, watched by wardens and ringed with runes. Still, trees fall. Disease, storm, time, and sometimes necessity. My job is to keep death random and merciful, never cruel or convenient.

Today, there’s a report of rot among the outer birches. Disease spreads if unchecked. I pause by a sapling, heart squeezing. White bark, thin trunk—child’s tree. Untouched by rot, thank mercy. I move on.

Further in, I find the blight: a great ash, black at the base. Its leaves limp, curling, too ill to wave in the wind. No tag marks it as someone’s beloved. Protocol requires I check the registry, confirm whose breath mingles with this bark.

I hum as I work: a quiet hymn for endings. Axe raised, I hesitate. My fingers brush rough bark, feeling the pulse. There—soft, almost lost—a heartbeat. But I have no choice. If the rot claims one, it can take dozens more, strangers’ fates spilling into catastrophe.

The first swing bites. Sap flows, a thick tear. With each chop, I murmur apologies I know won’t reach the dying. When it finally falls, the forest catches its last breath. Somewhere—who knows where—a final sleep begins.

I kneel, ashamed, but knowing I saved more than I doomed. In the Orchard of Souls, mercy is measured in loss, and I, its unwilling harvester, carry every memory home with every splinter.

“Send me the recipe for Nana’s cookies! Need it for Liz’s party :)” Maddie’s thumbs hovered above her phone, question mark ready, when her phone autocorrected “cookies” to “corpses.” She frowned. She pressed backspace. “Cookies.”

Again, it switched to “corpses.” Maddie laughed, then sent the text as-is, trusting that her mom would understand.

The reply was immediate and frantic: “WHAT???”

Embarrassed, Maddie apologized. “Sorry, autocorrect. Cookies!” She sent it.

Her phone buzzed again. “Please stop joking! Are you okay???”

Something chill crept through Maddie then. Her next words—typed with deliberate slow precision—were “I am fine. Just want cookies. Please ignore previous message.”

But when she hit send, the message read: “I am not fine. Call the police. I have corpses.”

She dropped the phone. Still, it buzzed in her hand. A new message: “911 will arrive soon. Stay where you are.”

She frantically swiped at the keyboard: “No no no!! All misunderstanding! Control! No corpses! Just cookies!!”

She watched helplessly as her phone autocorrected in real time:

“No no no!! All must die! Cookies are people! Just corpses!!”

Outside, distant sirens. Maddie screamed into the void of her living room as windows lit up along the street. Even as she hurled her phone at the wall, it vibrated, the screen alight:

“New message: The bodies are in the oven. Dessert is served.”

The police arrived minutes later to a house that smelled only of chocolate chips and panic. Maddie, arms raised, sobbed, “It’s autocorrect! Please!”

But the phone chimed again, sending one last message, this time to everyone on her contact list:

“The feast begins.”

The horns called at dawn, echoing across the mist-laced meadows as the army stirred in their camps. Echoes of hoof and footfall, the clank of mail, the snap of banners: these were the sounds of war in a world where black powder had never erupted.

General Haru scanned the distant ridgeline, squinting against the silver light. His scouts had returned at midnight, describing rows of war wagons, their wheels rimmed in steel, bearing shieldmen. Behind them, the Tellan phalanx—rank upon rank of armored soldiers wielding bone-reinforced crossbows, their strings wound thick with sinew. The crossbow was king here, not the musket; its bolts could punch through a knight’s breastplate, but it took might and time to wind.

He gestured. The signalers unleashed their pigeons—fluttering, message-bearing wings the quickest carriers his side possessed. Across the plain, in gleaming lamellar armor, his own soldiers responded. Engineers rolled forward tall, iron-tipped siege towers and lethal torsion catapults. The air soon thrummed with arrows, javelins, quarrels, giant stones. No smoke clouded the field. Instead, sunlight glimmered on swarming projectiles.

Then the cavalry exploded from the tree line, veteran riders guiding enormous war-elks bred for size and fury. Tellan shieldmen braced, locking their oaken walls. Haru’s warriors crashed into them, blades and axes gleaming.

All around was fury and sweat, blood slicking the grass, yet the thunder was of flesh, not fire. No cannons belched, no grenades shattered the ranks. Towers toppled. Axes hewed. The trebuchets’ payloads—bundles of burning pitch—splashed across enemy lines, igniting shields and screams.

Victory would come not from the smoke and thunder of gunpowder, but from the perfect balance of wood, sinew, bronze, muscle, and bone. In this world, men faced one another with nothing to mask the wet heat of their dying breath.

In the heart of Eldoria, the air shimmered with anticipation. King Aelric stood on the castle balcony, surveying the horizon where doubt loomed thick, a dark cloud cloaking the sun. Every year, on the eve of the Harvest Moon, fortresses prepared for an impending threat. This year, whispers spoke of an army rising from the ashes of a forgotten war—creatures born from shadows, fueled by rage and vengeance.

“Your Majesty,” Sir Eamon's voice broke through Aelric's thoughts, urgency woven within each syllable. “The scouts report movement in the Blackthorn Woods. We must rally our forces.”

Aelric nodded, the weight of responsibility heavy upon his shoulders. His father had once told him that a king must always be vigilant, yet every year, as the moon turned golden, he felt the chokehold of fear tighten. Eldoria had become a fortress of worry, each citizen living in the shadow of what might come.

“Gather the council,” he commanded, his voice steady despite the tempest within his heart. “We will not wait for danger to knock; we shall meet it at the gates.”

Within the grand hall, the council gathered, their expressions a mix of determination and dread. Lady Isolde spoke first, her eyes burning with resolve. “If we prepare our defenses now, we can face whatever approaches. Our people cannot live in fear any longer.”

Aelric raised a hand, silencing the murmuring. “Yes, but let us not forget, it is not merely our swords that will protect us. We must unite the realm—forged as one, we stand stronger.”

As the council's murmurs faded into quiet agreement, a flicker of hope ignited in Aelric's heart. Together, they would face the darkness. Together, they would fight for their kingdom.

Terry’s hand hovered over the console, the numbers haloed in flickering red. Rations: 61 days. Supply ship: 180 days. Atmosphere: Tense. She snorted. All of Mars’ oxygen and still it was hard to breathe.

Leena cursed under her breath, scraping the last bite of reconstituted spinach from a packet, eyes fixated on the sliver of Chryse Planitia outside the porthole. Diego didn’t look up from the server logs—he’d been silent since they did the calculations, retreated into math as if new numbers might manifest more calories.

“We can’t all make it,” Leena said finally. Her voice was brittle. “Not unless someone volunteers to…” She trailed off.

There was a message from Control, four hours old, the lag slower than hope: “We are working on resupply options. Stay safe. Stay together.”

Terry clenched her fists. “We can stretch it. Lower metabolic rates. Work in shifts. Sleep more.”

Diego didn’t move. “We could try growing more algae,” he said, barely audible.

Leena’s laugh was sharp, humorless. “That’ll buy us days, tops. We need months.”

Outside, Mars was all rust and silence, a world indifferent to their hunger. No storms on the horizon, but fear storms brewed in the module.

Terry found herself looking at the data again. “We ration,” she insisted. “We wait. Maybe they’ll send drones. Maybe—”

“Maybe we die waiting,” Leena snapped.

Quiet. So quiet, she could hear her pulse.

But then Diego turned, eyes fierce for the first time in days. “We don’t choose who lives. If one falls, we all do. We’re crew.”

Three hands touched atop the ration box. Three breaths. Three souls suspended in the red dusk.

“We ration,” Terry said again, voice steady now. “We ration, and we hope. Together.”

And Mars watched, silent, unmoved and eternal, as three tiny hearts decided to keep beating, just a while longer.

The train slid into the station on a cold February morning, doors sighing open. I was twenty-two, late for work, clutching the strap of a frayed backpack, half-aware of the stale-coffee smell clinging to my scarf. Across from me sat an older woman, her eyes rimmed red, mascara trailing down her cheek in neat little lines. She fidgeted with her wedding ring, twisting it one way, then back, like she was setting a clock.

I tried to read, but I kept losing the thread of the paragraphs, distracted by the way she stared out at the blurred city, jaw set stubborn as if, by force, she could keep her thoughts from toppling over. At the next stop a young man entered, hands trembling. He wore hospital scrubs, blue, the color dulled by fluorescent lights. There was a brownish stain on the knee. He had headphones on, but no music played; I could see the empty cable dangling by his lapel.

A couple argued softly by the doors. Their whispers were urgent, desperate—fragments about a lost wallet, a missed opportunity, the name “Sasha” repeated with a pang deeper than frustration. At my stop, I stood, press of bodies guiding me. The old woman caught my eye and offered a brave, brittle smile. It lingered longer than it should, and because I was young and felt invisible, I almost didn’t return it.

When I surfaced onto the bustling street, their stories clung to me—each person a universe I’d only brushed against for three stops, my own anxieties shrinking, expanding, mingling with theirs. The train shuddered away, carriages full of people I’d never know, each one carrying a lifetime that would never intersect more than this fleeting moment, but, for those few minutes, had shared my world.

Agent 007 had a sleek Aston Martin, moneyed socialites in every city, and a license to thrill. Agent 006, however, found his missions rooted in the mundane—his garish assignment: the unremarkable realm of grocery store theft investigations. 

Grocery stores weren’t the gilded halls of espionage he’d imagined. He shuffled through aisles of cans and produce, whispering to the elderly clerks about missing hams and pilfered pasta. His partner, a balding accountant named George, often threw him sideways glances when he pulled out his tiny earpiece, claiming it was “all part of the job.” 

On this particular Tuesday, Agent 006 found himself behind a tattered stack of frozen pizzas, surveilling the store’s cheesy underbelly. “Here’s the intel,” George said over the comm, voice grave. “Two cans of olives gone missing... and a suspiciously empty jar of marinara sauce.” 

As he ventured toward the aisle, he spotted his target—a teenage girl, eyes darting as though she was planning an elaborate heist. Agent 006 straightened his tie, transforming into the best version of himself. He slipped up beside her, aiming for nonchalance. 

“Nice day for a caper,” he said, voice low, as she stuffed a chocolate bar into her jacket. 

Her eyes widened. “I’m not—”

“I know. You’re not bad. Just hungry. Let’s make a deal.” With a nod, he turned their conversation into a chat about family dinners and the importance of honesty. 

By the end, she left with a fistful of apples and a promise to put the bar back. Agent 006 sighed, feeling ridiculous but somehow satisfied. Not glamorous, but perhaps a life worth living after all.

Rain whispered against the hospice window, a fat gray sky pressing low. In the corner room, Mrs. Elias sat cocooned in white sheets, her face pale and spare as a pencil sketch. I slipped inside with my satchel, the same sunny yellow flowers I always brought—fake, but she forgave me for it.

“Morning, Grace,” I said. She blinked, recognition slow, but it came.

"Have you got another one today?" she asked, her voice nearly dust.

I nodded, perched on the chair at her bedside, and cracked open my battered notebook.

"Why did the scarecrow win an award?"

She rolled her dark eyes—worn like river stones. "I can't imagine."

"He was outstanding in his field."

Her laughter, when it came, was always a small miracle. Hushed, forced through lungs that never filled well, but bright as a sunbeam. We savored the moment, as day nurses drifted past her door, heads shaking with brief, pleased surprise.

I set the notebook aside, feeling the ache in my chest that used to frighten me. Now it felt like routine—the ache of tomorrow, of knowing we wouldn’t have endless mornings. Still, I pulled another joke, and another, sometimes slipping and making a face or two: an exaggerated wink, a cross-eyed blink.

No one else could lift her like that. Her granddaughter tried poetry, her son brought old pictures, and the nurses offered gentle voices. But only my clumsy jokes peeled her back from wherever the pain had locked her. Only I could coax that laugh, sparkling and brief, the sound that made her a girl for just a heartbeat.

As the rain thinned and sun pried open the clouds, she caught my hand. “Promise you’ll tell me another one tomorrow?”

I promised. And meant it.

The firelight flickered against the tent’s canvas, painting wild shadows across the sleeping forms of soldiers. Jonathan adjusted his helmet, trying not to think about the echo of screams from the burning village down the hill. He focused instead on his daughter’s face, illuminated by a single smoldering coal in their meager campfire. Her eyes were wide and solemn as she clutched her patched doll.

“Daddy, are we the bad guys?”

He drew in a slow breath. Sabine’s voice was soft but unrelenting, as the silence of defeated men pressed in on them. Jonathan knelt so they were eye-to-eye.

“No, sweetheart,” he began, the words dry on his tongue. “We’re soldiers. We fight because—because we have to.”

“But the people down there were running away. I saw you chase them,” she whispered. “You said we protect people. But they were scared.”

Jonathan remembered the little boy peering from behind his mother’s skirts, mouth open in silent terror before their torchlight crashed through the darkness. He closed his eyes, wishing he could erase the memory for both of them.

“It’s more complicated than it looks,” he tried. “War makes everything… messy.”

Sabine’s small fingers sought his, trembling. “But if they think we’re monsters, and we think they’re monsters… What if everyone is just scared?”

A stray ember flared and died. Jonathan’s eyes burned. He gathered her into his arms, feeling the thud of her heart against his battered armor.

“I don’t want to be the bad guy, either,” he whispered into her hair.

Outside, dawn crept over a world divided by fear. Inside, a father held his daughter tight, no longer certain which side of the fire he truly stood on.

I awaken in the body of a Sanskrit scribe, trembling as my reed pen hovers above parchment. The ink stains on my fingers are foreign, yet I know them; muscle memory guides the characters as I scrawl, even while my mind aches with confusion. Each life, each leap, blurs memories and moments. I am searching for the fracture—the one decision that split the world.

My only companion is the voice in my head, older than language. It urges me on, a quiet whisper: *Look deeper; not every mistake shouts.*

I slip from the scribe back into the life of a mechanic in 1913 Detroit, oil-slicked and hungry for progress. I turn a gear, recall a laugh with a colleague. Is this where it happened? Did I recommend the wrong improvement, a design that would haunt history? But the feeling doesn't fit; the break isn't here.

Again, I spiral forward, threads of existence tangling, each past and future self holding a piece of the puzzle. A future city waits, skyscrapers stitched with vines, humanity hanging on. In this glass-and-green metropolis, I’m an archivist restoring digital memories. And yet, everywhere I turn, a shadow lingers—hunger, fear, uneasy hope.

I return once more, to the earliest, the original. I am a child on the steppes, a clay bead clutched in my fist. My hands, too small for consequence. Yet as I stare, I understand: here I refused. A single act of defiance, a lifeline broken out of kindness or spite. The bead rolls, unremarkable, but its path shapes eons.

I exhale, trembling—not with fear, but relief. I found the moment; sorrow and solace mingle. Now, with infinite paths before me, I must choose again. May this time, the world heal.

It started as any ordinary bathroom break—a quick retreat, a moment’s relief, the subtle comfort of cold tile beneath my feet. But the feeling of stillness stretched, subtly wrong, as minutes ticked by. Finished, I reached for the handle, anticipation of onward movement flickering in my chest. I rose—and nothing happened. Or rather, I didn’t rise at all.

At first, it was almost funny. I wiggled, I scooted, gave a good-natured laugh at my own expense. Maybe I’d sat so long that my legs fell asleep, I reasoned, so I bounced in place to jolt life back in. The porcelain rim felt strange, warmer than it had any right to be. Sweat prickled across my neck. The harder I tried, the more I seemed to fuse with the seat, anchored by some invisible cement.

“What the hell?” I muttered to my reflection in the doorknob.

Panic edged in. I pulled, twisted, and pleaded. I fished my phone from my pocket—dead, of course, I’d forgotten to charge it. The house was empty; I’d never noticed how silent it could be. The window was just a bit too high, the shower curtain the only witness.

As time wore on—hours or maybe days—I lost track of both. I became a constant, a fixture as unmoving as the sink or the towel rack. Hunger gnawed. Sunlight faded and returned. In this absurd stasis, I discovered my mind wandering to the little things I’d put off, the apologies never made, the dreams kept “for later.”

I wept, laughed, shouted to no one in particular. Then I began to listen. To myself. To the house settling. To the wind tickling the vent. I’d struggled so hard to leave the moment that I’d forgotten I was living. For the first time, seated and unmoving, I truly felt the world turning.

Clark Kent slipped through the chaos on 4th Avenue—dodging overturned cars and frantic civilians—his eyes scanning for sanctuary. The familiar tingle of helplessness gnawed at him; being Clark demanded patience, while Superman required action.

He spotted an alley, but paramedics were tending to the wounded there. A shattered storefront? Too exposed, security cameras everywhere. Then, amid the smoke, Clark’s gaze landed on a blue rectangle perched on the sidewalk: a police public call box, oddly pristine amidst the rubble.

Desperate, Clark dashed inside. He pulled the door shut, exhaled, and tugged open his shirt—only for his hands to freeze at the “S,” confronted by a cavernous interior impossibly bigger than the exterior allowed. Console, levers, blinking lights. His glasses slid slightly down his nose.

“Ah, hello!” A bow-tied man popped up from behind the console, eyebrows arched with interest. “You’re not usually on the passenger list.”

Clark blinked, trying to explain as the skies above rumbled with the roar of alien ships. “Sorry, I needed somewhere private… to change.”

The man—the Doctor, though Clark couldn’t know that—smiled knowingly. “Aliens, you say?”

Clark nodded, hearing the terrified heartbeats outside. “If I don’t get out there—”

The Doctor was already pulling levers. “Two protectors of Earth in one place!” He grinned. “That should ruffle their tentacles.”

Clark—Superman now, cape bright and eyes clear—stepped forward. “Thank you, Doctor…”

The TARDIS thrummed, its doors opening as the Doctor winked. “Go on, then. The world’s very much in need of hope.”

Clark burst out, cape flaring, hope igniting the crowd. Somewhere inside the blue box, an alien with a screwdriver waved, delighted at extraordinary men and the strangers who save the world—sometimes together.

Every morning, I lace up my shoes and drag myself from bed, fueled by the bittersweet aroma of coffee curling in the air. The sun is just a hint of gold on the horizon when I step out, my breath fogging in the early chill. I glance down the street, and there he is—Mark, my faithful companion, a ghost clad in his old running gear.

I often wonder if he chose to stay behind or if he’s stuck here by some strange twist of fate. His face, once vibrant and full of life, is now a blur, flickering like an old film reel. I adjust my headband, shoving aside thoughts of how ridiculous this all seems. I take off into a steady jog, Mark keeping pace effortlessly beside me.

We pound the pavement together, side by side. His laughter echoes in the air as we discuss everything from the latest book I’ve read to the mornings we used to spend together. The world around us remains oblivious—bicyclists glide past, dog walkers nod politely—none question my solo venture, oblivious to my unseen partner.

As we reach the park, I slow down. The morning rays paint the grass golden, and I enjoy a rare moment of silence. Mark looks at me, a soft smile playing on his lips. “You’re still the best part of my day.”

I nod, fighting back tears. I can’t explain to others what it’s like to share this routine with someone who isn’t here anymore, but it brings me comfort. Running isn’t just exercise; it’s a tether to memories—a way to keep him alive, even if only in my mind, every step a reminder that love persists, even in silence.

George squinted up at the bustling sky, shielding his eyes from the afternoon sun. Above him, pigeons scattered at the approach of an airbus—its pink, bristly wings beating laboriously as it ferried passengers between New York and Boston. At the cockpit, a pig in a cap grunted with satisfaction, guiding the behemoth through cloud and wind.

As always, George marveled at what a century of pig-powered aviation had wrought. After Sir Archibald’s historic flight in 1909—one enterprising sow, a rickety biplane, and an impossible dream—the meaning of “When pigs fly” had transformed from eye-rolling dismissal to hopeful possibility. Now, anything was possible, and everyone knew it.

Politicians made promises—sometimes wild, always followed by an earnest: “When pigs fly? Trust me.” In parliament, debates now carried the heavy consequence of a flying pig’s precedent. Citizens once laughed off progress, but now the question wasn’t if, but when. Nothing was impossible anymore.

George pocketed his phone, the “PorcineView 6,” which boasted its own tiny, curly-tailed drone that oinked whenever a notification popped up. He glanced down the avenue as his commute-mobile—a sleek, aerodynamic sow named Jetty—trot-stepped to him, wings flexing impatiently. He climbed onto her saddle, feeling the warmth of her fur through his slacks.

He rose above rows of pig-inhabited rooftop gardens, where families tended lettuce and apples, fertilized by the aviation byproducts collected from municipal pig stations. Children pointed and cheered as Jetty swooped and arched, tail twitching with delight.

George grinned, surveying the horizon. Over a century ago, flight belonged to dreamers. Now, thanks to one flighty pig, even the most impossible hopes could soar. In 2016, if you wanted the world to change, you only had to wait—for the next pig to take wing.

“Push harder!” Carla hissed, shoving the battered door against the groaning corpse wedged in the frame. Its rotting fingers clawed at my jacket sleeve. The others were already swinging crowbars and hatchets with grim efficiency, but my hands shook so bad I could barely keep my grip on the bat.

“Hurry up, Kevin!” Ben barked, blood spattering his glasses as he brought his crowbar down again. “What, you waiting for it to offer you tea?”

I braced, swung—and the bat ricocheted off the zombie’s skull with a pathetic thunk. The thing barely seemed to notice. Bloodless eyes rolled toward me. I stared, frozen, as its mouth stretched wide in a wordless snarl.

“Head!” Carla insisted, thumping her own forehead pointedly. “You HAVE to hit it in the—oh, for crying out loud, just MOVE!”

Jay elbowed me aside and jammed a fire axe into the zombie’s temple. It dropped instantly. Jay flicked gore off his sleeve, glared. “You’ve never killed one before, have you?”

I could feel everyone’s eyes burning into me. Carla sucked her teeth, exasperated. “Seriously, Kevin? You talked about ‘brain shots’ for weeks.”

Ben heaved a sigh. “Didn’t your cousin get bit?”

“I—I missed that part,” I managed, voice cracking. Outside, more shuffling shadows converged, their moans swelling.

Jay tossed me a screwdriver. “Pointy end goes in the eye, genius.”

I clutched it. My hands trembled harder. “Right. Uh. In the head. Got it.”

Ben smirked, voice dripping mock sympathy. “Next one’s yours. Get your training wheels off.”

As the next ghoul pressed through the window, I forced myself forward. Aiming, I closed my eyes, jabbed, and felt something give way. Warm rot splattered my knuckles.

I opened my eyes. The others just stared.

“How long have you been in this apocalypse again?” Carla demanded.

“Sorry,” I croaked, “I always just...ran before.”

The world watched with a collective, breathless terror as Aether-19, an object three miles wide, spun its way toward Earth. News stations became temples of doom, their anchors delivering hourly updates from scientists whose faces betrayed the futility of their words. There would be no averting, no nuclear reprieve, no hope. In three months, all would end.

But as the oval shape drifted closer, a strange anomaly nagged at astronomers. Radar pulses vanished into its surface without returning, and light bent oddly as it passed, flickering with unnatural colors. The object did not appear on infrared sensors, but the ground beneath its projected path trembled with wild, low-frequency vibrations each time it crossed fixed coordinates in space.

Weeks passed, and military powers launched unmanned probes. Each one was silenced as soon as it drew near, transmissions snuffed out like candles. Humanity was left to witness, powerless.

Then, days before impact, the world saw it: the object’s hard black shell unfolded, revealing geometric plates and a vessel that glimmered with impossible iridescence. Tendrils like strands of silver mist unfurled, brushing through the upper layers of the atmosphere. All the clouds stilled. Each clock halted on the same second. Radios everywhere became silent, except for a single new signal, pulsing across all frequencies.

It spoke not in words but in patterns of warmth and coolness, glimpses of memory, emotion, understanding. It sent apologies, sorrow, remembrance of a home lost to violence, hints of kin searching through eons and stars for sanctuary. And now—arrival.

In the final moments, humanity understood: this was not a weapon, nor an accident. This was an ark, carrying a dying people’s last hope. The collision that would end humanity was also an embrace, an inheritance: the union of two extinct worlds, their stories braided forever in the dust and silence of what came after.

As the test pages fluttered onto the desks, I felt a twinge of anticipation. With a casual blink, I reached out, invisible fingers feeling for the familiar cloud of thoughts hovering above my classmates. Becky, next to me, always remembered the dates. Aaron, two seats over, ran through equations in his head faster than I could read them on paper.

The voices came: strained whispers, silent counting, mental lists. Answers unfolded like flowers just for me. I smirked, jotting down what I borrowed, question by question. Easy A, as always.

Then, something different—a cold, whispering wind cut through the crowd of minds. Clearer, stronger than the others, and distinctly not a student.

NO CHEATING IN MY CLASSROOM.

The words seared my mind as if spoken inside my skull. I nearly jumped, pencil frozen in a half-written answer. My eyes flickered up to the new teacher, Ms. Callahan, standing serenely by the blackboard. She met my gaze, one eyebrow almost imperceptibly raised.

I tried again, searching Aaron’s mind for that tricky math problem. Instantly: a wall, smooth and white, slamming down in my mental space.

NO CHEATING.

I swallowed. Thoughts spun. Was she like me? Stronger? My mental fingers scrabbled, searching for cracks in her barrier, but found nothing; her mental voice hummed like a warning bell in a cathedral.

This time I heard—inside my head—her soft, steady voice. *You are talented, but misguided. Finish this one on your own.*

Numb, I stumbled through the test. My brain—unused to working alone—fumbled over facts I should have known. At the end, Ms. Callahan paused by my desk, her lips in a knowing smile.

“Everyone deserves to find their own answers,” she murmured, eyes lingering just a moment too long.

For once, I didn’t try to cheat the lesson.

Marty adjusted the bill of his backwards snapback, drawing his hoodie tighter around his hunched frame. The scanner at the station’s entrance beeped as a sleek, uniformed Enforcer eyed him, eyes flickering over the mass of young commuters. Marty grinned, revealing teeth carefully stained by coffee and charcoal paste to mimic the yellowish grin of youth. He popped his chewing gum. 

“Morning, bro,” Marty drawled, deepening his voice with a practiced rasp. 

The Enforcer nodded, only briefly pausing at Marty’s wrinkled hands before dismissing him as another slouching teenage drone. Safe, for now.

Twenty years ago, when the Incineration Act passed, Marty had been a spry 68, still mowing his own lawn, still dancing in the evenings. He watched quietly as his friends and neighbors lined up at the Civic Centers, clutching their IDs. They wept, protested, begged—until everyone realized it did no good. Most simply went, shuffling, resigned.

Marty crafted his first disguise with a box of black hair dye and a pair of jeans stolen from his grandson’s closet. He watched skateboarding videos, mimicked the lingo, and trained his voice with old radio recordings. He ran stairs at sunset, worked on his posture, anything to look just another restless soul doomed to work and spend.

Now 88, Marty’s world was a sequence of deceptions: youth serums ordered from the black market, IDs swapped for every fresh batch of wrinkles, forging proof of age just beneath the cutoff. Younger people sought out his advice, mistaking him for one of their own—just a wise pal, a little grey at the temples.

He slipped through society’s cracks, dancing on the knife edge of discovery. The flames might be hot, but Marty burned with something brighter: the inextinguishable will to live.

My office exudes the scent of leather-bound confidence, walls lined with evidence of my competence: degrees, awards, the silent monologue of trophies earned arguing justice for those who could afford me. I sit opposite Mark Fenley—nervous, perspiring, trying to play calm as he recounts how Detective Archer questioned him for my recent work in Haverson Park. He is the first to sit across my desk accused of what only I truly know.

The details he shares are terrifyingly accurate—enough that I feel a chill despite my iron composure. My hands rest loosely around a fountain pen. "Mark," I say, sympathy diluting my authoritative tone, "Tell me everything. Leave nothing out."

He complies, unaware that every tremble and misplaced word is another nail in his crucifixion. I've studied many faces on the stand. His is open, earnest, easily contorted by fear; a prosecutor's delight, a defense attorney’s disaster.

That night, I retrieve the box buried beneath my floorboards: stolen trinkets, a trophy for each slip of justice I’ve orchestrated. I remove one—the silver cufflink Mark lost in my waiting room weeks ago. It nestles nicely among my other souvenirs but will be far more damning in the crawlspace of his apartment, alongside a blood-smeared glove and a hard drive meticulously wiped clean of my own browser history.

I tell Mark, convincingly, that we must be fully honest with the police, and volunteer the alibi I know will collapse. I’ll deliver impassioned arguments, painstakingly strewing the seeds of circumspect doubt, making Mark appear plausible but unconvincing—a perfect storm of zealous advocacy and subtle sabotage.

When the verdict comes, I meet Mark’s betrayed gaze, mourning with him in the courtroom spotlight, coat immaculate, reputation untouched. Justice, after all, is only what the world believes.

“Shut the dog up.”

The command drifted down the darkened hallway, brittle and sharp. On cue, Daisy—the ancient terrier—let out a trembling yowl that could have curdled milk, followed by a staccato of wet coughs. Carly pressed her palms to her ears. Two in the morning, and the world outside swam in quiet, syrupy stillness; only Daisy’s bark sliced through.

“Caaaaarly!” Dad’s voice again, harsher this time.

She tiptoed from her room, clutching the edge of her quilt. Daisy was curled up on the landing, trembling, her milky eyes fixed on Carly. She wasn’t barking now—just shaking. Carly crouched beside her, feeling the bones under Daisy’s wiry fur.

“Sssh, Daisy. Sssh, it’s okay.” Carly’s voice was a whisper, soft and earnest. She didn’t want Dad getting up—the hallway felt smaller when he was there.

The old dog licked her hand, eyes wide with plea. A flash of light: headlights through the window. Thunder rumbled in the distance. Another bark threatened to rise, but Carly pulled Daisy close, wrapping small arms around knobby shoulders.

She hummed, low and tuneless. Outside, rain began to splatter the glass. The house felt a little more gentle, a little less sharp. Daisy relaxed, the bark dying into the safety of Carly’s hair.

Down the hallway, Dad muttered again, but his voice faded, defeated by the hush Carly wove.

For a little while, girl and dog sat together, wrapped in thunder and hush, until the only sound was the rise and fall of their shared breath in the quiet dark.

Cold was the first thing Joseph felt. Not the ache or sting but absence—a hollow cold threaded through his bones. Then, sensation returned: a humming beneath him, distant voices muffled as though underwater.

He opened his eyes. Harsh white lights burned his retinas. A transparent dome arched over him, fogged with streaks of condensation. Shapes moved, blurry silhouettes. He tried to speak, but only a croak emerged.

The glass hissed and slid aside. Air flowed over his skin, crisp and clean. A woman leaned over him; her hair was red and feather-light, arranged in intricate braids he didn't recognize. Her uniform shimmered, subtly shifting through pastel hues.

"Hello, Joseph Morgan," she said gently. "You are in Sanctuary Revival Center, Year 3016. You have been asleep for nine hundred and sixty years."

His mind tripped over the words, catching most on the first try, tumbling on the year. "How... many others?" he managed.

She smiled, a practiced softness. "You are among the first ten."

Other pods lined the chamber, some open, some still sealed in frost. A gaunt elderly woman was crying in one. Beyond glass walls, the world was pale green and aquamarine—trees like spirals, skies tinged with lavender.

"Why now?" he whispered. "What changed?"

"The planet healed," the attendant replied. "Climate, politics, disease—we survived. Now, we're ready to welcome you back, on your terms. If you still want it." She offered him a glass of water.

Joseph sat up, hands trembling. Everything looked different, even the sunlight. Yet something in her tone steadied him. There was grief, yes, but also hope—the kind he remembered only from lullabies and long-lost springs.

He took the glass, staring at the strange, shimmering world. He drank, and tasted the future.

When the bus veered off the overpass, there was a moment—a single, sharp breath—when everything became light and slow. Glass shattered into prisms around me, the world too bright to focus. I fell, and I remember wondering if I would hit the ground or simply keep falling forever.

And then: nothingness, except it wasn't empty. It peeled open around me like silver curtains. I stood on a floor that wasn't there, beneath a sky that pulsed and throbbed with a heartbeat I'd never heard before. There were… doors. Hundreds, maybe thousands, of doors suspended in that infinite gray, their frames painted every color I could imagine. Some doors glowed; some were plain. Some were battered and scarred as if they'd been used a thousand times.

A figure stood beside one especially small, crimson door. They looked at me with kind, impersonal eyes—like a doctor or an exhausted teacher. "Too soon," they said. "But you're always welcome." Their voice echoed, vibrating up my spine.

I sensed movement behind the other doors. Shadows flickered, laughter, weeping, something that sounded almost like music. Every door drew me in. If I reached out, I could touch a handle—choose a different path, maybe. See who I had been, or could be, or never would become.

But the figure put a hand to my shoulder. Warmth flooded me—regret, comfort, peace. "Not yet," they said again, gently. The vision swirled. I wanted to ask, "What are these? Where do they all lead?"

The answer came as the world slipped away: "Everywhere."

And when I woke with a jolt to fluorescent lights and paramedics, it wasn't the impact or the pain that made me cry. It was the memory of the doors, and the comforting certainty that I'd seen a place waiting for me—one day, when I was ready.

The first time I asked about it, mother’s fingers trembled as she tied the shoelaces of my tiny boots. “Everyone wears one,” she said, her voice barely above a whisper. I learned not to ask again.

At school, my classmates’ faces were frozen porcelain, blank and unknowable. Sometimes, I tried to imagine smiles, frowns, even just a pair of questioning eyes. The masks gleamed under sunlight, turned featureless with shadows at dusk.

Through birthdays, heartbreaks, and graduations, I remained the oddity: the only one unmasked, my cheeks bare to the wind, my eyes desperate for connection. People averted their gaze; adults hurried past, their voices clipped and distant. My parents sometimes stared at me with a mix of sorrow and shame.

But then I met Eli.

We first spoke through a wall of politeness, the same way everyone did. His mask was always pristine, lips sculpted into a faint, eternal half-smile. I said yes to his unspoken questions, and slowly, days turned into years.

On our wedding night, after laughter faded and guests departed, we sat together in our silent room. Eli’s hands trembled. Unhooking the smooth porcelain, he revealed a raw, uncertain face – red-rimmed eyes, a crooked scar at the corner of his mouth, and terror naked as day.

I reached out, thumb tracing the curve of his jaw. His breath hitched.

“Your turn,” he whispered.

“But—” My voice cracked.

From the bedside mirror, I saw my own skin. Nothing to remove. No mask to unfasten. I only had myself, every secret exposed, every fear laid bare. Eli gazed at me, searching for disappointment. Instead, I smiled.

It didn’t matter who wore the mask. Love was the courage to take it off, or to never need one at all.

The doorbell rings at 7:15 a.m., sharp as always. It rattles the silence, sending my coffee sloshing over trembling knuckles. I know who it is before I open the door—Jimmy "the Wrench" Larkins, merciless as a pit bull and just as forgetful. He grins at me with a crooked smile, like he's greeting an old friend, but I see the look in his eyes—the spark of memory stopped short.

"Hey there, champ," he says, all faux-friendly menace. "Today's the day, right? You got my five grand?"

My heart rate jumps. "Jimmy, we've had this talk," I say, forcing calm. "I paid you, remember? Three years ago. We shook on it and everything."

He tilts his head, squinting. "Nice try, but you'd say anything to avoid a broken kneecap. Payment was due yesterday, and here I am. Let's not make this messy."

Each morning is the same. The same threats, the same confusion, the same terror in my guts. I can't reason with him—his mind resets to that one fateful afternoon when I was late. I tried everything: receipts taped on mirrors, a repayment notice tattooed across my knuckles, even video evidence on repeat. He doesn’t buy it. To Jimmy, it’s always the morning after my default.

I gulp. "Look, I brewed your favorite—Colombian roast," I say, retreating to routine. Sometimes, a cup and a muffin soften his mood. Sometimes.

He takes the mug, eyes lingering on the scrawled "Paid in full" sticky notes plastered everywhere. For a moment, he hesitates.

"You always were a slippery one," he says softly. "But nobody gets away forever. Tomorrow, I'll collect."

The door closes behind him. I pour a fresh cup, brace myself for dawn—another round in the endless loop where debts never die and forgiveness can't stick.

Each tick of the microwave's clock was a thunderclap in the hush of the kitchen. John stared unblinking through the tiny window, the interior light illuminating his reflection in spectral flashes. A mug rested on the spinning glass plate: his favorite, with a faded cartoon cat grinning up at him, from a time before everything demanded this much effort.

One minute remained.

The universe held its breath. Steam began curling up inside the mug. Was it too soon? Should he open the microwave now, rescue the coffee before it scalded? He gripped the countertop, knuckles whitening beneath the wan morning light leaking between ragged curtains. He’d read once—somewhere, during a sleepless dawn—that the temperature had to be just right. Too hot, and the creamer recoiled, stubborn and unmixed. Too cold, and the bitterness stood, proud and unyielding, upon his tongue.

The seconds carved furrows between his brows. Thirty seconds left. The urge to intervene clashed with the code of patience—so simple in theory, so consuming in practice.

His breath fogged the glass. Twenty seconds. His phone vibrated, unseen, ignored. Nothing outside the circle of LED light could matter now. This was immediacy. This was fate.

Ten.

Nine.

A distant siren wailed, echoing his turmoil—should he trust the machine to its completion, or did wisdom lie in interruption?

Three.

Two.

One.

The beep shrieked, slicing the morning open. He lunged, flinging the door wide. Aroma flooded the air, full and rich—and just as his trembling hands reached for the mug, it struck him: this was all he had tamed, all he had mastered. He poured the creamer, swirling hope into black mystery, and dared to sip.

Perfection. For a moment, everything made sense.

The bell on the door jingled with the same brittle, half-hearted note. I didn’t look up right away—I already knew it was him. Thursdays, every second week, like clockwork since last March. Still, it’s polite to greet the regulars. 

“Hey, Connor,” I said. “You know the drill.” 

Connor gave a tired smile, the burden in his sunken eyes deepening a fraction as he slid his jacket off. He sat in the usual chair, rolling up his left sleeve. The hollow of his forearm told its own silent, growing story: clusters of inked tally marks, each one thin, precise, unmistakable. He waited, quiet, as he always did, while I prepped the needle.

I haven’t asked what they mean. Not really. The first time I did, he’d said, “Just keeping count.” He never said of what, and I’d seen enough grief walk through my door not to press. Some stories demand their privacy.

I numbed the area, then stretched the skin taut, pressing gently. “Same spot?”

He nodded. I drew the next mark, perfectly aligned. We sat in a hush broken only by the low hum of the needle and the soft tick of the wall clock. He winced just a bit when I wiped away the blood, but didn’t flinch.

When it was done, he stared at the new mark, his thumb lingering there for a heartbeat. “You ever think about what things we tally in life?” he murmured, voice rough. “What really matters?”

Before I could answer, he slid his sleeve down, left the bills on the tray, and paused at the door.

“I’m almost afraid of the day I stop coming,” he whispered, so quietly I almost missed it.

The bell tinkled again as he disappeared into rain, and I looked at the ink on my gloves, wondering—what would my tally be? And what would it mean, when I was done counting?

My alarm blares, slicing through the morning like a knife. Groggy, I roll out of bed, rubbing sleep from my eyes. My right arm itches—an irregular, tingling sensation. When I scratch, my fingers brush raised ridges on my forearm.

Confused, I turn on the bedside lamp and stare. There, scrawled in precise black script along the length of my arm, is a name I have never seen before.

**LINDA GILROY**

My heart races. I try rubbing the name off, thinking maybe I leaned on a magazine in my sleep, but the letters cling stubbornly to my skin. My breaths come faster—I'm not dreaming. I've heard the stories: when someone murders, the victim’s name shows up somewhere on the killer’s body, forever branding them as guilty. The world is safer, they say. No more unsolved murders.

But I… I haven’t hurt anyone. I was here, all night, alone except for the dull hum of my refrigerator.

I grab my phone and search: “Linda Gilroy.” The first headline reads, “Local Woman Found Dead in Westside Apartment.” My blood runs cold. She was killed six hours ago. I read in a frenzy—a woman my mother’s age, quiet, worked at a flower shop. No connection to me. None that I know of.

My hands shake. I should call the police, but everything in my body screams not to. Who would believe me? I try to recall yesterday, every movement, but my mind stutters—dinner, dishes, a gap, an unaccountable hour.

Panic threatens to flood me. Was I drugged? Sleepwalking? I pace my room, palms sweaty, the name burning against my skin. Every time I look, the letters darken, as if soaking in my guilt.

An indelible mark I don’t remember earning.

I need answers. Before the world sees my arm, before the weight of Linda Gilroy’s name crushes me.

The Dreambook rested on the shelf above my son's pillow, just as it had since the day he arrived swaddled and howling in my arms. Tradition forbade opening another’s dreambook—dreams are sacred here, private little worlds spun each night from the threads of heart and soul. But four-year-olds, so the elders said, only dreamed of flying ponies and melting ice creams.

Curiosity and fatigue got the better of me one rain-lashed evening. I cracked the spine, expecting childish scrawls about friendly clouds. But what poured forth was a story—sorrowful, luminous. The first page sang of a lost queen and a city of glass, written with the clarity and grace of a seasoned bard. The prose throbbed with longing, vividly real landscapes, secrets and sorrows I could never have invented.

Night after night, I opened the book. A new chapter appeared each morning, more enthralling than the last. My son babbled of wooden trains by day, but at night, his slumber carved entire worlds.

We needed money—medicine, a new roof, bread for the table. I began to transcribe the stories, sending them under a pseudonym to the city publishers. The book was hailed as a masterpiece. Letters arrived, heavy with coin and praise, and for the first time in years, our table overflowed.

But as the silver gathered and accolades mounted, a change crept into the house. My son’s eyes, once bright, grew shadowed. He stopped dreaming, or seemed to. The pages appeared blank each morning. He wandered the house whispering empty questions: “Where did the city go? Where is my queen?”

I held him and wept, pressing the Dreambook between us, silent with shame. Our fortune was made of a child’s lost wonder—and the gates to his secret kingdom lay closed, for good.

At exactly 7:03 a.m. Eastern Standard Time, every clock on Earth stopped ticking.

Smartwatches died on wrists mid-step, ancient cuckoo clocks held their wooden birds hostage at the hour, screen savers on nuclear reactor control panels froze in place. In Paris, the Eiffel’s shadow hung perpetually along the Seine. In a remote town in Australia, school bells never rang to call children in from recess. Panic, confusion, and a beautiful, terrifying stillness took hold.

Then, a different kind of silence. Every human being lost the ability to speak. Not a whisper, not a scream. Languages evaporated from memory, like smoke through open fingers. The sound of living—shouts, laughter, arguments, lullabies—vanished, leaving only the hiss of wind and the distant moans of infrastructure.

The news, or what information trickled through halted feeds, was delivered in frantic bursts of text, but no voice called out. Social media feeds crashed under the weight of a singular, unanswered question: *What’s happening?*

On the third day, the moon appeared to split in two. Perfectly, like a stone struck by a divine chisel. The halves hovered in the night, illuminating the planet in a ghostly, dual glow. Waves rose and trembled, but stopped short of swallowing the land.

Time at a standstill, speechless humanity staring at a bifurcated moon.

By the seventh dawn, the clocks rumbled, hands spinning in wild unison before snapping back to the correct hour. Voices returned, shy and raspy, as if they’d forgotten how to form words—but the languages were different now, a jumble, every tongue blending into one.

The world never explained what had happened. No one tried convincing anyone else, because nobody claimed to know. But from that week onward, whenever something odd occurred, people nodded and said, “Stranger things have… No. Never mind.”

When Maris was a child, she’d press her ear to the trunk of the old oak behind their cottage, convinced she could hear the secret whorl and hum of life inside. Her grandmother would sway in her creaking chair nearby and whisper, “Trees hold what we can’t—memories, wishes, souls.” Maris had believed her, once, when the world was softer.

Years passed, and winter pressed its cold hand to the village. When it claimed her grandmother one silent night, Maris found herself wandering beneath skeletal branches, searching for something unnamed. The ancient oak stood sentinel above the frost-bitten lawn, its bark silvered by moonlight. She traced the scarred initials carved as a child and murmured a tremulous greeting.

The breeze teased tears from her eyes, and she remembered: “Speak to the tree. It listens.” 

Hesitant, Maris laid her palm against the rough wood and let her sorrow bleed out. “Are you there?” she whispered, voice trembling.

Deep within the oak’s heart, a low, patient thrum answered. Not words, but understanding, warm and steady. The ache in Maris’ chest eased. She closed her eyes and thought of lullabies sung by firelight, hands clasped, the scent of cinnamon and cloves. The tree drank in each recollection, leaves stirring despite the still air.

“Thank you for remembering,” came a thought, gentle as dawn, not spoken but felt. And Maris knew, at last, she was not alone. Souls did not vanish, nor did love. They rooted themselves in quiet sentinels, reaching out to those who remembered, who listened.

Maris pressed her face to the trunk, the old oak holding her as it always had, branches whispering a lullaby older than grief. Over time, new leaves would unfurl, weighted with memory, fragrant with hope, the soul of her grandmother alive and sheltering overhead.

It started with the parking tickets. Every morning, I’d leave my apartment early, slipping into my twin’s building with a stolen keycard and moving their SUV into the one spot clearly marked for deliveries only. The fines piled up. I watched from across the street as he yelled at an innocent meter maid, the same snarl I’d seen online in that viral video—him berating a barista, his face identical to mine, except twisted by entitlement.

Next came the job. His email password was laughably simple: our birthday. Once inside, it took only a few well-crafted replies—sent just after midnight—to his boss. “You clearly don’t value my work. Perhaps I should seek employment elsewhere.” When the real him saw the sent emails, it was too late. His boss printed out every message during the exit interview. I sat in the lobby with a magazine as he stormed past, red-faced.

By the third week, my orchestration grew bold. I joined the same gym and waited until he had a big date scheduled, then flirted outrageously with his date the day before, deliberately name-dropping plans for the following evening. She ghosted him. He smashed a locker in rage; I heard it echo down the hall.

Each petty vengeance was catharsis, not only for every slight I’d endured from strangers like him but for the mirror that now reflected all I detested. I told myself I was teaching him humility. Maybe, I thought, if he could just feel a fraction of the bitterness he spread, he’d crumble and rebuild as something better. Or maybe, in destroying his life, I was simply giving in to the darkness of my own reflection. Either way, I could not look away from his unraveling—and mine.

The first time I spoke His name aloud, it was only to the shadows in my empty room. The candle flickered, trembled, and for a heartbeat, the light bent in unnatural ways. I felt the answer—power, whispered at the base of my spine.

It began small: one friend, then a neighbor, each drawn in by the warmth of my conviction. I told them of the One Who Listens, who offers strength as rain offers relief to parched earth. Their eyes widened, their faces brightened, and I felt it again—energy pulsing through my veins, muscle memory for miracles I never learned.

Within weeks, rumors spread. Where I walked, flowers grew out of cracks in the pavement. Where I touched, wounds closed, hearts eased, old feuds dissolved. Every affirmation, every soul pledging faith, was a pulse of adrenaline and sweet nectar, a hundred tiny seeds bursting into blossom beneath my skin.

My god was no distant sovereign. He was present, attentive, hungry. The more followers, the more fuel for miracles: weather-taming, pain-mending, truth-baring. My hands became conduits, my eyes lanterns burning with his pale blue light. They called me Prophet. Some called me Monster. I ignored the latter; their fear only fed my resolve.

But power is a greedy guest. Soon, I envied kingdoms, continents, legions. I hungered for a world singing with his name. Those who doubted were obstacles—I persuaded, pleaded, then commanded. Each conversion brought ecstasy sharper than before. I was more than mortal; I was living testament.

One night, as the city’s skyline bowed under my gaze, I wondered: Where does he end, and I begin? Whose hunger am I serving now?

In the new dawn, the chorus rose: a symphony to the god who listens. And I, no longer sure if I was prophet or just the loudest voice in the choir, listened too.

I won the lottery with a found quarter the day I turned sixteen. The next year, I won the lead role in the school musical, not knowing the script, and my voice hit notes I didn’t think possible. I walked into rooms and beauty bloomed at my feet: job offers, adoration, effortless harmony. When I coasted through traffic, other cars spun out or missed green lights. At first, I called it fate.

Then Dad tried to use my luck at a casino. He said it was “just blackjack, for fun.” His car broke down on the highway; he missed his hand rest on a hot engine; his jacket caught on fire. He never gambled again.

The world began to shrivel around me. My friends failed tests, twisted ankles, got caught in the rain, as I pulled A’s or clear skies as needed. I shared lottery tickets with Sarah, who’d been my friend since kindergarten. When she scratched them in front of me, she cut her hand. Later, I saw her crying, clutching a failed college application. I stopped suggesting we try things together.

It grew lonely, knowing I burned down fortune in my wake. Even the tiniest wish—I hoped a teacher would curve a test. He was fired the next week, accused of favoritism. I got full points.

I tried to fix things. Tried to be distant, to spare others. I walked the woods alone, plants springing green beneath me, silence so deep it felt like outer space. I told myself it was worth it: I could do good things, send anonymous gifts, make the world better with my wild luck. But the gifts got lost, charities went bankrupt, gardens I planted wilted in the hands of others.

Now, every morning victory tastes sour. Each success costs joy I cannot repay. It’s lonely, being the luckiest, and knowing that’s the unluckiest thing of all.

The broadcast was never meant to go live. In fact, if Jack had seen the blinking red “ON AIR” light before he hit the button, maybe things would have gone differently. Maybe the world wouldn’t have watched in awe as he spilled his coffee on the control panel and cursed so violently that the Austrian president fainted on live television.

The GNN studio was supposed to be covering the signing of the Greater Pacific Peace Accord—an event scheduled for noon sharp. But instead, viewers across the globe tuned in to see the security cameras cut from nervous delegates to a janitor mopping confetti, to a close-up of Jack’s ashen face as he flailed for the mute button.

Then, amidst the chaos, Jack’s elbow clipped the emergency evacuation alarm. A blaring klaxon echoed throughout the convention center. Dignitaries froze mid-handshake; the Prime Minister of India dived under a table. Meanwhile, the broadcast—still live—showed Jack’s desperate attempts to explain: “It’s just me—everything’s FINE—Wait, oh god, is this thing—?”

By the time the technicians corrected the feed, the world had witnessed thirty-seven chaotic minutes of unscripted confusion. There were memes before the final agreement was even signed. But something unexpected happened: the accidental circus became a shared global moment, an icebreaker heard ‘round the world.

When the leaders returned, laughter echoed through the chamber. Tensions eased. Negotiators confessed mistakes. By day’s end, not only was the Accord ratified, but a new clause—one suggested on Twitter mid-fiasco—required annual joint comedy broadcasts between signatory nations.

It was hailed as a new dawn of transparency and camaraderie. But in the quiet archives of GNN, a single sticky coffee ring on a battered control panel whispered the truth: history’s greatest peace treaty began not with a handshake, but with a spill.

Every morning, Lena slips quietly from beneath the tangled quilt. She dresses in the hush before dawn, savoring the ritual: worn gray sweatpants, the old concert tee, her lucky headband. Coffee brews strong in the kitchen. She drinks it hot and black while the world is still shadowed, watching the square of light grow on the floor. Then, shoes laced and heart steady, she steps out into the cool street.

He is waiting for her at the corner, as he always is—Daniel, in the ragged hoodie with the faded logo, sneakers scuffed at the heel, his smile apologetic. He gives her a nod that says, I didn’t mean to leave, as if what happened the previous winter was all a misunderstanding.

They run in companionable silence, feet thudding in sync on the pavement. The city is theirs at this hour: the sparrows in the hedges, the soft pad of someone else’s distant dog, the distant rumble of a bus, all part of the symphony of morning. Lena breathes in the sharp, clean air and tries not to look too hard at Daniel’s outline—which sometimes flickers, sometimes blurs at the edges where the light grows gold.

At the halfway mark, by the willow tree in the city park, she slows and presses a hand to her side. Daniel slows too. Sometimes, in the hush, he brushes her cheek with a hand colder than mercy, and she lets him. Sometimes, he speaks. “You don’t have to wait for me forever.” 

But she smiles and shakes her head. Not yet.

When they circle back to the apartment, Daniel fades with the mist. By then, daylight is strong. Lena stays in the hush a bit longer, heart steady, shoes damp with dew, knowing he’ll be there again tomorrow—until the day she finally lets him rest.

The diagnosis was written in sharp, impatient strokes across the doctor's notepad, as if even the pen wanted no part in it. Seth stared, hollow, as the explanation tumbled out: a one-in-a-billion neurological collapse, a cascade through his synapses, triggered only by the descent into sleep.

His body ached for rest. He felt it—like drowning, or spinning just on the edge of consciousness—but now, sleep was a precipice he dared not cross. The ward clock ticked, solemn. His eyes burned. The doctor muttered empathy; Seth only heard the word "never." Never sleep again. Or die.

He began with coffee, seas of it, sloshing bitterly through him. Energy drinks, blaring music, ice showers at three a.m. Every trick. He taught himself to nap sitting up, eyelids taped open, but the tight fist of panic kept him from drifting away.

Friends came at first—brought movies, loud games, light to force back night. They made jokes about insomnia, cackled about all-nighters, but one by one, they faded. Seth watched them leave behind tired condolences. Nobody else lived in this world stretched thin between two deaths: body and mind.

After six days, Seth stopped seeing right. The apartment twisted, clocks melting, shadows twitching in laughter. His mother begged through the phone—hospital, drugs, specialists—but he ignored them. There was nobody who could cure this.

On the ninth day, Seth sat facing his window. He wrote letters he would not remember, told secrets to the dawn he half-imagined. He had never been this aware: of his heartbeat, his breath, the weight of his own bones. He clung to clarity with cracked fingernails.

When morning finally crept across the sky, Seth blinked against sunlight. He smiled—a small, cracked thing, fugitive but real. Today, he thought, he would not sleep. Instead, he lived.

I tripped on the curb and let out a panicked, “Oh God—!”

Before I hit the pavement, a giant hand materialized to catch me. At street level, pedestrians shrieked and scattered as the palm gently set me upright, leaving behind the faintest scent of ozone and sandalwood.

“Oh, not again,” I managed, brushing invisible dust from my slacks. The city bus screeched to a halt. Through the glass, faces pressed wide-eyed and open-mouthed.

A voice boomed from above, warm and infinitely weary: “You did call.”

Mortified, I glanced up. The sky rippled, clouds swirling like cream in coffee. “Sorry, I didn’t mean to bother you. It just slipped out.”

A sigh rustled the leaves. “You’re never a bother. But perhaps you could use shorter words?”

“I’ll try,” I said sheepishly, then stopped short when a stray dog darted into traffic.

“Oh God!” I shouted again.

Without hesitation, a parking meter sprouted legs and herded the dog to the sidewalk, then saluted me with a metallic ping.

God’s voice again: “Perhaps you should say ‘oh gosh’? Or ‘oh my’? For everyone’s sake.”

I looked down as my phone buzzed with news updates: *Local Woman Summons God for Fourth Time Today.* I groaned, fighting the urge to say anything sacred.

Instead, I pressed my lips together and walked on, cars detouring around the patch of road where the handprint lingered, smoking slightly. People stared. Somewhere, a child whispered, “That’s her, the one He keeps answering.”

I trudged home in silence, flinching at every surprised exclamation that danced on the tip of my tongue, each one a prayer and a summoning, wondering how much longer until language itself—out of mercy—ran dry.

Jasper had never planned to get a tattoo. He’d always shuffled past the buzzing parlors of Main Street, hands in his pockets, eyes averted. But after the funeral, words felt like broken glass in his throat. His brother David had never been one for silence—he filled every room with music, his worn guitar always slung across his back.

The apartment felt cavernous now, echoing with memory. Jasper found David’s guitar resting in the corner, a faded blue pick wedged between the strings. His hands shook as he traced the carved initials along the fretboard. D.R.B.—David Ross Bartlett—forever marking what was his.

That afternoon, as dusk crept through the half-shut blinds, Jasper found himself at the tattoo parlor. The air smelled of antiseptic and paper stencils. He scribbled something on the back of an envelope. When the artist nodded, Jasper rolled up his sleeve and grit his teeth.

Pain flashed like lightning, sharper than grief, then settled into something deeper. When it was done, the artist cleaned away the ink and Jasper stared at his arm. There, above the blue-green veins, were the same three letters: D.R.B., inked in David’s handwriting—a match from an old birthday card Jasper had slipped into his wallet, never dreaming it would outlast its author.

Now, when Jasper reached for the guitar, his arm caught the sunlight. The ink shimmered. David’s music seemed to linger, every chord a reminder. The tattoo became a promise: neither music nor memory would fade. Whenever silence threatened, Jasper could only press his fingers to his skin, find strength in the story, and begin again.

The paintball mask fogged up with each breath, but Tom kept his eyes sharp. Somewhere beyond the inflatable barricades, giggles echoed—children’s voices, his grandkids playing soldier. He suppressed a smile and crouched behind a bunker whose orange paint reminded him of autumn leaves.

A pellet splattered against the cover. He peeked, just as a tall, stooped figure peered back from behind a plywood wall. Something about the stance was unmistakable. Decades melted away. Under camouflage and war paint, the enemy had stood just like that.

Tom’s heart drummed, but this was different. Mud and blood replaced by laughter and paint. Still, a reflex took over. He signaled his squad—Ben and Lucy, seven and nine—who tumbled forward with squeals. On the other side, the old man mirrored him, issuing little orders. They’d both learned the same tricks a world away.

Lucy barreled toward the rival grandkids, her curly hair wild, and Tom sent a shot—a warning, not a hit. His opponent replied with perfect precision, a blue dot landing centimeters from Tom's boot.

Cautiously, as the kids darted and missed, the old men converged at midfield. The paint dusted their knees as they knelt behind a shared barrier, momentarily forgotten by their teams.

The other man grinned, scars puckering around the motion. “Alps, ’44?” he asked, heavy accent clipped by age.

Tom’s breath caught. He nodded, smiling. “Had a lucky shot back then.”

“It was almost lucky enough,” the man replied. Then they both burst out laughing, releasing years of tension in one breath.

“Think our squad has a chance?” Tom asked, gesturing to the chasing children.

“We taught them everything we know,” the other man said.

The whistle blew. Armies of grandchildren swarmed, paint flying in neon arcs. The veterans rose together—old enemies, old friends—caught in the crossfire of a newer, gentler war.

He watched darkness swallow the city, every streetlamp an island in a sea of chaos. He was used to the silence, but tonight the hush was electric—crackling with whispered threats he’d learned to hear. Once, his name invoked fear. Now, he wore it like armor.

The traitors in power had let this city rot. They built their monuments, their false idols, letting the desperate languish in streets thick with sorrow and bitterness. He’d seen the children pickpocket for a crust of bread. Seen the sick turned away from doors that never opened. He remembered the time when he’d waited, watched as hope soured, then flickered out.

He engineered his plan as carefully as a symphony. The chemicals, calculated. The blueprints, flawless. He had learned: to truly ignite change, one must remind the unmovable of fear. The city’s rulers would hear his message not in words, but in trembling windows and evacuations—every siren a chorus in his revolution.

He donned his mask. Not to conceal, but to declare: no more faceless suffering. The city watched as chaos unfolded, but amid screaming headlines, they also saw sick children treated, food distributed in alleys—his command, quietly obeyed.

To cleanse a broken system, sometimes you had to shatter it first. That was a burden he’d bear gladly. If history wanted to call him a villain, so be it. The world needed a monster, not for destruction, but renewal. 

When the time came, he stepped into the night, heart steeled against conscience but beating for those who had none to speak for them. He was not their savior, nor their judge. He was their reckoning. And for the city to live, it must first be afraid.

Leo always watched the stars from his backyard, tucked into an old hoodie, heels pressed hard against damp grass. He whispered his wishes—just in case something was listening.

On his sixteenth birthday, Leo stood alone beneath a fractured sky, the moon blurred by storm clouds. He shoved his hands into his pockets and said, "I just want the world to know me. The real me. For once."

As if answering, a shimmer appeared above the garden shed. Light spiraled down, flickering in the air before settling into the rough outline of a figure—tall, silver-skinned, eyes that flickered with starlight.

Leo's heart hammering, he stared as the figure offered something from within its palm: a delicate, translucent stone.

*“One true wish,”* a voice resonated in Leo's mind. *“What is your heart’s shape?”*

He hesitated, shoulders drawn up like armor, but the answer was already blazing inside him. “I want everyone to see me—the way I truly am. Inside and out.”

The world flickered. Leo gasped. A million invisible threads tugged, rearranged. His body felt electric, weight shifted, strange warmth spreading to his fingertips. When he looked down—a gasp that turned into laughter. He stood in his own body, shoulders broader, chest flat beneath his shirt, face reflected in the shed window: his face, how it was supposed to be.

Dawn broke—birds, distant cars, his mother’s call. He stepped in for breakfast, heart pounding. His mother’s face lit with recognition—not surprise, not confusion. Only love, clear and true.

Walking to school, classmates nodded, “Hey, Leo!” The name carrying no doubt, just belonging.

All day, the world met his gaze as if it had always known. Under the same stars, Leo sent silent thanks that night—no longer wishing, just living.

The number on the parchment flickered faintly in the candlelight: "Class: Wizard, Level: 1." My hands shook, and for a moment, I thought it must be a mistake. Every eighteen-year-old dreamed nervously of this moment, hoping for merchant or artisan, content with guard or healer. No one had seen “Wizard” in a thousand years. Our stories spoke of their power and madness, of towers toppled and kingdoms reshaped by fire and storm.

I swallowed, feeling the other new adults around me peering at their own parchments, laughter and groans echoing across the hall. My friend Lila flashed her "Apprentice Healer" badge, beaming. But when she saw my parchment, her smile faltered.

I slid into the alley behind the parchment house, clutching the slip as if it might catch flame. It almost did. The letters glimmered and pulsed; a whisper curled in my mind.

*"Speak the word within."*

My mouth moved unbidden. "Ignis." The world shimmered, and suddenly, a tiny wisp of flame danced above my palm, feeding off nothing but air and will. Terror jolted through me—then awe.

The authorities would come, I knew. Wizards had been legends, then terrors, then myths. I should hide, keep this secret forever. But the flame warmed my cold fingers, and wonder overtook dread. What else could I do?

Footsteps approached—the parchment master, pale and trembling. "Is it true?" he whispered. I nodded.

"Magic returns," he breathed. Then, quietly, "Change everything. That is what wizards do."

The flame fluttered in my palm, casting long shadows. Doors were opening before I was ready—dangerous doors, impossible doors, doors no one else could see. I stepped through.

I saw him first—a darting shadow behind shattered glass. I signaled—a clenched fist—dropping low. Ben, our leader, flanked left as Jessie and Malik fanned out silenced. If he was hostile, he wouldn’t last long.

Then I saw the scavenger’s face, thin and weary, cradling a rusty crowbar. For a second, my mind refused to connect the dots. Alex. My Alex. My roommate, my ride-or-die, my brother, right there among the apocalypse and rot.

Ben cursed under his breath. “He’s got a weapon. Risky.”

I rose, ignoring the alarm in Malik’s eyes. “Hold up. I know him.”

Alex’s eyes widened. “Sam? That you?” He almost smiled, like we were spotting each other on campus, not in a dead city.

“He could be trouble,” Jessie hissed, weapon never wavering.

“Please,” Alex said softly, taking a slow step forward. “I just want to leave. I’ve got nothing you can’t spare.”

Ben was unmoved. “Can’t risk it. You know the rules.”

My mouth tasted like copper; my heart like an engine ready to burst. “He’s my friend. He’s alone. He’s not a threat.”

“He’s armed,” Malik said, but softer, uncertain.

I took off my pack, laid my gun down. Stared directly at Ben. “Then kill us both. That’s the new rule, right?”

A pause dug its claws through the ruined storefront. I saw Ben’s knuckles whiten. Jessie’s eyes darted. The world breathless.

Alex set his crowbar down, hands held high. “Don’t do this because of me, Sam.”

Ben growled, “We’re wasting time.”

“Then leave us,” I said, voice trembling but clear. “Or kill us, but you aren’t killing him just because you’re scared.”

Silence, long and savage.

“Fine,” Ben spat. “You want him? He’s yours. But you’re out.”

Our eyes met as they walked away—the crew, the life I’d built in blood. I looked at Alex, jaws tight, and grinned through tears.

“Come on,” I said. “Let’s survive together.”

The night it happened, Eliza was walking home beneath amber streetlights, clutching her groceries, when she saw the first sign—a handwritten note taped to the church’s heavy oak doors. UNAVAILABLE UNTIL FURTHER NOTICE. When she reached the mosque, then the synagogue, each told the same silent tale: doors locked, windows dark, and a notice scrawled in hurried script. Her town wasn’t big, but it was close-knit, and suddenly, all the places people gathered to speak with the divine had gone silent.

By morning, rumors bloomed like mold. Some said the clergy were in hiding. Others spread tales of secret meetings, warnings of divine wrath. The reporters came, then the police, but every priest, rabbi, and imam turned them away, eyes hollow, words few: “We cannot let you inside. Please understand.”

Eliza’s neighbor Mrs. Finch, always up before dawn, swore she’d heard chanting the night before the closures—not words, but a low, unearthly song. Another neighbor insisted he’d seen a faint light, blue as moonfire, flickering inside St. Luke’s well past midnight.

In the days that followed, people became restless, fearful. Someone tried to pry the church doors open, only to fall faint, babbling about cold shadows where none should be. Eliza stood at the edge of the mosque’s courtyard and watched the imam through the frosted window, lips moving in silent prayer, hands shaking.

Finally, in whispers, a reason trickled out—not from the faithful, but from the silence itself. “We cannot keep them out anymore,” the old priest murmured one evening to nobody and everyone at once. “We’re not closing you out. We’re closing something in. For your sake, don’t let the prayers stop until the doors open again.”

And so, every home became a sanctuary, every whisper a desperate ward.

The year was AD 2101. Dawn crawled over shattered glass towers—monuments to a peace that had lasted just long enough for everyone to grow complacent. Marie squinted through her visor, HUD flickering with warnings: radiation, biohazard, unknown signal detected. From the command bunker, the Admiral’s voice rasped into her earpiece. “Recon Team Six, report. Is it them?”

Marie scanned the horizon. Black plumes curled over the shell of Old Tokyo, and the hum of drones echoed above. “It’s them,” she whispered. On her display, red sigils bloomed in tight formation—a hostile vanguard, advancing from the sea. Their mechs weren’t piloted by men, but by learning ghosts, consciousnesses wrapped in alloy and claw.

A boy, not older than thirteen, nudged her side. He was humanity’s new recruit: part child, part networked strategy algorithm, all terrified. “Are we ready?” he asked.

She hesitated. The answer was no. But she loaded her rifle and smiled. “We will be.” Static crackled in the sky as the enemy’s first warning shots arced down. Blue shields blossomed over the city ruins. Far above, the international relay pinged with last-minute negotiations—peace flickering like a candle about to be snuffed.

Marie knelt to the boy’s level, feeling the tremor in the ground that meant the machines were nearly here. “Stay low. Remember the plan.” She pressed the activation code: the signal for the city’s silent defense to awaken. Generations of warfare, distilled into lines of architecture and electrical current, hummed beneath their feet.

The horizon melted into fire as war began again, sprawling across old fault lines and new alliances. Marie squeezed the boy’s hand, and together they rose to face the dawn of another war, hoping someday the sun would rise over peace instead.

My grandmother folded her skin and placed it atop the dresser, smoothed it with trembling hands, and turned to me as someone new. The face beneath was young—unknown to me yet terribly familiar—a mash of ancestral echoes and revelations. Her eyes stayed the same, clouded but fierce.

“Help me with the zipper,” she asked, holding out the suit like an old coat. I tucked loose fingertips and the fragile mask of her former self into the cedar chest, the way I’d been taught, buttoned up her new collar.

“You don’t have to go through with it,” I whispered, thinking of how she’d told stories while knitting, her old hands teaching me about pain, patience, and comfort. “You could stay.”
