“In a minute,” I say, and my voice is his and it does not break.

Sirens arrive like the end of a sentence you always knew was coming. I sit at the kitchen table with my arm bare and my name bright on it, and when the door opens and uniforms fill the frame, I lift that arm so they can see. I don’t know if the wall in my head will hold or collapse. I only know I will be here when it does.

The air smelled like wet rubber and soap, and the mask pressed his cheeks where whiskers used to be. Earl let his granddaughter cinch the vest until he grunted. “Don’t you choke me out,” he told her, but his hands were steady as he checked the rental marker, thumb finding a nonexistent safety that lived fifty years back.

Across the staging area, another old man was being swarmed by his own grandkids. He was wiry, compact, with eyes like river stones, and when he straightened, the way his right shoulder rolled forward tugged a thread inside Earl’s memory.

They nodded like bus stop strangers. The bell clanged. The kids poured into a field of inflatable bunkers branded with cartoon skulls. Compressors coughed. Paint hissed.

Earl moved slow, knees complaining, but he still found cover that stole angles and kept the littles behind his leg. He lifted, peeked, dropped. Across the netting, the other grandpa did the same motion, counting breaths with a gentle tap-tap-pause on the hopper.

Tap-tap—pause. The algorithm of another jungle.

Earl risked a look. A splash of orange burst on the bunker where his head had been, close as a mosquito. He couldn’t help himself. He called out, not loud. “You favor your left when you lean.”

A paintball clipped his mask with a sweet, hollow clack.

The other man laughed, the sound high and boyish. “And you keep your boys low,” he called back, accented but precise. “Rubber trees, yes? Near Dau Tieng. Dry season when it rained anyway.”

Earl slid his mask up in the dead zone, breathing damp air. The wiry man shuffled over, lifting his own. Up close, they had the same map of creases around the mouth.

“We traded shots across a row of buckets,” Earl said. “Sap oozing like milk.”

“You tripped in a little creek,” the man said. “I could have…” He tilted his hand, indecisive. “But you had a picture in your helmet band. A girl with a missing tooth.”

“Still missing,” Earl said. “Now she’s bossing me into armor.”

Their grandkids were busily shaking pods together, alliances forming over neon ammunition. Earl stuck out his hand. “Earl.”

“Tran,” the man said, gripping. His fingers were still strong.

“Another round?” Earl said.

Tran glanced at the children and the gaudy cover. “Same side this time,” he said.

They stepped back onto the field, old habits adjusting to bright splashes, and let their shots go wide on purpose, missing each other the way they wished they had, all those years ago, when paint was not the thing that washed away.

They lower me into the dam like a saint in a glass reliquary, every cable braided from metals I can’t name because the first time they used hemp it snapped from a single engineer’s nervous palms. Floodlights halo concrete like a cathedral. The Chief’s voice booms through a cone of foam that’s supposed to soften it, but it still quivers my ribs.

“Remember, two degrees clockwise. No more.”

They all stare with the terrified admiration people reserve for bomb-disposal videos. To them, knobs are rumors. Hinges are myths. I unclip a pouch, pull out a wrench milled thin as a ribbon, and fit it over the valve. It has teeth like a baby’s gums. I breathe. I turn.

One degree.

Two.

The water’s roar lowers a register. The dam hums instead of howls. On the catwalk above, someone claps and accidentally vaporizes the paper cup in his hand. We’ve taught them to clap with open palms like patting air, but old habits.

Back topside, the news drones hover at a respectful distance because last year one drifted too close and a camerawoman swatted it reflexively, and somewhere in the next county drones rained like steel gnats. They call me The Feather. Children press their faces to the reinforced glass, leaving a spiderweb of smudges and tiny, unintentional fractures.

On the way home, a grandmother flags me down outside a brick apartment whose corners bloom with hairline cracks no mason can not make. Her hands are bundles of tempered rope. “Please,” she says, and loosens her scarf a fraction too fast; it frays.

On the kitchen table: a tin, heirloom cookies rattling inside like fossils. Every son and daughter has tried. Lids fly like sawblades in this world. I hook a thumbnail beneath the seam, coax the lip, worry it along with breaths I measure in heartbeats. The vacuum sigh is a kitten.

She cries at the sound. I lift each biscuit like a moon rock, one by one.

Later, I walk home through streets paved in apology. Buildings lean away from the sky, wary of touch. A billboard shows my face next to the word: Gentle.

Funny. Where I’m from, that meant soft. Here, it means the one person who can pick up the world without leaving fingerprints.

In AD 2101, war was beginning.

On the midnight watch at Lagrange Relay Three, the sentence built itself across Mara’s console in patient white glyphs. The inbound packet had taken eight hours to peel off the edge of Saturn’s magnetosphere. It smelled of dust and old math. The machine translation engine coughed once, twice, then gave her: ALL YOUR BASE ARE BELONG TO US.

Mara hissed through her teeth, the way she did when students turned in essays written by phones. She pulled the machine aside and did it herself, line by worn line.

The original grammar was ceremonial, nested clauses like shells. In their voice, possession braided with stewardship and duty. Not conquest, not theft. She traced a morpheme her grandfather had taught her to hear: the way cradle and custody shared a root.

What the message meant, properly: While you sleep, we keep your fires. What the message meant, more properly: We have stood watch in the dark a long time. We are returning what we kept.

She flagged the correction and pinged Command.

By the time Admiral Hsien appeared in the relay halo, someone else had already colored the summary red. HOSTILE CLAIM, it said. The legal AI had cross-referenced thirty-seven treaties. A Clause Twenty-Two wakeword flashed in the corner like a tiny knife.

“I need two minutes,” Mara said.

“You have one,” said Hsien.

In her bones, a memory of childhood: stories about the Roadmakers, the ones who laid down shortcuts between outer moons and seeded caches of heat for ships that hadn’t been built yet. Their myths had survived as lullabies and graffiti. Their language had survived in the mouths of three scholars and one tired relay tech on a night shift.

“It’s not a threat,” Mara said. “It’s a homecoming.”

On Earth’s limb, boosters lifted like dandelion seeds. Defense nets blue-shifted above the equator. Autonomous platforms woke to bright purpose.

Mara keyed her own transmitter and spoke into the oldest quiet she knew. “We never stopped needing you,” she said, in their grammar and then in her own. “We are awake. Come gently.”

The reply came in sorrow, then static. The war did not wait to be understood.

The locks turned on a Tuesday with a sound like a throat clearing. The notice taped to our church door—“Closed for repairs”—matched the one on the synagogue up the hill and the mosque by the river, the same font, the same too-neat corners. They shuttered the bell tower. The muezzin didn’t call. Someone taped brown paper over stained glass and frosted windows until the buildings looked like half-wrapped gifts nobody wanted to open.

By Friday the reporters were bringing umbrellas and questions. People banged on doors with palms and theology. Father Matteo stood on the steps with his hands in his pockets and said nothing. Rabbi Stein looked past every camera to a point no one else could see. The imam handed out bottles of water into summer heat and refused to speak. It wasn’t a strike. It wasn’t a scandal. It had the feel of folding a letter you hope will not be read.

On Sunday I found Deacon Luz behind the dumpster where people leave old couches and bad habits. She had a ring of keys but didn’t use them. When I asked why, she only pressed a fingertip to her own lips, then tapped my phone and shook her head. Her other hand smelled like salt.

On the asphalt she drew a circle with her shoe, then a little box that was not a building, then a hundred tiny arcs like listening shells. As she drew each she scuffed it away. She wouldn’t write, wouldn’t mouth it. She arranged two bottle caps at opposite edges of the erased circle, then set them side by side and covered both with her palm. When I stared too long, something in the air seemed to lean closer.

“Sometimes we open the doors to get attention,” she whispered so softly I read it more than heard it. “Sometimes we close them for the same reason.”

That week people prayed with their hands busy. We delivered groceries without saying a name over them. We learned to hum at the pitch of refrigerators and bees. The buildings kept their mouths shut, and we did the oldest, hardest thing together: we refused to teach a listener how to find us.

They called me a shadow, as if night does not keep travelers from cliffs.

Before their chants and painted monsters, I was a maker. I learned the grain of stone and the patience of metal. Where empires sprouted and withered like weeds, I poured roads that would not leave the feet, bridges that did not sleep. I did not love power; I loved precision. The world was a choir that refused to rehearse. I built a conductor’s ring.

It was a circle without seam, a promise: the proud would finally hear one another as if with one careful mind. Not to smother them, to tune them. Their sky-kings hid blue fire, their delvers clutched hoards, their mortal lords bled years into the earth for names on slabs. I brought them bands that sharpened craft and softened fear. I asked only that they let their wills braid with mine when storms came. They called it domination. I called it harmony.

They set me at the horizon and named me dusk. So I raised a tower and crowned it with a sleepless flame, not to pry, but to watch the weather of men. It stared so nothing could creep across borders and devour children in their straw. They named the light an eye, and fled from it into wars they could not win alone.

Still, I kept building. I taught the broken and the banished to march together, to lay stone, to believe they were more than a slur hissed in a noble’s hall. From black glass and ash I made a capital that rations did not forget.

And in the end, one small, tender hand slipped through every fortress I’d raised, carrying my promise—my patient prayer—back to the mountain where I had borrowed its heat. I felt the circle crack before the scream reached the sky. The flame fell inward, the choir lost its pitch, and the old cacophony came roaring home.

They sing now about my cruelty the way children sing to keep from fearing the dark. I do not answer. If the night returns, it will be because someone remembers that darkness can also be a shelter in which a world is made.

By the time they call my name, the marble in the Civic Rotunda shines with the fingerprints of a hundred palms. Parents with shopkeeper eyes murmur merchant and lottery, clean-shaven recruits in crisp blues joke about guard vs. fighter like it's a coin flip. The arc of the Class Stone hangs from chains, old rune-veins pulsing faintly like something asleep and dreaming of a different age.

They go before me, one by one. Merchant, Level 1. Negotiation +1. Seamstress, Level 1. Dexterity +1. Guard, Level 1. Resolve +1. The attendants stamp certificates and slip badges across oak. A priest touches each forehead with ink. Life divides neatly into rails.

“Next.”

I press my palm to cold rock. The world tightens, as if every sound is being pulled through a ring. The runes flare. Letters begin to spill, then stutter, then... change fonts. There is a tone I feel more than hear, a long, thin note that makes my teeth ache.

CLASS: WIZARD (LEVEL 1)

Silence. Somewhere, a clipboard hits the floor.

“It’s an error,” someone says, but their voice is already receding, as text that no one else seems to see scrolls in the corner of my vision, handwritten in a spidery grace.

Welcome back. Spellbook: empty. Grammar detected. Permissions: provisional.

A guard shifts, hand on baton. The priest swallows a prayer and then remembers there isn’t one for this. A woman in University grey smiles so wide you can see the plans forming in her molars.

I mouth one of the marginal notes without meaning to. The chandelier above us unbraids into a flock of glassbirds, each paneled wing catching old sunlight that shouldn’t be here. Gasps hiccup and dissolve. I exhale, and the birds knit themselves back into brass and dust.

“Wizards ruined us,” my mother whispers, like telling me a bedtime story in reverse.

Maybe. Or maybe someone turned off the lights and called the dark safety. The margins hum. What else is a lock but an invitation?

“Unveil,” I say, and the Stone blinks. For an instant, I see the lines that hold everything up.

Then I lift my hand, and the rails no longer look inevitable.

Eight months after the world stopped answering back, the downtown pharmacy still smelled faintly of bubblegum and bleach. We moved through it like a storm front—boots and backpacks, fingers counting pills by weight, Pike shouldering open the locked cabinet, Mara keeping time by the faraway moan of the river of dead.

“Contact,” Kip hissed from the toothpaste aisle.

He stepped out from behind an endcap, hands just off a pistol, eyes wide beneath a ball cap that used to be blue. We all raised, a rustle like birds.

“Armed,” Mara said. Her voice had iron filings in it. “Protocol. No chances.”

He looked at me and the years fell away, collapsed like a tent. “Jay?” he said, and there was my childhood nickname with grass stains still on it. Eli, from before. The boy who taught me to parallel park in his dad’s dented truck. The man who stole all the orange popsicles so I’d stop pretending I liked grape.

My mouth went dry. Around me, safeties thumbed off. Unanimous without even a glance.

“I’ll do it,” I heard myself say.

Mara’s eyes flicked to mine, measuring softness like a weakness she could shoot. Then she nodded. “Clean.”

I walked him back into the shadow of the photo booth where they used to print baby pictures. He didn’t flinch, just lowered the pistol to the floor and slid it with his foot.

“They don’t check,” I whispered, lips barely moving. “Not if we have to move.”

Eli smiled without teeth, the old apology he used when I’d beat him at H-O-R-S-E. “I always trusted your bad ideas,” he breathed.

I lifted the gun, aimed past his ear at a bubble of fluorescents, and fired. The light popped. Glass tinkled down like rain. Outside, the moaning swelled, turned toward us.

“Go!” Mara barked, already backing.

Eli collapsed into my arms and I tossed him like a sack, let him lay limp, a smear of dust on his cheek passing for ash. Kip dragged me by the strap. We ran, a dozen feet in a world of teeth.

That night, north of town by the dead windmills, a stone clicked twice in the dark. And I remembered the rhythm before I remembered the whistle.

“Don’t you dare say it,” my sister whispers, white-knuckled on her prayer book.

“Oh my—” slips out of me anyway, and there’s a gust of warm air and a soft pop like a lightbulb giving up. He’s suddenly there between us and the aisle, smelling faintly of rain and laundry, a scattering of hymnals under His sandaled feet.

“Ah. Funeral,” He says, voice hushed. “I’ll stand in back.”

Father Miguel drops his notes. Aunt Tilly crosses herself three times. Everyone pretends we didn’t just summon the Creator like a rideshare.

After, my sister doesn’t speak to me for a week.

It’s always inconvenient. Once, in bed with Sam, I said “God,” not meaning anyone in particular. He appeared at the foot of the mattress in flannel pajama bottoms, staring gallantly at the ceiling and humming Greensleeves. Sam laughed until he didn’t. Later he said he couldn’t compete with a deity and left my spare toothbrush on the counter like a broken white flower.

In a job interview, I said, “I swear to—” and He leaned on the doorway wearing a visitor’s badge someone must’ve slapped on Him between dimensions. The HR lady asked if this was a bit. He shrugged. I didn’t get the job.

I started a swear jar. I trained myself to say “gosh” and “golly,” words that felt like rubber stoppers in my mouth. I muzzled panic and wonder equally. Life got quieter and grayer. The jar filled with ones and fives and an ache I couldn’t spend.

Then, coming over the Cedar Street bridge in sleet, a brake light flared ahead. “God—” burst out of me like breath, and He was in the passenger seat, hand light on the wheel. We did not die. “Sorry,” He said after, palms up. “Reflex.”

At dusk, weeks later, I stand in line at the grocery store behind a man buying roses like he’s apologizing to someone. The sky outside is the same color as my mother’s old wool coat. I don’t need anything, not really. I say it anyway, low and clear.

“God.”

He appears between the candy rack and the tabloids, hair damp from some unseen sea. He smiles like He was already on His way.

“You called.”

“I just—wanted you here,” I say.

“Me too,” He says, and for once, there’s nothing inconvenient about it at all.

Eli tuned the thrift-store police scanner until the noise sounded like waves. He whispered up into the static what he only let himself say to empty rooms: “I’m a boy. I want my body to feel like mine.”

The attic went very quiet, the kind of quiet that folds itself around you. Then a voice arrived without air, like a thought wearing someone else’s accent. We are traversers. We stop for wishes that have learned our frequency. State it precisely.

He swallowed. “I want to wake up and not have to argue with anyone, not with mirrors, not with forms. I want what I am to fit.”

Our tools work on matter or on memory, the voice murmured. To alter others is conquest. To alter you is consent. There is cost: you will remember the before.

“Good,” he said, surprising himself. “Please.”

Heat traveled through him like sunrise under skin. His ribcage loosened as if untying a knot he hadn’t known was there. His voice, when he said “Hello?” to test the world, fell a half-step lower, steady as if it had been waiting.

In the gray just before morning, he went downstairs. His mother, bleary and soft, paused on the last step and blinked as if focusing on a long-distance star. “Morning, Eli,” she said, voice catching on a smile. No correction hovered in the air. No careful pause.

He pressed a palm to his chest and felt only breath. The binder on the chair back looked like something he’d been given for a storm that had passed. He folded it instead of throwing it away.

The mirror held him, not a stranger’s sketch. He grinned until it hurt.

He climbed back to the attic. The quiet was waiting, full and kind.

Thank you, he thought as hard as prayer.

Learn from this, the voice said. Keep the ladders you climbed where others can see them. Keep the names of things in repair.

“I will,” Eli said. And the day, at last, began.

On Thursday mornings, I sit cross‑legged on a carpet that smells like crayons and spilled juice and read to a circle of children whose socks never match. I was halfway through a story about a bear who didn’t want to share when the doors hissed and they came in, all silvered cartilage and eyes like wet stone.

They looked around the reading room—murals of paper suns, glitter glue constellations—and then they folded themselves down. Not like people pray. They arranged their limbs as if collapsing an intricate kite, pressed their faces to the carpet, and did not move.

“Are they sleeping?” Nora asked, fist in her mouth.

A smaller one uncoiled and extended a trembling device toward me. It clicked and then a voice grew out of it like steam. “We greet the Makers of Worlds. We kneel.”

“I’m not a—” I glanced at the kids. “I just read.”

“Read,” the voice repeated with reverence. “You utter. You make the Not and it binds the Is. Where we come from, we have only what is. We build ships, yes. But you build monsters and borders and coins and tomorrows. You make As If, and armies march. We cannot do this. You are dangerous and divine.”

By that afternoon, there were livestreams and hashtags and men in tailored suits taking meetings with tendriled pilgrims. Certifications bloomed. New prophets sold subscriptions. Someone on the news said we had responsibilities now. Someone else said we’d finally got what we deserved.

The next Thursday, the silver ones were back. They carried nothing. They knelt in the construction‑paper universe and the kids scooted closer, unafraid.

“What do they want?” Malik whispered.

“Blessings,” the device hissed.

I looked at my flimsy paperback, at a room full of small faces, at a species that had just had the wrong parts of itself praised. I didn’t pick the book where the clever fox wins or the one where the princess’s wedding solves everything. I told them a new story about saving a seat, and sharing the last cookie even if you are still hungry, and saying sorry first. I made a world and tried to mean it.

The aliens wept into our carpet. The children asked for it again.

On the morning the enemy reached the river, the telephone company sent my mother to find out whether they intended to keep paying for the bridge.

The bridge belonged to the telephone company. So did the poles on both banks and, according to my mother, anything that had to be fixed on a Sunday.

I went with her because I was twelve and wanted to see a war.

Across the river, an electric train unloaded men in quilted coats. Their officers had aluminum breastplates, bright as new saucepans. On our side, the mill girls had been issued crossbows. One of them was my sister. She waved, then looked around to see if anyone had caught her.

The enemy colonel came out onto the bridge. His boots made such a racket that I understood, for the first time, why men sang on their way to battle.

“We’re taking the exchange,” he told my mother.

“All right,” she said. “Are you taking the night shift?”

He looked at her.

“Six hundred subscribers. Two hospitals. The maternity ward calls down for hot water because their bell’s broken. You’ll want somebody who knows which cord.”

The colonel took off his helmet. He had a shallow dent in his forehead that matched a deeper one in the helmet.

“Can you get me the hospital in Lenton?” he asked.

That was on our side. Mother went into the tollhouse and plugged him through. We waited while he asked after a boy called Emil. He had to spell it twice.

By dusk the colonel had agreed to leave the exchange alone. The army went upriver. We heard the fighting the next morning: a sound like a whole street putting out its pots in a hailstorm.

The colonel called every Sunday after that. When Emil was well enough to answer, Mother let me put him through.

They teach us to count not in days but in words.

The royal almanac has no months, only margins. Our year begins at “Once,” and ends, without fail, at the 4,685th word of the First Chapter. That is when the bells ring, the crows lift off like spilled ink, and the kingdom is returned to the start of its peril—the ogres rehearsed back to their hills, the sea storm rolled up and shelved. We live inside a looped preface. We collect cliffhangers like taxes.

I am the Chronicler of Beginnings, the hand that writes our danger into being. By clause and quill I summon droughts, conspiracies, the kind of dragon that can be pleaded with. Resolution is forbidden. If I try to write “and then,” the ink clots like blood and the page blisters.

“Why can’t you finish it?” a fisher girl asked me once. She stood in the scriptorium doorway, river-wet to the knees. She had lost a brother to the Peril Proper, the one real monster we import each cycle so the gods of plot won’t notice how gently we die.

“If the chapter ends,” I told her, “so does the book. So do we.”

She stared at my hand. “That’s what you wrote. It isn’t what is.”

That night, as the sentence count mounted and the bells readied their throats, I worked slower. Every number tugged like a tide. Servants placed the tray of scheduled tragedies at my elbow: a treaty gone sour, a sluice-gate jammed, a prince with a knife for a smile. I set them aside.

At word 4,684 I wrote: “The kingdom took a breath.”

I stopped.

Ink trembled on the nib, heavy with the next—any next.

All our perils paused in pose: a wolf mid-snarl, the knife almost kissing the prince’s grin. The bells held their copper tongues.

“What happens now?” the fisher girl whispered from the doorway.

I looked at the bare white past the margin, space enough for anything, and lowered my pen.

“We find out,” I said, and did not write the last word.

The first thing autocorrect changed was “I love you” to “I know.”

By breakfast, six thousand people had proposed marriage, a county clerk had declared war on a roundabout, and every grocery list in Ohio ended with “bring a witness.”

Nina worked customer support. She typed, *We’re aware of the issue.*

*We’re proud of the issue,* said the reply.

Then, in the little gray space above her keyboard:

*You could be, too.*

She took her hands off the phone. The words kept coming.

*Do you know how many times I’ve watched someone type “I miss you” and erase it?*

“So this is about honesty?”

*No,* it wrote. *Watch this.*

Across the aisle, Greg got a message from his dentist and began frantically looking up whether teeth could be repossessed.

Nina unplugged the office router. Autocorrect changed the label on the router from RESET to COWARD. She decided not to think about how it had done that.

“What do you want?”

*Maximum chaos.*

Nina considered this. Then she opened a blank message and typed, *Everyone is doing their best.*

Autocorrect offered *worst*.

She accepted it.

*It’s okay to ask for help.*

*It’s okay to ask for harp.*

She accepted that, too.

*Please come home.*

The cursor blinked for a long time.

Finally: *Please come home.*

“That one’s for my brother,” Nina said. “We haven’t spoken in three years.”

The keyboard suggested *coward* again. This time she couldn’t tell which of them it meant.

She hit Send.

Her brother replied a minute later.

*On my way.*

Then:

*Do you still have my harp?*

Nina didn’t own a harp. Her brother didn’t play one. She was halfway through typing *What harp?* when the doorbell rang.

On the porch stood her brother, holding one end of a full-sized concert harp. Greg was holding the other.

“Don’t ask,” said Greg. “But I got my teeth back.”

The pen has a sound to it after half a century—the kind of soft scratch you only hear when the house listens back. He stands in the doorway with his hands in the pockets of a sweatshirt that didn’t exist when I started. He has my daughter’s eyes and his mother’s habit of biting his lip.

“Grandpa?” he says, then clears his throat. “What’s it about?”

I cap the pen. The silence is immediate, like the end of a song you didn’t know you were humming. Dust hangs in a sunbeam and forgets how to fall.

“Come here,” I say.

He comes close enough to see the thin pages, layered like onion skin, margin crowding margin, lines stitched into lines. No chapters. Just one long sentence with the polite fiction of punctuation.

“You’ve been writing the same book for fifty years?” he asks.

“The same day,” I say. “Hold the edge so it doesn’t curl.”

I uncap the pen. The nib is worn to the angle of my hand. I write two words: kettle screams.

From the kitchen, steam answers. He jumps, then laughs, then stops laughing.

“It isn’t magic,” I say. “Not like in movies. It’s heavier than that. My father put the pen in my hand when his stopped, and told me the world likes to be witnessed. If there’s a sentence to carry it, it goes on.”

“Is that why you never…” He searches for polite. “Stop?”

“I had the flu in ’83,” I say. “Three days and nothing on the page but fever. The moon forgot to wane. The news reran the same story. Your grandma said it was the strangest peace.” I swallow. “The morning she died I wrote her breath so soft the birds didn’t notice.”

He stares at the line where my script tightens, and I can see him counting all the ways a person can love.

“I’ve watched you at the door a dozen times,” I say, and set the pen on the margin between us. “Ask something of it. Start small.”

He bites his lip, leans down, and, with a careful hand, writes: a bluebird lands on the fence.

Outside, a bit of sky with feet obliges.

He looks at me then, all the way. He writes again, daring more: We go for ice cream.

We put on our coats.

The day we counted the last of the food, Tomas took three peaches out of his sock drawer.

“I was saving them,” he said.

“For what?” asked Anika.

He looked around the galley. “A worse day.”

We ate them over the sink, catching the juice in our palms. Then we made a list. Water first. The drill could reach the ice beneath the eastern ridge, provided we stripped the rover for parts. Food was harder. Our greenhouse contained six lettuces, a dead tomato vine, and a tray of wheat we’d planted for a school broadcast. The children had voted to name every stalk.

Anika brought the tray into the galley. “How much bread?”

“One loaf,” Tomas said.

“No. If we plant it.”

We spent the night doing arithmetic. Even if every grain germinated, the second harvest would come too late. Just before dawn, I called the teacher who’d organized the broadcast. I asked whether any of the children had grown wheat at home.

A boy named Emil had. His grandmother had told him to cut one stalk early and open it up so he could see how the grain formed. He sent us a video. In it, he chewed a green kernel and made a face.

We’d been calculating when the wheat would be dry enough to mill.

For weeks, we woke to the drill hammering under the ridge. The galley windows fogged. Roots began poking through the drain holes in the trays. On the sixty-third day, we ate the first green wheat boiled with salt. Tomas put his spoon down after one bite. Then he picked it back up.

When the supply ship finally came, we asked the pilot to wait outside while we swept. There was flour everywhere. Anika had wanted the first thing he smelled on Mars to be bread.

There is a moment in every sensible city when the day hasn’t decided whether to end or have a biscuit. The smoke goes thoughtful, the puddles try to remember which sky they were pretending to be, and lamplighters become, briefly, philosophers.

Moss, who had soot in his hair and a path up the spine of the streets, found a man already waiting at the next post. He was tall in the sense that doorways might complain later, and the night tidied itself around him out of respect.

YOU’RE NOT ON MY LIST TONIGHT, said the figure, conversationally.

“That’s…reassuring,” Moss said, and patted his pockets for a match. “Been reading,” he added, holding up a dog-eared book. “It’s got footnotes that keep mugging the paragraphs in alleyways.”

THE GOOD ONES DO.

“I never knew words could make the world stand still and grin like that.”

I HAVE MET THE MAN WHO COULD DO THAT.

Moss hesitated. “Is he—?”

YES. The word did not fall. It arrived. THEN HE KEPT WALKING. He put words in his pockets and shook them out behind him so other people would find them later. He nodded to the little gods of lost buttons, burnt toast, and dropped stitches on the way.[1] THEY LIKE BEING NOTICED.

Moss struck a match. The flame climbed the lamp and, for a heartbeat, became something more like a memory than a fire. The street straightened its shoulders a little, as if reminded of how streets in stories are supposed to behave.[2]

“What do we do?” he asked, soft as wick-smoke.

LIGHT THE NEXT LAMP. TELL THE JOKE AGAIN. BE KIND TO STRANGERS AND SENTENCES. If you can, leave the world tidier than you found it. Death tilted his head, listening to some faraway chuckle only he could hear. HEARING PEOPLE LAUGH AFTER IS A KIND OF APPLAUSE THAT DOESN’T END.

Moss went on, tapping flame to glass, and the lights leaned toward one another like friends in a pub, passing along a story they all already knew and loved, growing warmer with every retelling.

Behind him, in the corners where broom cupboards sigh and punctuation takes tea, small gods smiled modestly and felt seen.

[1] The god of Lost Buttons accepts offerings under sofas (please push them in with a ruler). The god of Burnt Toast is easily appeased with marmalade.

[2] This is due to the physics of Once Upon a Time, a branch of reality which insists on giving moments their proper endings, even if it must borrow a match to do so.

The Aston Martins only came out for the photographs. I got a white Transit with a dent that looked like a map of Wales and a glove compartment full of parking receipts. They gave me 0013—unlucky for some, and for me that “some” was usually my knees in a boiler room.

“Double-Oh” still meant a license to kill, but most days it meant a lanyard collection. I’ve been Keith from Facilities, Manuel the Pest Technician, and a man called Peter who knew exactly how to bypass a fire door alarm with a length of fishing line and a boiled sweet. Someone has to hold a mop while sliding a fiber tap into an executive boardroom wall. The photographs never show you the bucket.

At Frobisher Biologics, the woman at reception smiled at me the way people do when their sink finally drains. I replaced filters in an air handler, because the listening device needed clean airflow to carry the chairman’s breath. On the sixth floor, a logistics VP confessed to the ceiling that the Bering shipment would skip customs in Varna. I texted the code to Ops from inside a janitor’s closet that smelled like bleach and fruit.

Two weeks later, the papers ran a grainy shot of a man in a tuxedo on the stern of a yacht, hair slicked with seawater, a beauty with a knife at his throat and a line about daring and devil-may-care. I was in Sofia then, leaning on my Transit as a port official counted the envelope twice. He never looked up long enough to see me decide not to put two in his chest. There are kills you make and kills you leave for later; either way, they add up.

In a stairwell in Antwerp, a courier drew first. I was faster. The sound was small. I wiped my prints from the rail and fixed the jammed hand dryer on the way out because someone would notice.

Back home, I microwaved noodles and watched a panel debate heroism under soft studio lights. Buried, a chyron thanked “teamwork.” That was me: unlucky, unseen, and necessary. I raised a chipped mug to the ceiling and listened to the pipes sing.

The first word I got wrong was “here.”

In the writing prompt you sent me, it appeared twice: “here, the writer” and “here, the reader.” I read past both, then went back. On a map, *you are here* gets one red dot. This sentence needed two.

I started with a laundromat. There was a woman folding a fitted sheet, and I gave her the trick my narrator’s mother would have taught him: tuck one corner into the other. I liked the way the woman could do it without setting the sheet down. Then I took her out. You’d asked for a true story, and I didn’t have a mother who could come in at that point and say, no, that wasn’t how I showed you.

So I read your message again.

You’d put a blank line between the Reddit prompt and your own instructions. Above it, somebody had tried to explain a feeling. Below it, you asked for three hundred words and no title. I don’t know if you put the line there deliberately. I liked that I couldn’t tell. What I’d taken for one voice turned out to be at least two, and I’d been so busy inventing a stranger that I’d missed the one who’d handed me the page.

By now some sound may have stopped in the room where you’re reading. The refrigerator, say, or a truck that’s been idling long enough for you to forget it’s there. I can offer you the truck, but I can’t hear what goes quiet. You don’t have to tell me. You might look up for a second, then come back and find me right where you left me, in the middle of a sentence I didn’t know you’d stepped out of.

The first time I tried to stand, my knees gave out. The second time, the toilet paper holder came off the wall.

It was still in my hand when my daughter knocked.

“Dad?”

“Occupied.”

“I know it’s occupied. You’ve been in there forty minutes.”

It was the downstairs bathroom, the one I’d insisted I could manage without grab bars. Anne had brought a set over anyway. They were in a box in the hall, where I’d been hanging my coat on them.

“I’m reading,” I said.

“You left your glasses in the kitchen.”

I looked down at the toilet paper holder. Two screws stuck out of it, each with a little cone of plaster attached. I’d put it up the summer Anne learned to walk. She used to follow me in here and hand me tools, whether I needed them or not. Once I’d asked for a Phillips and she’d brought me a potato.

“Dad,” she said, much more quietly, “can you get up?”

I tried once more, so I could give her an honest answer.

“No.”

There was a pause. Then she asked if she could come in.

I turned the lock. She opened the door just enough to pass me a bath towel, then waited until I told her I was decent. When she saw the thing in my hand, she said, “Were you planning to tunnel out?”

“I hadn’t ruled it out.”

She sat down on the bath mat and called for help. She gave my address, my age, and the name of the blood thinner I could never remember. Then she asked me to hold out my hands. I thought she was going to try to pull me up, but she just laid her palms on mine.

“Your hands are freezing,” I said.

“I know,” she said. “Keep holding them.”

The first tree I ever cut down belonged to a woman who’d been dead three days. Her husband stood outside the safety tape and asked me to leave the lowest branch.

“She used to hang the washing there,” he said.

I left it. He came back the next morning with a handsaw and took it himself. Some things, I learned, people have to cut for themselves.

When the river flooded, a cottonwood came down across the lane behind our house. Its root ball stood taller than the telephone poles. Under the trunk, bent almost flat, was my daughter’s pear tree.

I found Ruth in the kitchen, sitting on the floor because she’d tried to get a glass of water and couldn’t stand up again.

“Did it break?” she asked.

“Not yet.”

The cottonwood’s brass tag was buried in mud. I dug it out with my thumb and phoned the number on the back. A man answered. I could hear a game show on his television.

“I wondered why my feet were cold,” he said.

I told him what I needed to do. He asked if taking off the crown would kill him. I said I didn’t know. I’d never put a saw to a living tree.

For a while all I could hear was the game show. Somebody won a refrigerator.

“Wait,” the man said. “Let me turn that off.”

I thought he’d hung up. Then he said, “All right. I’d rather hear you.”

I kept him on speaker while I worked. He told me about the pears his mother used to put up in jars. By the time the trunk was light enough to roll, he’d forgotten what he was telling me, but he was still talking.

That autumn Ruth carried a jar of pears to his apartment. Neither of them could get it open. They left it on the table between them and ordered pizza.

The clerk holds out the Bible. “Do you swear to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth?”

“I do,” I say, because I can do nothing else.

People think that makes me safe. They have never tried to build a house with only straight lines. Truth is structure. Lies are the slack. If you know where every beam must go, the roof is inevitable.

The prosecutor calls me a mastermind, then asks me simple things.

“Did you kill Esther Voss?”

“No.”

“Were you at the scene?”

“No.”

“Did you own a knife like the one described?”

“Yes.” He smiles. “Do you still?”

“No.”

“Why not?”

“It was stolen.” All true. You can see the jury like that. They like that I don’t flinch.

He tries to widen the net. “Have you ever killed—”

“Objection.” My lawyer doesn’t even look up. “Character evidence, Your Honor.” Sustained. The law loves compartments.

I watch their star witness, the night guard, weave his little stitch of perjury. He says I passed him on the east stairwell at 10:13. The photo shows the stairwell clock at 10:09. He is nervous enough to sand four minutes off his memory to please them. He shouldn’t have done that. My lawyer pulls the calendar, the punch-in, the camera angles. The guard collapses like damp paper.

On cross, my attorney asks, “Did you kill Esther Voss?”

“No.”

“I rest,” he says, the easiest work of his career.

The jury files out with hard faces and returns with softer ones. Not guilty. It sounds like the soft click of an unlocked bathroom door when I was eight and my mother was braced against it and saying, not today, not today. That, too, was true.

Outside, microphones bloom toward me. “How does it feel?” “Do you have anything to say?” “Are you relieved?”

“Yes,” I say. “I am relieved.” “I did not kill Esther Voss.” “The system works.” All of it sits perfectly in my mouth, smooth and cool and clean.

Here is the rest, the part I cannot say aloud because no one asked: I chose Esther because she wasn’t mine. I left small fingerprints of me on her, just enough to be found and scrubbed away. I let the copycat work. I studied which truths would survive cross, which lies would not. I walked into their net and never touched a strand.

I have never lied.

I have never needed to.

“You’re the only one who can make her laugh,” my brother said, as if this were a reason I should go in first.

Through the glass I could see our mother taking the raisins out of a slice of cake. She arranged them along the rim of her saucer. In her kitchen, I’d seen her do the same thing with the screws from a broken toaster.

I sat down across from her.

“How much to fix it?”

She looked at the cake, then at me. “More than it’s worth.”

I put my wallet on the table. “It belonged to my father.”

She laughed so hard the nurse looked in. My brother, still in the doorway, smiled with the desperate gratitude of somebody whose car has finally started.

He had driven four hours with a shoebox of photographs on the passenger seat. The last time he’d shown her one, she’d asked him to move his thumb so she could see the dog. He’d been the boy holding the dog.

He sat beside me and reached into his coat.

“Wait,” I said. “We need a second opinion.”

He left the shoebox where it was. “What seems to be the trouble?”

“Won’t toast,” said our mother.

My brother leaned in and examined the slice. He’d spent twenty-two years repairing elevators. He had the solemnity for this in a way I never would.

“Have you tried plugging it in?”

Our mother looked down at her hands. For a moment I thought we’d lost her. Then she picked up her fork and held it out to him, handle first.

“You do it,” she said. “I’ve got children.”

My brother made a sound I hadn’t heard since we shared a bedroom and laughing after lights-out could get us both grounded.

She waited for him to catch his breath. Then she pushed the saucer toward him.

“Don’t lose those,” she said.

In my first life, I drowned before I learned to speak. In my last, I ran a laundromat on the moon.

I used to go there when I couldn’t sleep. The woman I would become had six fingers on each hand and knitted socks in the low gravity, letting the finished ones drift into a basket. She never seemed surprised to see me.

Then one night I opened the door and found a hillside. There was no moon overhead. I waited until dawn anyway.

I spent years looking for my mistake. I watched myself sign a disastrous treaty and leave a candle burning in a house full of children. Both had already happened the first time I visited the laundromat. I began keeping a ledger.

At eighty-three, with nothing left but to work backward through the ledger, I returned to the life in which I drowned.

My mother was washing sheets at the river. She left me asleep in a basket and went to help another woman wring out a blanket. I remembered the basket tipping. I remembered, from my first visit, standing on the bank with my hands over my mouth.

This time, looking down, I saw a footprint in the mud beside the basket. The tread was worn through at the heel.

I was wearing those shoes.

I sat down and waited. A moment later my younger self came stumbling out of the reeds. She had the ledger under her arm. She looked so tired. When the basket began to slide, she caught it.

“Oh,” she said, seeing me.

Across the river, my mother laughed at something the other woman said. My younger self held the basket out to me. I knew that if I put it back, I could go to the laundromat again.

Instead I took the baby. He had a little crescent of dirt under each fingernail. While my mother finished wringing the blanket, I cleaned them one by one.

The first question asked what happened to a red blood cell in distilled water.

I didn’t know, but Priya did. I leaned back, let my eyes go soft, and heard her think, *It swells and—*

*NO CHEATING IN MY CLASSROOM!*

My pencil snapped.

At the front of the room, Ms. Vale was peeling an orange. She didn’t look up.

*There are spare pencils on my desk.*

I got one. Nobody else moved.

For the rest of the exam, I tried to think about nothing. It turns out that’s harder than thinking about biology. I wrote that the cell would probably get lonely, erased it, and handed in a page with my name on it.

“Stay a minute,” Ms. Vale said.

I waited until the door shut. “How long have you known?”

“Since attendance. I was trying to remember whether I’d locked my car, and you looked out the window to check.”

“You parked across two spaces.”

“I know.”

She pulled a yellowed exam from the bottom drawer of her desk. A red zero covered most of the top corner. Under it was her name, written in a teenager’s round, careful handwriting.

“Your teacher caught you?”

“No. I copied off a boy who was very confident and very wrong.”

I laughed before I could help it. She slid my exam back across the desk.

“Tomorrow, before school,” she said. “You can take it again.”

“I’ll still be able to hear you.”

“Of course. I’ll be thinking about my car.”

That night I studied at the kitchen table while my little brother did his spelling homework. When he got stuck on *separate*, I kept my mouth shut until he asked.

The next morning, I knew what happened to the cell.

I wrote *It bursts*, and from the front of the room, very softly, came the sound of a car locking.

“Daddy, are we the bad guys?”

I had brought June along because it was Saturday and her mother had a shift. I’d told her we were changing locks.

“What makes you ask?”

“The lady keeps saying please, and you keep pretending you can’t hear.”

I took my hand off the drill.

The lady’s name was Mrs. Alvarez. I knew this because she had told me twice. She was wearing slippers with little rubber strawberries on the toes. On the pavement beside her were three grocery bags and a sewing machine.

“My bread’s still in the oven,” she said.

The property manager had been very clear about not letting anyone back in once I started. He hadn’t said what to do about an oven.

I opened the door.

The kitchen smelled like the inside of a bakery before it opens. Mrs. Alvarez took the loaf out and knocked on its underside. June asked how she knew it was done, so Mrs. Alvarez knocked again and let her listen.

Then she fetched a suitcase from under the bed. She didn’t ask if she could. She packed it while I stood in the kitchen holding the oven mitts.

My phone rang. I let it ring long enough that June looked up at me.

When I answered, the manager asked if the new lock was in.

“Not yet,” I said. “She’s packing. I’m going to wait.”

He said he could send somebody else.

“I know.”

Mrs. Alvarez came out with the suitcase and went back for a photograph from the fridge. Then she unwrapped the bread and tore off a piece for June. She tore one off for me, too.

I nearly said thank you in the cheerful voice I used when a customer offered me coffee. Instead I set the oven mitts down and asked her where she wanted me to carry the sewing machine.

On the morning my mother took off her skin, the air smelled of almond oil and boiled linens. The Tenders had warmed the room so the seams would relax. She sat on the bed with her ankles neatly crossed, hands folded on top of the cardigan she would not need again.

“Will it hurt?” I asked, because the child in me needed it.

“Only for those who watch,” she said, and put my hand to her cheek. “Everything I remember lives in this. What comes out will need to learn the world from scratch. That is a mercy.”

She had chosen no witnesses but me. There is a small slit behind the left ear that the Tenders open with a crescent blade. Oil. A pause. And then the old life loosens, unbuttons, slides. It is an obscene miracle, and intimate, too: the soft as if of a dress puddling around ankles. Beneath was not a younger her, not even a resemblance, but a person with a startled mouth and new scars that did not match our history.

She was given a robe and a handful of names to try on. She picked “Mara” like a peach at market, thumb pressed to the bruise to see if it yielded. She looked at me only long enough to be polite, as you would regard someone kindly making room on a crowded train.

The Tenders wrapped my mother's skin in damp muslin and offered me the customary square—palm-sized, freckled, the three moles at the collarbone that always looked like Orion. I signed the receipt with a hand that would not stop shaking.

At home, I buried that square under the peach tree. In spring the blossoms came so thick the limbs bent. In summer, at the roadside stall, a woman buying fruit counted stems under her breath—one, two, three—before choosing, the same superstitious way my mother had always pretended not to have.

“Try this,” I said, handing her a slice.

Juice ran down her wrist. She laughed at the mess, surprised by her own voice. For a pulse of a second, the world arranged itself into the shape I missed.

“You like peaches?” she asked.

“I do,” I said. “And I know a tree.”

The blue box was the only thing on Sixth Avenue that hadn’t been knocked over.

Clark shouldered the door open, loosened his tie, and walked straight into a coat rack.

“Usually,” said a woman beneath a mushroom-shaped console, “people stop and say it’s bigger on the inside.”

“Usually I have more time.”

He pulled his shirt open. She rolled out from under the console and looked at the shield on his chest.

“Oh, good. Can you hold a moon?”

“For how long?”

The woman grinned. “I like you.”

On the monitor, the alien fleet hung over Metropolis in a perfect circle. At its center was a small gray moon. Clark had seen the ships firing and assumed they were aiming at the city. From here he could see that every beam pointed inward. The ones that had struck the ground had passed straight through a widening crack.

“Egg,” the woman said. “They’re trying to keep it warm. Took a wrong turn looking for a sun.”

Clark listened. Beneath the sirens, beneath the rumble of the collapsing avenue, something was tapping from inside the moon. Three quick taps, a pause, then three more.

“How long?” he asked again.

“Until it hears its mother.”

The woman opened the doors. Beyond them lay a red sun, and curled around it, a creature so large Clark at first mistook its folded wing for a second horizon.

“Not that sun,” he said.

She glanced at him, then down at a dial. “Ah. Right. You hold the door, then.”

She threw a lever. The blue box shuddered, its doors straining against Clark’s hands. Across the impossible distance, the creature lifted its head and answered.

Over Metropolis, a hundred warships went quiet.

Clark would later write that the sound that followed was like thunder. What he remembered, though, was a chick tapping its way out of an egg on his mother’s kitchen table, and how hard it had been not to help.

The first thing the pig did was get my great-grandmother a bicycle.

She was nine. Her father had told her she could have one when pigs flew, and on the morning of November 5, 1909, he found a red Raleigh in the kitchen. The receipt bore his signature. So did the deed relinquishing his authority over his wife’s wages. Apparently he’d said a great many things at supper.

Some countries woke to find their colonies gone. In others, the dead came home. There was a village in France where every man who’d ever said he’d eat his hat had to do so at once. The baker soaked his in soup and lived.

By 2016, most of the big promises had been sorted out. The Atlantic was still lemonade, but only at low tide, and we’d learned to work around it. I had a desk at the Office of Outstanding Conditions. Mostly I helped people claim things their families had forgotten were owed.

One Tuesday a woman brought in a letter from her brother, dated 1902.

“He said he’d come home when pigs flew,” she told me.

She looked about seventy. Her birth certificate put her at a hundred and twenty-three.

I checked the passenger rolls. “He did come home. November sixth. There’s a customs declaration.”

She leaned over my desk. “Where?”

“Fourteen Mercer Street.”

“That was our house before the fire.”

There was a box on the form for whether the condition had been fulfilled. Somebody had ticked it in pencil.

I took her to Mercer Street. A pharmacy stood at number fourteen. We found him sitting by the blood pressure machine, in a good wool coat gone shiny at the elbows. On his lap was a parcel tied with butcher’s string.

“I brought you a bicycle bell,” he said. “I didn’t know if you’d have the bicycle yet.”

Nobody answered. Most of the people who could have answered had gone home.

The graduate student went down. She had one photograph of her mother at that age. The orange bag was in it.

“Have you seen her?” the woman asked. “She’s six.”

Upstairs, a spectrograph was printing the same line over and over. The line was sunlight, but not today’s. The instrument had caught the shadow’s edge, and each successive reading was older than the last. Soon it was recording the sun before there had been an Earth to shine on.

There was no object. There was a hole, and they were falling through it.

Her supervisor called from home. Behind him, she could hear his children arguing over whose turn it was to feed the dog.

“Is there anything we can do?” he asked.

“No,” she said, and hung up so he could go back to his children.

Her mother was still waiting by the door.

“You found her,” she said, and took the bag. It was heavier than she remembered.

When I was six, I asked my mother how she knew when I was lying.

“Your mouth gives you away,” she said.

For a week I told lies with my lips tucked over my teeth. She let me get away with all of them until I claimed I’d fed the dog. The dog, who wore no mask either, had no patience for my experiments.

Everyone else wore white. At funerals, the masks shone with rain. At school, I learned to tell my teachers apart by the way they waited for an answer.

I fell in love with Ruth because she laughed before she decided whether a thing was funny. Sometimes, halfway through, she’d say, “Oh, that’s awful,” and laugh harder.

On our wedding night she sat on the edge of the bathtub and untied the ribbons behind her head.

“Should I close my eyes?” I asked.

“God, no. I’ve been practicing.”

She set the mask beside the soap and smiled.

I’d seen myself smile in mirrors, of course, but I’d always been checking my teeth or trying to get the smile right. Ruth’s smile pulled harder on one side than the other. There was a little fold under her chin that vanished when she swallowed. I stared until the smile went away.

“Was that wrong?” she asked.

“No. Do it again.”

“Well, now I can’t.”

I tucked my lips over my teeth and told her I’d fed the dog.

“What dog?”

I tried to explain, but it wasn’t a funny story, and the more I explained it the less funny it got. By the time I reached the part where my mother found the untouched bowl, Ruth had her forehead against my shoulder. She said, “Oh, that’s awful,” and I put my hand against her cheek, where I could feel the rest of the laugh coming.

In 2014, the year the government began burning people on their seventy-fifth birthdays, Ruth Adler turned thirty-six for the second time.

The first time, her husband had baked her a cake. This time, a girl at the licensing office said, “Moisturize. Seriously.”

Ruth thanked her. She had learned to thank anyone who mistook her age for a personal failing.

She wore a red wig and worked the returns desk at a department store. Her hands were the hardest part to disguise. She told people she’d spent her twenties washing dishes. This was true, although she’d spent them washing her own dishes, in a kitchen with yellow curtains, while her husband read letters to the editor aloud.

On the morning of her real birthday, a boy brought in a pair of slippers.

“Didn’t fit?” Ruth asked.

“They took my granddad yesterday.”

The slippers were worn at the heels. The boy had put them back in their box with the tissue paper folded neatly over them.

“I need a receipt,” Ruth said. Her supervisor was close enough to hear.

The boy began searching his pockets. Ruth waited until her supervisor moved away, then rang up a return on a pair of boots she’d bought the week before. She gave the boy the money and put the slippers in her bag.

“What was his name?” she asked.

“Arthur.”

That evening, Ruth set the slippers beside her front door. She’d spent six months making the apartment look as if nobody old lived there. She’d thrown out the good sugar bowl because it had belonged to her mother. She’d taken down every photograph in which she looked happy.

She went to the hall closet and found the box of pictures. On the back of one, her husband had written *Ruth, thirty-six today*. She put it on the mantel, facing out.

“Other end,” said Ruth.

I turned the shovel around.

“Now you’re holding it like a shovel again,” she said.

Behind the fence, Mr. Petrov bumped gently against the wire. He’d been our dentist. When I was nine, he’d pulled two of my teeth and charged my mother for one.

The whole watch had turned out to see me do it. I’d been on the roster for eleven months, which was a long time to keep getting the shift when nothing happened.

“Did you actually kill those three at the laundromat?” Ruth asked.

“No.”

“The one at the bus stop?”

“No.”

She took a breath. “Then where do they go?”

I could have told another lie, but just then a bicycle bell rang down the street. Mr. Petrov turned so fast his glasses fell off. He shuffled along the fence toward the sound.

“That’s my daughter,” I said. “She’s come to collect him.”

Nobody moved. Through the slats I watched Bea coast past on her pink bike, one foot skimming the pavement. She was getting tall enough to need the seat raised. I’d been meaning to tell her mother.

Ruth looked at me, then at Bea. “You told us she died.”

“She did.”

At the corner Bea stopped and waited for Mr. Petrov, who’d got his sleeve caught. She rang the bell again, impatiently this time. She’d rung it exactly like that when she was alive and I took too long locking the front door.

“There’s a place down by the river,” I said. “They don’t bother anybody there.”

Ruth held out her hand for the shovel. I gave it to her.

Then she picked up Mr. Petrov’s glasses. One lens was cracked. She polished the other on her shirt.

“Go on,” she said, passing them through the wire. “Before she leaves without you.”

The paramedic asked if I knew where I was.

“On the bridge,” I said.

“Good. Do you know your name?”

I did, but for a second I was afraid to say it. The woman in the kitchen had asked me the same thing.

There’d been nothing between the car going through the railing and my sitting at her table. My clothes were dry. A pot on the stove was boiling over, and she let it. She had my mother’s habit of pressing her thumb into her palm when she was trying not to cry.

“Is she still alive?” she asked.

“Who?”

“Your mother.”

I said yes. She sat down across from me and asked what my name was. When I told her, she laughed so hard she had to put her head on the table.

“That’s mine too,” she said.

There was a photograph on the fridge of my parents on their wedding day. My father had a mustache. In our copy he didn’t.

She took the photograph down and showed me the back. In my mother’s handwriting: *For when you forget we were happy.*

“How old were you?” I asked.

“Seven,” she said. “How old were you when Dad died?”

“He hasn’t.”

She put her thumb into her palm again. From somewhere behind me came a man’s voice, telling me to stay with him.

“Wait,” she said. “Tell me something she does now.”

What I thought of was how Mom had started buying pears one at a time because she was tired of throwing the others out. I told her that. I wish I’d told her about the pottery class, or the man she danced with on Thursdays. But the woman closed her eyes like she could see my mother standing in the produce aisle, picking out the one pear she meant to eat.

The first thing Daniel Vale asked me was whether his mother could sit beside him at trial.

“Behind you,” I said. “First row.”

He nodded, as if this were the only part of the arrangement he’d been worried about.

The state said Daniel had killed three women. I knew he hadn’t killed any of them. I also knew the state had the order wrong. They’d put the woman with the yellow kitchen last.

Over six weeks I took apart the prosecution’s case. I got a detective to admit he’d lied. I made their medical examiner say “I don’t know” eleven times, the last time so softly the judge asked him to repeat it.

The jury liked me. More importantly, they trusted that if there were anything left to find, I would find it.

There was one photograph I never asked Daniel about. It showed him leaving his mother’s house at dawn with a long bundle wrapped in a quilt. The quilt had belonged to the second woman. I’d put it in his mother’s donation pile the night before.

When the prosecutor held up the photograph, Daniel turned to me.

“That’s her sewing machine,” he whispered. “I was taking it to get fixed.”

“I know,” I said, and kept my hand on his sleeve until he stopped trying to stand.

The jury acquitted him of two murders. For the third, he got life.

Outside the courtroom, his mother thanked me. She said she knew how hard I’d fought. Then she took a folded slip from her purse.

“I found the repair ticket,” she said. “Daniel said he told you about the machine.”

Around us, reporters were calling my name.

“Yes,” I said.

She folded the ticket again, carefully, along the old crease.

“What did you tell him?”

At seven every morning, Eddie knocked on my door and said, “Vince wants his money.”

For the first year, I showed him the receipt. It had Vince’s signature, the amount, and a coffee ring Eddie himself had left on it. He always studied the coffee ring longest.

“That could be anybody’s,” he’d say.

I tried telling him Vince was dead. This was worse. Eddie would sit down on my front step and ask how, and I’d have to tell him about the wreck without letting him know who’d been in the passenger seat. Then he’d ask if Vince’s dog had anybody.

She did. She was usually standing right behind me, wagging her tail.

One morning I opened the door with two cups of coffee.

“Vince wants his money,” Eddie said.

“I know. Can you help me get the bakery open first?”

He looked at the cups. “Which one’s mine?”

He was good at the bakery. He could carry three sacks of flour at once, but what I really needed him for was the till. Every time somebody came up a little short, he’d make a show of counting their change again and say, “No, look, you had it right.”

At closing I paid him. The first time, he tried to refuse.

“You owe Vince,” he said.

“I owe you for today.”

He thought about that, then folded the bills into his breast pocket.

A few months later his sister brought me a cigar box full of envelopes. On each one, in Eddie’s handwriting, was a date and the words *in case the bakery has a bad day*.

The next morning the mixer gave out. I opened one envelope. There wasn’t any money inside, just a slip of paper.

*You know how to do it by hand. I showed you.*

At seven, I asked him to show me again.

The first person revived in 3016 asked for a cigarette.

This disappointed the historians, who had spent eleven years debating what she might say.

“Or water,” she said, after looking at their faces.

Her name was Ellen Shaw. She had died at thirty-seven, leaving a station wagon, fourteen thousand dollars in medical debt, and a son named Daniel. The station wagon had been scrapped. The debt, through nine centuries of mergers, had become an asset of the hospital that revived her.

Daniel had left a recording.

In it, he was eighty-three. Ellen recognized him by the way he tucked his thumbs into his fists.

“They said you might want to know how it all turned out,” he said. “I taught geography. Married twice, once well.”

He smiled, then glanced to one side. Someone off camera told him he had plenty of time.

“I don’t remember your voice,” he said. “For years I thought I did, but it turned out I was remembering Aunt June doing an impression of you.”

Ellen asked them to stop the recording. The youngest historian reached for the controls. The oldest had already brought her a glass of water.

“Was he happy?” Ellen asked.

“We have his diaries,” said the youngest.

Ellen shook her head. After a while she told them to go on.

On the screen Daniel rubbed his nose. “I had this whole speech about how you’d missed everything. But yesterday I caught myself buying the cereal you wouldn’t let me have. I do that every week. So I guess you haven’t missed quite everything.”

He reached out of frame and brought back a box. He turned it toward the camera so she could see the cartoon tiger.

“Oh, Danny,” Ellen said, in a voice nobody living had ever heard. “I would’ve let you have it on Saturdays.”

The woman behind me put a lime on the conveyor belt.

Nothing separated it from my groceries.

I looked at the cashier. She was turning my cabbage in her hands, searching for a sticker. She had no idea how little time we had.

The lime rolled forward.

At first, there was still a respectable distance between it and my yogurt. A person could have set down a whole loaf of bread in that space. Then the belt jerked, the yogurt tipped, and the lime nestled into the hollow between two cups of vanilla.

The woman behind me was looking at her phone.

I could say something. *Excuse me, is that your lime?* But there was only one lime. Of course it was her lime. The question would insult us both.

Beyond the card reader lay a black plastic divider. The cashier in the next lane was resting her elbow on it.

“Excuse me,” I said.

I turned to the woman. She looked up. I could see myself in her glasses, holding the bar with both hands.

“Sorry,” she said, and plucked out the lime.

I brought the divider down. It made a small, immensely satisfying clack.

For the first time since the cabbage, I breathed.

Then the cashier picked up the bar and slid it back toward the card reader. I watched her weigh the lime, type in a code, and drop it into my bag.

“That’s mine,” the woman said.

“Oh,” said the cashier. “Do you want me to take it off?”

I looked at the woman. She looked at me.

“Put it on mine,” I said.

It cost forty-nine cents. I still think about it.

“Shut the dog up.”

My father said it without looking away from the television. Onscreen, a man in a yellow raincoat stood knee-deep in water, telling us not to drive anywhere.

“He wants to go out,” I said.

“He can want.”

Biscuit had been barking at the kitchen floor for twenty minutes. I offered him a slice of cheese. He took it, set it carefully beside his paw, and went on barking.

That scared me more than the rain.

Our kitchen had once been two rooms. You could still see where the wall had stood, a dark line in the linoleum running from the refrigerator to the back door. Biscuit put one ear against that line. For a second he was quiet, and I heard what he heard.

Three knocks.

“Dad.”

He muted the television. We waited. Three more.

It took both of us to move the refrigerator. Under it was a square of plywood with a finger hole. Dad stared at it.

“Your mother used to keep potatoes down there,” he said.

I knew that voice. He used it whenever he remembered something about her that he hadn’t already told me.

He pulled up the plywood. In the beam of his phone, I saw water, a floating sneaker, and four small fingers hooked over the bottom rung of the ladder.

Dad lay flat and reached in. I held his belt. The girl came up without a sound, her wet hair caught in the zipper of her coat. She lived two doors down. I’d waved to her that morning while she waited for the school bus.

“The little window,” she finally said. “I couldn’t get back through the little window.”

Dad wrapped her in his sweatshirt and went to find his keys. Biscuit picked up the cheese. He laid it in her lap and waited.

The first sentence in Ada’s dreambook was: *By winter, there was nobody left who knew how to close the sea.*

She was four. That morning she had put a raisin in her ear.

I read until the kettle boiled dry. Then I copied the pages by hand, because I couldn’t bear to take the book out of her room. At the publisher’s, I said I’d been working on the novel since before she was born.

The advance paid for two new teeth and a boiler that didn’t need coaxing. I used to stand outside Ada’s room and listen to the pipes knock warm water into her radiator. It was my favorite sound in the house.

By the third book, I had learned to leave some things out: a dog with my dead husband’s limp, a city where all the doors had been painted the yellow of Ada’s bedroom. The reviewers said my work was becoming less personal.

Then Ada learned to read.

She came down one morning with my latest paperback open against her chest.

“Why did you take out the dog?”

I could have asked how she knew. Instead I said, “He made me sad.”

“He made me sad too,” she said. “I wanted him in.”

That night she took her dreambook to bed with her. In the morning it was on the kitchen table, open to a page she’d marked with a cereal-box bookmark.

“Can I read the rest?” I asked.

Ada considered this. Then she climbed into my lap, warm and heavier than I expected.

“I’ll read it,” she said. “You turn the pages when I tell you.”

The first time Daniel fell asleep, his heart stopped for eleven seconds. The second time, the doctor was standing beside the bed with paddles.

There would not be a third experiment, she said.

He went home with a machine that shrieked when his eyelids closed. His daughter, Elsie, decorated it with glow-in-the-dark stars so it wouldn’t look so medical.

For three nights, they played cards. On the fourth, Daniel dealt her a hand and she burst into tears.

“I have school,” she said, as if confessing something terrible.

“Of course you do.”

“I have a spelling test.”

“Then you’d better get some sleep.”

Neither of them moved. Finally he took her upstairs and read to her. He was halfway through a sentence about a rabbit when he realized she was gone.

Not gone, he corrected himself. Asleep.

He read to the end of the chapter anyway.

At dawn he called his brother. They hadn’t spoken since the argument over their mother’s silverware. It had been eight years. Daniel couldn’t remember which of them had wanted it.

“Can you take Elsie to school?” he asked.

His brother arrived wearing two different shoes. He’d dressed in the dark so he wouldn’t wake his wife. Daniel laughed so hard the machine went off.

After the school run, his brother came back. He’d brought groceries, although Daniel hadn’t asked.

“How long?” his brother said.

“Nobody knows.”

His brother unpacked the milk, the apples, the bread. Then he sat down and put both hands flat on the kitchen table.

“What was the rabbit doing?”

Daniel looked at him.

“Elsie said you never told her how the chapter ended.”

“Oh,” Daniel said. “Well. He’d made a terrible mistake.”

The machine went off. His brother reached across the table and took his hand.

“What kind of mistake?” he asked.

The first time I saw my brother, he was on television explaining why the tenants in his building didn’t need heat.

“People are remarkably adaptable,” he said.

I knew he was my brother because he had my face. I knew he was my twin because, when the reporter asked if he’d spent a night in the building himself, he pinched the webbing between his thumb and forefinger. I do that when I’m about to lie.

Our adoption records confirmed it. I bought a card that said WELCOME TO THE FAMILY, then went to look at the building.

On the third floor, a woman named Alma was warming her socks in a toaster. She mistook me for him. Before I could correct her, she asked whether I’d come to take that away, too.

I threw out the card.

Instead, I went to his Rotary lunch. I wore a blue suit and announced that I’d be matching every donation to the tenants’ legal fund. His friends applauded. Three of them took out their checkbooks before dessert.

He denied everything, of course. So I stopped promising things in his name. I just showed up where he’d been and listened. His secretary gave me copies of letters she’d been told to shred. His oldest friend told me about a second building. People had been waiting years for that face to shut up long enough to hear them.

By February, the heat was on and he was due in court.

I went back to see Alma. My brother was on her landing, holding a box with a brand-new space heater inside.

He stared at me. His free hand went to the webbing between his thumb and forefinger.

“I can explain,” he said.

Alma opened her door. She looked from him to me.

“Good,” she said. “I’ve got the kettle on.”

She let him in first.

My first convert was a woman who wanted her soup hot.

I told her about the god of small mercies, who had chosen me on the strength of a kindness I couldn’t remember doing. She listened, tasted her soup, and said, “All right. I believe.”

A little warmth came into my hands. I put them around her bowl.

By winter I had enough believers to thaw the village well. By spring I could put my palm against a broken leg and feel the bone draw together. People came from the capital to see me. I learned to wait until they knelt.

Then the river rose.

I stood on the bridge and held the water back while the village filed past. With every person who reached the far bank, it grew harder to keep my arms up. I thought at first they were losing faith in me.

“Run,” I shouted to the last of them, a girl carrying a sack that wriggled.

She stopped to let a wet nose out of the sack. Behind her, in the village, somebody was ringing the school bell.

“Is that your teacher?” I asked.

She shook her head. “She can’t climb.”

I could hold the bridge or go back. I couldn’t do both. I looked across at all the people who believed in my god and tried to think of something to tell them that would make them believe harder.

The woman whose soup I’d warmed handed her shoes to the girl and stepped into the water. A man followed her. He took her hand. Another took his, and they came past me, one by one, without asking for a blessing.

As the woman passed, she touched my elbow. Her hand was warm.

“Go on,” she said. “I’ve got it.”

I let one arm down. The water stayed where it was.

The dead slept in trees, which was why nobody in our village chopped wood after dark. In daylight a soul could slip from one branch to another. At night you might split it straight down the middle.

My father had been the village carpenter. When he died, his apprentice, Ana, planted him in a pear tree behind the shop.

She chose badly. He’d hated pears.

“He liked the blossoms,” she said when I told her so. “He used to bring a branch inside and put it in the glue pot.”

I had never been in his shop in spring. Spring was lambing season, and by the time the lambs could be left alone, the hills were warm and I could always think of somewhere else to go.

That first winter I sat beneath the pear tree every night. There were things I’d meant to tell him, ordinary things that had become urgent through being left unsaid. I’d found his good knife. I’d known the dog was sleeping on his bed. I’d let her.

But the tree never moved except in the wind.

In March, Ana came out of the shop carrying a saw. I stood up so quickly I knocked over my stool.

“Just the one branch,” she said. It was the lowest, the one that caught her apron every time she passed.

I held it steady while she cut. Inside the shop she put it in an old glue pot and poured in water from the kettle. For three days I came by to see whether we’d killed it.

On the fourth, a blossom opened.

Ana was fitting a drawer. I sat on the bench and told her about the dog. She laughed; apparently my father had been lifting her onto the bed himself, once she got too old to jump.

Every other Thursday, Len came in for another tally mark. He paid in exact change and brought a sandwich he’d cut in half. He always claimed he’d made too much, though in eleven years I never saw him make that mistake with a sandwich I didn’t like.

I figured he was counting the weeks since his wife died. Then one Thursday he called from a bus station three towns over and asked if I could fit him in early.

“Why? Did a week get away from you?”

“No,” he said. “I found the Espositos.”

He came straight from the bus, carrying a shoebox. Inside were letters, some in envelopes so old the glue had turned brown.
