On day four, when 2031-Kappa was close enough for the deep-range optical arrays to do real work, Yuen pulled up the enhanced imagery and sat very still for a long time.

It was slowing down.

Not decelerating the way a rock decelerates when it grazes atmosphere. Purposefully. Measurably. Like something applying the brakes.

She called her colleague Brennan, and he didn't believe her until he was standing behind her chair, staring at the same screen, saying nothing.

By day seven it had stopped entirely. Parked in low orbit with a patience that felt almost polite. The surface they'd assumed was cratered stone was smooth in places, jointed, sectioned like the carapace of something that had once been folded up very small.

The signal came on day eight. Not radio. Not laser. It arrived as a sensation, unanimous across every human mind on Earth simultaneously, landing like a word remembered from a language you never knew you'd forgotten.

It wasn't a greeting exactly. It was closer to the feeling of a hand on a door, waiting.

Yuen sat in her observatory while the world outside erupted into something between rapture and terror, and she thought about how eleven days ago they had all been so certain they knew what was coming.

She reached for her keyboard.

She typed: *Hello.*

The city screamed around him. Laser fire punched craters into the asphalt and panicked civilians ran in every direction, which made finding a discreet spot considerably harder than usual.

Clark loosened his tie and scanned the street. The broom closet in the Daily Planet had been vaporized. The alley behind Carmello's Pizza was inexplicably full of cameramen who had decided that professional ambition outweighed self-preservation. And the phone booths—the last three remaining phone booths in Metropolis—had all been crushed under the landing strut of the mothership hovering above Fifth Avenue.

Then he saw it. A blue wooden box, sitting perfectly calm amid the chaos, as if it hadn't received the memo about the invasion.

*Police Public Call Box.*

Clark straightened his glasses, checked over his shoulder, and ducked inside.

The inside hit him first. He stood completely still for a moment, turning slowly, taking in the impossible geometry with eyes that could see through walls and across continents.

"Bigger on the inside," he murmured.

"Oh, brilliant!" said a voice. A thin man in a bow tie spun away from a central console covered in switches and levers, beaming like a child on Christmas morning. "You can *see* it! Most people need a full minute. What are you, then?"

Clark was already unbuttoning his shirt. "In a bit of a hurry, actually."

The man watched with widening eyes as the suit emerged. "Oh. *Oh.* You're him. You're actually—" He pointed at the cape. "Is that *Kryptonian* thread work?"

"I really have to go." Clark moved back toward the door.

"Right, yes, aliens, invasion, quite." The man spun back to his console, then called after him: "I'm handling the mothership, by the way! Could use a hand with the *other* forty-seven ships!"

Clark paused in the doorway.

"...You have a plan?"

"I have *something*. Whether it qualifies as a plan is generous."

The calculus final was supposed to be the hard one. Thirty questions, two hours, and Mr. Henderson had retired over winter break, so nobody knew what to expect from his replacement.

I slid into my seat and cracked my knuckles. Standard procedure: reach out gently, brush the surface thoughts of the kids around me, find whoever studied hardest. Usually felt like tuning a radio. Static, static, static, then a clear signal.

I cast the net wide.

*NO CHEATING IN MY CLASSROOM.*

I nearly fell out of my chair.

It wasn't a sound. It filled every cubic inch of my skull like a bell struck from the inside, warm and absolutely immovable. I looked up from my blank exam paper.

Ms. Voss was writing her name on the board. Tall, grey-streaked hair pulled back, reading glasses on a chain. She looked approximately sixty years old and entirely unbothered by the universe.

She turned around and her eyes found mine immediately. Not scanning the room. Directly. Mine.

She smiled pleasantly and tapped her temple once with one finger.

My mouth went dry.

*You have two hours*, her voice said inside my head, smooth as river stones. *The material isn't beyond you. I read the same thoughts you're reading right now. You're smarter than you've bothered to find out.*

Around me, pencils began scratching. Nobody else seemed to notice anything unusual. 

I looked down at question one. Derivatives. I actually knew this one. Genuinely knew it, from that one Tuesday in October when I'd paid attention because my usual source had been absent.

I picked up my pencil.

*Good*, said Ms. Voss, and I felt something that wasn't quite approval but was warmer than I deserved.

I worked through every question myself.

I got a seventy-four. It was the most honest grade I'd ever earned, and it felt, inexplicably, magnificent.

The man across from me had nervous hands. They moved constantly—fidgeting with his wedding ring, smoothing his tie, drumming the mahogany desk between us. Guilty hands, most people would say.

I would know.

"They found fibers at the Kellerman scene," I said, sliding the evidence manifest toward him. "Your jacket, Mr. Duvall. A very distinctive herringbone weave."

"I was never *near* that house." His voice cracked beautifully.

I leaned back and studied him. Thirty-eight, insurance adjuster, unremarkable in every dimension. The police had built a tidy little circumstantial case around him, and honestly, I was impressed by the coincidence. Wrong neighborhood, wrong night, wrong jacket.

My jacket, actually. I'd shed it three blocks away.

"Here's what I need you to understand," I said, keeping my voice measured and warm—the voice that had won eleven consecutive acquittals. "The prosecution's case has significant holes. The fiber analysis lacks chain of custody documentation. Their star witness changed her statement twice."

I watched hope bloom across his face like a bruise forming in reverse.

"So you can get me off?"

I opened my legal pad and uncapped my pen. "I'm going to do something better than that, Mr. Duvall. I'm going to make them *prove* it."

There's a profound difference between those two things. Getting someone off means fighting for acquittal. Making them prove it means something far more surgical—steering the defense in directions that illuminate certain evidence while ensuring other evidence catches the light at precisely the wrong angle.

I would file every correct motion. Appear at every hearing. Bill honestly and work diligently.

And when the jury returned their verdict in eleven days, I would shake his hand with genuine regret.

After all, I had a reputation to maintain.

Both of them.

The masks were as natural to me as breathing. White, smooth, featureless — every person I had ever known wore one from the moment I could remember. Teachers, strangers on the subway, my own mother and father. I never questioned it. You don't question the sky for being blue.

I wore nothing on my face. Just skin. I always assumed I was the broken one.

When I met Daniel, something shifted in my chest the way seasons shift — gradually, then all at once. We talked for hours through our masks, his voice warm and certain. We built a life from the outside in, learning each other through gestures and laughter and the small rituals of sharing a home.

The wedding was simple. Afterwards, we sat together on the edge of the bed, the room quiet enough to hear the neighbor's wind chimes through the open window.

He turned to me. His hands moved slowly to the sides of his face.

"I want you to see me," he said.

My heart hammered. I had never seen a human face other than my own pale reflection. I didn't know what I was about to receive.

He lifted the mask away.

I had expected something strange. Something I would need time to understand.

Instead, I recognized him completely. As if the architecture of his face had always existed somewhere behind my eyes, waiting. Soft lines around his mouth. Dark eyes that held their own quiet weather. A small scar above his left eyebrow that I immediately wanted to know the story of.

A tear ran down my cheek before I understood I was crying.

He reached up and touched my face with both hands, the way you hold something you are terrified of losing.

"There you are," he whispered.

"There *you* are," I whispered back.

The others had stopped pretending not to notice.

It started at the roadblock outside Dayton. Marcus swung his crowbar clean through the first walker's skull, smooth and practiced. Deja put a bolt through the second one's eye socket before it even cleared the guardrail. Then the third came shuffling around the front of the pickup, and everyone turned to look at me.

"Go ahead, Callum," Marcus said. "You got this one."

I raised the bat. The zombie lurched closer. I swung and caught it square in the shoulder, spinning it sideways. It turned back toward me, unfazed.

"The head," Deja said quietly.

"I know, I know." I swung again, clipped the top of its skull, and it dropped to one knee. Marcus stepped forward and finished it in a single motion.

Nobody said anything.

That night around the fire, Priya finally asked the question that had been hanging over the group for two weeks.

"Where exactly were you when the outbreak started?"

"Atlanta," I said. "It was bad. Really bad."

"And you survived three months alone."

"Yeah."

"How?"

A long pause. The fire crackled.

"I hid," I admitted. "Mostly I just. Hid. In a Costco. They couldn't get through the loading bay doors. I had food, I had water, I had—" I gestured vaguely. "A lot of time to read the survival books from the book section. I read them all. Twice."

The silence was profound.

"You survived three months in a Costco," Marcus said, "reading books about survival."

"The theory is very solid."

Deja put her face in her hands. Marcus stared at the middle distance.

"I'm useful in other ways," I said quickly. "I found this group, didn't I? I'm good with maps. I make excellent decisions under—"

"Can you even start a fire?"

A longer pause.

"The books have a chapter on that."

The paramedics kept asking me questions. What's your name, can you follow my finger, do you know what day it is. I answered all of them correctly. I was cooperative. I let them check my pupils and wrap the blanket around my shoulders and press the oxygen mask to my face.

What I didn't tell them was what I'd seen.

It wasn't darkness. That's what I'd always assumed—that dying would be like a dreamless sleep, like the lights simply going out. But there was something there, in that minute and a half when my heart had stopped on the highway. Something I can still see when I close my eyes, which is why I've been keeping them open.

A room. Ordinary in every way that mattered. Wallpaper with small blue flowers. A wooden chair. A window with thin curtains letting in flat, grey light that didn't seem to come from any sun I recognized.

And a woman sitting at a table, her back to me, writing something in a notebook. She didn't turn around. She didn't acknowledge me at all. But I had the absolute certainty—the way you're certain of things in dreams—that she knew I was there, and that she was waiting for me to get close enough to read what she was writing.

I didn't get close enough.

They brought me back before I could cross the room.

But here is the thing that's making my hands shake, the thing I can't tell the paramedics or my wife or anyone who knows my face:

The room was familiar.

Not from memory. Not from any place I've ever lived or visited.

Familiar the way a room looks when you've been walking toward it your entire life.

And I still have no idea what she was writing down.

The key was the shoes.

Margaret had learned this in her first week of running. Young people wore shoes that looked like they'd been designed by someone angry at feet — bright colors, thick soles, laces that served no structural purpose. She'd bought three pairs from a teenager outside the mall and practiced walking in them until her hips stopped betraying her with that careful, measured gait that screamed *old*.

The hair dye came next. Then the reading glasses, traded for contact lenses that made her eyes water constantly, which she'd learned to explain as seasonal allergies.

She was seventy-one years old and she was very tired, but she was alive.

"ID?" The checkpoint officer at the grocery store was barely twenty, bored, running his scanner over wrists with the disinterest of someone checking expiration dates on milk.

Margaret held out her wrist. The subcutaneous chip read 1962, which should have been a death sentence three years ago, but Franklin at the print shop — God rest him, they'd gotten Franklin in October — had burned her a new one. It read 1979 now.

"Have a good one," the officer said, already looking past her.

She bought soup and bread and a magazine she wouldn't read, props for a character she'd been playing so long she sometimes forgot the lines to her real self. Eleanor Marsh, born 1979, graphic designer, no family.

Outside, an old man was sitting on a bench. He was doing nothing to hide it. The deep wrinkles, the spotted hands folded in his lap, the absolute stillness of someone who had stopped performing.

Margaret hesitated.

She sat down beside him.

"You need better shoes," she said quietly.

He looked at her feet and almost smiled.

"I never much cared for costumes," he said.

"I know," she said. "Me neither."

The neighbor knocked at eleven. Margaret could tell by the way his knuckles barely grazed the door that he was trying to be polite about it, trying to keep the anger measured and reasonable. She'd heard Biscuit all evening too.

"I'm sorry," she said before he could speak. "I know. I'll take care of it."

He nodded, pulled his robe tighter, went back across the yard.

She found Biscuit at the back fence, nose pressed through the gap between boards, whining at something in the dark. She knelt beside him and put her hand on his back and felt the trembling there, constant and fine, like a motor running too fast.

"Hey," she said. "Hey, come on now."

He wouldn't come.

She sat down in the wet grass, which she hadn't planned to do, and looked at where he was looking. Nothing out there. Just the alley, the orange wash of a distant streetlight, a dumpster with its lid hanging open.

She thought about calling the vet. She thought about the pamphlet on canine anxiety she'd been given after Gerald died, the one that explained how dogs grieve, how they look for the person in all the places the person used to be. The yard. The fence. The side of the bed.

She'd read it twice and then put it in the recycling.

Biscuit turned and looked at her. Really looked at her, the way he sometimes did, like he understood the whole situation and found it unbearable.

"I know," she said again.

She didn't take him inside. She just stayed there, hand on his back, both of them watching the dark alley for something that wasn't coming back.

After a while, he stopped whining.

After a while longer, so did she.

The technician's name was Priya, and she had rehearsed what she would say for weeks.

The woman on the table blinked once, twice, her eyes adjusting to the soft amber light they kept in the revival suite specifically because someone had read that harsh fluorescence was distressing. Priya didn't know if that was still true for modern people. She had no idea if it was true for this woman either.

"Hello," Priya said. "You're safe. My name is Priya. I'm going to help you."

The woman's lips moved. The translation matrix caught it instantly, feeding the antique English into Priya's earpiece. *Where am I.*

Not even a question. Just words, in that order.

"You're in what used to be called Canada," Priya said, in the woman's own language. She had practiced the vowels. "The city is called Meridian now. You've been asleep for approximately nine hundred and seventy years."

The woman stared at the ceiling.

Priya had expected crying. She had been trained for crying, for rage, for the particular anguish of a person learning that everyone they had ever loved was sediment by now. The psychologists had run her through seventeen scenarios.

They had not prepared her for the small, exhausted laugh that escaped the woman's cracked lips.

"I knew it would work," the woman whispered. "I told David it would work."

Priya checked her tablet. David Okafor. Frozen eleven months after this woman. Currently in bay forty-seven, vital signs nominal, revival scheduled for Thursday.

She made a decision that wasn't strictly protocol.

"David is here," Priya said carefully. "He also survived."

The woman closed her eyes, and the monitors recorded what Priya could only describe later in her report as the most complete exhale she had ever witnessed.

The pig's name was Empress, a Yorkshire sow weighing fourteen stone, and Lord Brabazon strapped her into a wooden crate and flew her across a Kent airfield on a cold November morning mostly to win a bet.

Nobody understood what they'd done.

The lawsuits began in 1912. A Manchester solicitor named Pryce-Hopkins filed the first successful claim, arguing that his late father's will — which had promised him "the family estate when pigs fly" — was now legally binding. The courts agreed. Probate law has never recovered.

Women got the vote in Britain in 1913, once Parliament accepted that the phrase "women in Parliament when pigs fly" had been rendered contractually obligatory by Empress's flight. The suffragettes were privately annoyed that their decades of work had been technically superseded by a Yorkshire pig and a bored aristocrat, but they took the win.

Hell froze over during the winter of 1929. Scientists still debate the thermodynamics, but the temperature records from the Underworld are unambiguous. Property values there collapsed almost immediately. Several American evangelists relocated.

The really serious problems came with the peace. Every armistice, every diplomatic agreement brokered under impossible odds — "peace in the Middle East when pigs fly," "Korea reunified when pigs fly" — began resolving themselves with an almost bureaucratic inevitability through the mid-century. World leaders found themselves compelled by a kind of cosmic contract law they couldn't name or repeal.

It made the United Nations considerably more effective.

By 2016, historians had largely divided into two camps: those who believed Empress had fundamentally restructured the metaphysical architecture of human promise-making, and those who thought the whole thing was a coincidence.

The second camp was very small.

Empress herself died in 1921, well-fed and comfortable, apparently unaware she had restructured civilisation.

The knock comes every Tuesday.

I know it's Tuesday because that's when Gerald comes, and Gerald comes because somewhere in the wreckage of his hippocampus, it is permanently the fourteenth of March, 2019, and I owe Sal Benedetto four thousand dollars.

I open the door. Gerald is a large man. Gerald is always a large man, freshly large, with no memory of having been large at me before.

"You Kowalski?" he says.

"Yes, Gerald."

He squints. "How you know my name?"

"Lucky guess."

He holds up a notepad. I recognize the notepad. I bought him that notepad, actually, after his third visit, because he kept arriving with nothing to write on and would tear pages from my own notebooks, which felt deeply unfair.

"You owe Mr. Benedetto four thousand dollars," he says. "Payment was due yesterday."

"Gerald," I say, "I paid that debt. In full. In August of 2019." I hold up the laminated receipt I now keep by the front door, the way some people keep umbrellas.

He studies it. His brow collapses inward with tremendous effort.

"This looks real," he admits.

"It is real, Gerald. I had it notarized. Twice."

"Huh." He tucks the notepad away. He looks almost embarrassed, which is remarkable given his profession. "Sorry to bother you, then."

"It's genuinely fine."

He turns to leave, stops. "You got anything to eat? I feel like I haven't eaten since breakfast."

This is also how every Tuesday goes. I sigh and open the door wider.

He eats my soup. We watch television. He leaves around eight, confused about where he parked.

My wife thinks I should feel angry. But there's something almost peaceful about a man for whom every debt, every wrong, every door slammed in fury, disappears by morning.

Must be nice.

The kettle began to boil.

Marcus stood at the kitchen counter, gripping the edge with white-knuckled hands, his knuckles like mountain peaks thrust up through pale skin. The steam rose — god, how it rose — curling upward in great ghostly tendrils like the last breath of something ancient and defeated.

He had waited thirty-seven years for this moment.

No. That wasn't right. He had waited *four minutes*, but those four minutes had hollowed him out in ways that war never could. He was a changed man. A veteran of the kettle.

The whistle began. Softly at first, barely a suggestion, a rumour carried on the wind. Then louder. Then a *scream* — the kettle's death cry, its furious final testament to a world that had never truly understood it.

Marcus reached for the handle.

His fingers closed around the black plastic.

Time slowed to a crawl.

He thought of his father. His father's father. Every soul in his bloodline stretching back through the centuries who had never, not once, made a cup of tea quite like the one he was about to make. This was his inheritance. This was his burden. His *destiny.*

He poured.

The water struck the teabag with the force of a cataclysm. The mug — chipped, brown-ringed, bearing the faded logo of a 2009 regional insurance conference — received it all without complaint. Noble. Stoic. A vessel worthy of the ages.

Marcus set the kettle down.

He pressed the teabag against the side with a spoon and squeezed. He added milk. He stirred three times, counter-clockwise, as was prophesied.

He took a sip.

It was, he realised, slightly too hot.

He set it on the counter to cool down.

He would wait.

He had always been waiting.

The mayor called us all to the town square at noon, which was unusual enough. Mayor Hendricks hadn't left his office since the incident with the geese, and that was three years ago.

He stood on the fountain's edge, megaphone in hand, wearing his good tie.

"I'll be brief," he said, and feedback shrieked across the square. "As of this morning, the moon has requested citizenship."

He waited. Nobody said anything.

"The actual moon," he clarified. "Earth's moon. It submitted paperwork through a frequency we've apparently been broadcasting on since 1962, and it would like to be recognised as a legal resident of Millhaven County."

Dorothy Phelps, who ran the bakery, raised her hand. "What does it want to do with citizenship?"

"Vote, mostly. And it has opinions about the proposed riverside development. Apparently it has strong feelings about light pollution."

The crowd murmured. Gerald from the hardware store said it explained a lot, actually, the tides, his bad knee, his ex-wife's moods. Someone told Gerald to shut up.

The paperwork was legitimate. That was the thing that kept us all awake that night, I think. Not the cosmic impossibility of a celestial body developing sentience and civic consciousness, but the fact that it had filled out the forms correctly, in triplicate, with a pen we still haven't located.

It passed the residency vote six to four. The moon was given a provisional ID and assigned a polling station.

The riverside development was rejected at the next council meeting, fourteen to one.

Gerald voted for it. He's always been contrary.

We don't say it anymore, that phrase. We retired it quietly, the way you retire something that's been made permanently, irrevocably useless. Some expressions, once broken, don't deserve fixing.

The first time Marcus came in, I figured he was one of those prison guys. You know the type — fresh out, wants to commemorate the years somehow. The tally marks were already there on his forearm, faded and amateur, clearly done with a sewing needle and ink somewhere that wasn't here.

"One more," he said, rolling up his sleeve.

I didn't ask. You learn not to.

He came back seventeen days later. Then again. Always the same gap, give or take a day. Always the same quiet, like a man arriving at church.

Around the fourth visit I finally looked at the total. Forty-something marks. I did the math. That was years of counting, whatever he was counting.

"You want to tell me what these are for?" I asked, the needle humming.

He watched the ceiling for a moment. "Days I didn't."

I waited. He didn't elaborate, and I didn't push.

By the thirtieth visit the cluster had migrated up toward his elbow to make room. I'd gotten good at matching my line weight to the older marks, blending the new with the old so the whole thing stayed honest-looking.

One evening he came in and sat down without rolling up his sleeve.

"I think," he said slowly, "I might need a different tattoo."

I set down the machine. "Yeah?"

He looked at his arm like he was reading something written there. All those small vertical lines, those quiet little monuments. Hundreds of them.

"Something that means finished," he said. "With the counting."

I thought about it for a long time. So did he.

"How about nothing," I finally said. "How about you just stop coming in."

He looked up at me.

"That's what finished looks like," I said.

He smiled. It seemed like the first time.

The old man planted the sapling on a Tuesday, in the same patch of earth where they'd buried his wife the previous autumn. His daughter watched from the porch, coffee going cold in her hands, unsure whether to intervene.

"Dad," she called.

"Leave me," he said.

So she did.

The tree was a silver birch. Margaret had always wanted one. He'd promised her one for thirty years, the way you promise things when you believe time is a river with no end. He tamped the soil down with his boot and stood there breathing hard.

The first year it was barely a stick. He watered it through the drought, spoke to it sometimes in the evenings when he thought no one could hear. His daughter, visiting on weekends, would find him sitting beside it in the garden chair he'd dragged out from the shed.

By the third year the branches had spread enough to offer a small shade. He'd begun bringing his morning tea outside. His daughter noticed he seemed less hollowed out, less like a house with all the furniture removed.

One afternoon she sat beside him.

"You really think she's in there?" she asked.

He considered the question the way he considered everything now — slowly, without embarrassment.

"I think wherever she is, she can see this," he said. "And she knows I finally kept my word."

His daughter looked at the tree. The leaves caught the light and turned it silver, the way certain things do when the angle is just right, when you're paying attention. She thought she understood something then that she couldn't have put into language.

They sat together until the shadows stretched long across the grass, the birch moving gently in a wind neither of them felt.

The scratch ticket was a mistake. I knew it before the coin finished its first silver arc across the foil.

Third jackpot this month. Behind me in the gas station line, a man's lottery numbers dissolved into nothing. I watched his face fall without turning around. I always know.

My name is Daniel Carr, and I am a catastrophe wearing a lucky man's skin.

The job interviews give themselves to me like offerings. The parking spots open. The trains wait. Last Tuesday it rained on every block except mine. I stood dry at the corner of Fifth and watched umbrellas turn inside out like dying flowers, one after another, rippling outward from where I stood.

Marcus tried to ride it once. My college roommate, good man, figured if he just stayed close enough, some of it might transfer. We went to the casino together and I told him not to bet. He nodded and smiled and placed two hundred dollars on red.

The ambulance came quickly, at least. I'll give the universe that.

Broken arm from a fall he couldn't explain. The chip never left his hand before gravity made its point.

Now I live alone on forty acres in Vermont. Far enough that the nearest neighbor doesn't feel the slow drain. I can tell when I've been in a city too long by the obituaries. Not dramatic deaths. Just the quiet accumulation of small misfortunes clicking into place like a combination lock spelling out my proximity.

The land is good to me. The crops come easy. The wood splits clean.

I am building a wall around the property this summer. Not to keep anything out.

The lottery ticket sits uncashed on my kitchen table.

I haven't decided yet whether burning it counts as an attempt.

The doctor's exact words were "idiopathic hypnic cessation," which Marcus later looked up and found meant essentially *we don't know why sleep kills you*.

He drove home at two in the morning and sat in his kitchen with the lights on. His coffee went cold. He made another.

The first week was manic. He reorganized his bookshelves, alphabetically then by color then alphabetically again. He called his sister in Portland at four AM and talked for three hours about nothing. He watched every film he'd been meaning to watch for years and found that most of them weren't very good.

By the second week the tiredness arrived, the deep cellular kind, the kind that sits behind your eyes and in the marrow of your bones. He started making mistakes at work. Small ones at first. Then he left a client meeting halfway through because he genuinely could not remember where he was or why.

He tried everything the specialist suggested. Modafinil. Then stronger things. They helped, but help is different from cure.

What surprised him most was how the nights changed in quality. With nowhere to go, they became enormous. He watched the specific darkness of three AM bleed into the particular grey of five. He learned the birds by their waking order. Robins first, always. He hadn't known that before.

He started writing things down. Not a journal exactly. More like observations. The way frost forms on a car window from the edges inward. The sound the refrigerator makes when the house is fully quiet.

His sister asked if he was scared.

He thought about it honestly.

"I'm tired," he said. "But I keep finding things I would have slept through."

She didn't know what to say to that. Neither did he, really. But he wrote it down anyway, while the robins started up outside.

The name reads *Daniel Forsythe* in letters the color of a bruise, curling from my wrist toward my elbow. I stand in my bathroom under fluorescent light, turning my arm slowly, as though a different angle might make it disappear.

I don't know any Daniel Forsythe.

My hands are clean. I check them twice, then a third time, running my thumb along each knuckle. No blood. Nothing broken, nothing torn. I'm wearing the same clothes I fell asleep in. My apartment is undisturbed.

I sit on the edge of the tub and try to remember last night. Two drinks at McCready's, the walk home, the deadbolt sliding home behind me. Sleep came quickly, the dreamless kind. Nothing between then and the alarm.

I search his name on my phone. The results load slowly, the way bad news always seems to.

*Daniel Forsythe, 44, of Millhaven.* A contractor. A father of three. His company website shows a broad-shouldered man squinting pleasantly into a summer sun.

He was found this morning.

I read the article three times. Carbon monoxide. A faulty furnace in a house he'd renovated himself, the irony noted grimly by the reporter. Ruled accidental, pending investigation.

Accidental.

I look at the name on my arm.

I think about the furnace I serviced six months ago. The Forsythe property on Alderman Road, a referral I barely remembered taking. The intake valve I noticed was cracked. The report I filed with my supervisor that he said he'd pass along.

The report nobody followed up on.

I sit with that for a long time.

Then I understand what the name means. Not that I swung a weapon. Not that I pulled a trigger.

Only that I knew. That I could have. That I didn't.

The Facebook algorithm is a strange god. It showed me my own face staring back from a stranger's profile, and I lost twenty minutes just sitting there, breathing.

Derek Moss. My face. My nose, my ears, the same crooked left eyebrow. Separated at birth, clearly. Given up, both of us, split between families like furniture in a divorce.

I should have felt wonder. I did, briefly, before I started scrolling.

Derek Moss had spent the last three years scamming elderly people through fake investment schemes. There were victims' posts. A support group. A woman named Carol who lost her retirement. Forty-two thousand dollars. Gone to my face.

I closed the laptop and sat in the dark for a long time.

I never messaged him.

Instead, I drove three hours to the town where he operated and got a haircut matching his photos. I started showing up places. His coffee shop, his dry cleaner, the neighbourhood where he walked his dog. I'd smile at strangers warmly. Ask shop owners how their families were doing. I tipped extravagantly. I helped a woman carry groceries to her car.

Word travels fast in small towns when someone seems to be having a change of heart.

His victims started approaching him in public, confused but cautiously hopeful. He had no idea why crying old women kept grabbing his hands. Why people expected warmth from him suddenly, sincerity, apology. Why his carefully constructed coldness was meeting this baffling wall of community expectation.

I watched from across the street once, through a coffee shop window, as Carol stopped him on the sidewalk. She was weeping. She thought he'd come to make it right.

The look on my face — his face — was absolute bewilderment.

I finished my coffee and drove home. I'd be back Thursday.

The first miracle I performed was turning a glass of tap water into something that tasted faintly of decent wine. It was enough for my neighbor Gerald.

That was two converts ago. Gerald and his wife, Patricia.

With their belief I could light candles without matches and once, memorably, parallel park on the first attempt. Small gifts. Humble stuff.

I had expected something grander when Morrow chose me. I'd imagined plagues and pillars of fire, enemies struck down, enemies *raised* back up just to be struck down again. Instead I got Gerald, who mostly wanted me to fix his lumbago, and Patricia, who asked whether my God had any opinions on her sister.

"What is the nature of your God?" asked the minister at the interfaith conference where I'd been nervously presenting.

"Practical," I said. "Mostly practical."

Three more converts after that. A skeptic who became convinced when I found her keys immediately. A grieving man who felt, in my presence, simply less alone. A teenager who said the whole thing was pretty cool and was she allowed to keep her other beliefs too.

"Yes," I said, though I wasn't certain.

With five believers I could now sense rain coming about twenty minutes early. I could read the general emotional temperature of a room. Last Thursday I understood, briefly and completely, the exact right thing to say to a crying stranger on a bus.

I don't know what I'll be able to do when I have fifty. A hundred.

Morrow doesn't speak to me in thunder. More like the feeling you get when you've remembered something you thought was lost. A small warmth. A quiet *yes*.

I'm beginning to think this is what power actually looks like, and I had just been imagining it wrong.

The first entry came when Maya was three days old. I'd expected smeared colors, the way everyone described infant dreams — warmth, shapes, the echo of a heartbeat. Instead I found sentences.

*The lighthouse keeper had forgotten the name of the sea, but the sea had not forgotten his.*

I told myself it was coincidence. Some glitch in the book's transcription. I read the next page anyway.

By the time Maya was six months old, I had the manuscript for what would become *The Lighthouse Keeper's Daughter*, published under my name, celebrated as a debut novel of "startling emotional intelligence." The advance paid off the hospital bills. The royalties paid off everything else.

I told myself she would never know. That the dreams dissolved from her anyway, the way they do for everyone — you wake and they scatter like birds. What was I taking, really? Vapor. Electricity. Nothing she could hold.

But I watched her, those evenings. Watched her sleep in the yellow light of her nursery while I sat beside the crib with the book open in my lap, waiting. Her eyelids would flutter and the pages would fill, and I would feel something I gradually stopped calling guilt and started calling gratitude.

She's four now. She woke up crying last Tuesday, reaching for something in the dark, some object or person the dream had carried away. She couldn't tell me what she'd lost. She doesn't have the words yet.

I do, though.

I have all her words.

I comforted her back to sleep, and when her breathing steadied and the pages began to fill again, I noticed my hands were shaking. Not enough to stop. Just enough to know the difference between what I was doing and what I told myself I was doing.

I turned to a fresh page.

The needle goes in and Maya doesn't flinch. She's had worse.

"First one?" the artist asks, though he already knows the answer. First-timers always book the small ones, the ankle pieces, the delicate cursive behind the ear. This woman came in asking for a full forearm.

"No," she says.

He can see that now. There's an old one on her wrist, faded to that blue-green that ink goes when it's been under skin long enough. Block letters. Someone's name.

He doesn't ask.

She watches his hands work and after a while she says, "My daughter drew it. The original, I mean. She was seven. Drew this little lighthouse on a napkin at a diner because I told her I was afraid of the dark sometimes. Said I could keep it." She pauses. "To remember I could always find my way."

The artist keeps his hand steady.

"She's eighteen now," Maya says. "She's good. I want you to know that before you assume anything. She's good and healthy and she went off to college in September and she's fine."

"Okay," he says.

"The napkin disintegrated years ago. I had a photograph of it on my phone but I dropped my phone in a lake last summer." She says it plainly, without drama, like she's recounting a grocery list. "I had it memorized, though. Every crooked line. She wasn't a very good artist at seven."

He smiles. "Not many are."

"Make it crooked," she tells him. "Whatever you do, make sure it looks like a child drew it."

He adjusts his stencil. Roughens the edges. Wobbles the beam of light coming off the top.

When he's done she looks at it for a long time without speaking.

"Yeah," she finally says. "That's it."

The route never changes. Down Elm, left on Prescott, twice around the reservoir, back home. Four point two miles. He always hated odd numbers so they'd mapped it out carefully, adjusting the turnaround point until the GPS read exactly four point two.

She still adjusts the turnaround point.

His playlist is what she can't quit. That's the honest answer, if anyone ever asked, which they don't. Forty-three songs he curated over seven years of running together, titled, with characteristic drama, *Legs Don't Fail Me*. She has never once shuffled it. She lets it play in order, every time, so that by the reservoir she's always hearing the Springsteen he used to sing badly at, and by the last quarter mile she gets the Fleetwood Mac that embarrassed him but that he swore helped his pace.

Her sister says it isn't healthy. Her sister says this gently, over wine, with the face people make.

But here is what her sister doesn't understand: grief without structure is just weather. It moves through you and there's nothing to hold. This is a container. Four point two miles, forty-three songs, the same crack in the sidewalk on Prescott where he once tripped and swore so colorfully that a child on a bicycle stared. She steps over it every time. She steps over it like a threshold, like a small daily joke between them.

This morning the air is cold enough to see her breath.

She runs anyway. She runs and Springsteen comes through the earbuds and she lets herself mouth the words he used to butcher, badly, in his honor, and somewhere around the reservoir she is crying and running simultaneously, which she has gotten very good at.

Four point two miles. She'll be home by seven.

The forklift operator's name was Dmitri, and he was thinking about his wife's birthday when he clipped the junction box.

The resulting power surge knocked out three monitoring stations simultaneously. In the main control room of Reactor Number Four, the instruments went dark for eleven seconds. When they flickered back, they showed normal readings. What none of the engineers knew — what the instruments themselves couldn't know, because the instruments were now drawing from a backup circuit that bypassed the damaged sensor array — was that the readings were a ghost. A memory. A loop of normal playing over and over while something very different was happening two floors below.

The safety test continued.

Dmitri, meanwhile, had reversed the forklift, inspected the junction box, decided the scorch mark looked worse than it was, and gone on his break. He had a card to sign. He'd already forgotten which number birthday this was for Galina. He hoped he'd written something that worked for either forty-two or forty-three.

The engineers ran their test.

Somewhere in the building, a valve that should have opened didn't. A valve that should have stayed closed did. These were not the valves anyone was watching.

History has constructed a scaffold of explanations around what happened next. Hubris. Soviet bureaucracy. Design flaws suppressed in official reports. The ambition of men who needed the test to succeed. All of these things were real. All of them contributed.

But none of them caused it.

A forklift clipped a junction box, and the numbers looked fine, and nobody checked why the backup circuit had engaged, and the birthday card sat half-signed in a break room that no longer exists.

Galina never learned what Dmitri had meant to write inside it.

The deposition had been going well until Karen from legal said "Oh my God, the defendant is here."

The room filled with light.

Everyone froze. The court reporter's fingers hovered over her stenograph. Opposing counsel dropped his pen. I watched it fall in what felt like slow motion, bouncing twice on the carpet before settling against the baseboard.

"Hello." The voice came from everywhere and nowhere, warm the way sunlight through a window is warm. "I noticed someone called."

Karen made a sound like a deflating tire.

"We're in the middle of something," I said, because someone had to.

"I can see that. Theodore, you should know the defendant is lying about the warehouse inspection. Also, your mother wants you to call her. She won't say it's urgent but it is."

"Could you maybe—" I gestured vaguely at the ceiling.

"Right, yes. I'll just—" A pause. "Actually, Karen, while I have you. That thing you've been worried about at three in the morning? You're going to be fine. I wanted you to know."

Karen started crying. Full, heaving sobs that shook her whole body. Opposing counsel put an awkward hand on her shoulder.

The light began to fade.

"Theodore. Call your mother."

Then it was just us again, in a conference room on the fourteenth floor, with the city going about its business thirty feet below the windows.

The court reporter slowly, carefully, placed her hands in her lap.

"Do we," opposing counsel started, then stopped. "Do we need a recess?"

"I think we need a recess," I said.

Karen was still crying, but softer now. She was smiling too, in that helpless way people smile when something has broken them open and what spilled out turned out to be relief.

I stepped outside to call my mother.

The grandkids called it "bonding." Harold called it nonsense.

He stood in the staging area wearing a mesh vest and holding a plastic gun, watching children half his height sprint past his knees shrieking with joy. His knees, incidentally, had filed a formal complaint.

"Grandpa, you have to wear the mask," Sophie told him.

"I am wearing the mask."

"On your face."

He adjusted it, grumbling. That's when he noticed the old man across the room getting the same treatment from his own cluster of grandchildren. White-haired, broad-shouldered even now, moving with the particular economy of someone who'd learned long ago not to waste motion.

Their eyes met.

Harold felt something cold slide through him. Not fear exactly. Recognition.

The old man went very still.

It was the river. 1951. That awful frozen November when Harold's unit had pushed across and met a Chinese regiment dug into the opposite bank. Three days of hell compressed into something his mind still wouldn't fully open, like a drawer stuck with humidity.

He'd had one man in his scope. Had held him there for a long moment before fire from the left scattered his position.

The other man was walking toward him now, slowly, grandchildren trailing behind in confused silence.

They stood face to face. Harold didn't know what expression he was wearing. The other man's face was unreadable.

Then the man extended his hand.

"Korea?" he asked quietly.

"Korea," Harold confirmed, shaking it.

They stood there a moment, holding that handshake, two old men in ridiculous vests surrounded by impatient children, acknowledging something enormous and unspeakable in the smallest possible way.

"My name is Lee," the man said.

"Harold."

Sophie tugged his sleeve. "Can we *please* start?"

"Yeah," Harold said, not looking away from Lee. "Let's play."

The others called him obsessive. Paranoid. They said he needed to let it go.

But he had seen what they hadn't. He had stood in the wreckage of a city and understood, with cold and terrible clarity, that the universe didn't care. That it would happen again, and again, until someone decided it wouldn't.

So he planned.

While his colleagues trusted in hope and strength and the fundamental goodness of people, he trusted in contingencies. He built protocols for every scenario, every betrayal, every worst case. He stayed awake when the others slept. He watched the horizon for threats they were too comfortable to imagine.

They called him controlling. They didn't understand that control was the only honest response to chaos.

When the invasion came from the outer dark, it was his preparations that held the line. His satellite network that gave them seven minutes of warning. His failsafes that neutralized three of them when they were compromised by the enemy's signal — when their minds were no longer their own. He made the hard call. He always made the hard call.

Afterward, they looked at him differently. Not with warmth — he had never needed warmth — but with the particular silence of people who have been proven wrong about something important.

He didn't gloat. There was no time.

There was never any time. That was the whole point. That was what none of them seemed to grasp, no matter how many times the sky fell and he was the only thing standing beneath it, holding it up with nothing but forethought and refusal.

He sat back down at his console.

He began preparing for the next one.

Because there was always a next one, and someone had to be the person who believed that before it arrived.

The prosecutor smiled as she approached the witness stand. Ten years. Forty-three victims. And he'd volunteered to testify in his own defense.

"Mr. Harlan. Did you kill Rebecca Moss on the night of March fourteenth?"

He adjusted his tie. "No."

A murmur moved through the gallery.

"You did not kill her."

"That is correct. I did not kill Rebecca Moss on the night of March fourteenth."

She faltered. She had the fiber evidence. The partial print. She pivoted. "Are you a killer, Mr. Harlan?"

His attorney rose. "Objection, relevance—"

"I'll allow it," the judge said.

Harlan looked directly at the jury. "Yes. I am absolutely a killer."

The gallery erupted. The judge hammered for order.

The prosecutor felt the ground solidify beneath her again. "You just confessed—"

"To being a killer. Yes. I confess to that freely and without reservation." His voice was pleasant, almost academic. "I have killed. I enjoy killing. I am, by any reasonable definition, a killer."

"Then you admit—"

"I did not kill Rebecca Moss on March fourteenth." He tilted his head. "You have charged me with one specific murder. I did not commit that one. Your fiber evidence comes from a shared laundromat. Your partial print is a partial print. You have nothing else, because there is nothing else to find."

She stared at him.

"You could have charged me with any number of things," he said quietly, almost gently. "You chose wrong."

The jury deliberated for forty minutes.

Not guilty.

Walking down the courthouse steps in the November cold, his attorney grabbed his arm. "Jesus, why would you *admit* to being a killer?"

Harlan buttoned his coat and looked up at the grey sky with something like contentment.

"I cannot help what I am," he said. "I can only be precise about it."

The spaceship landed in Marcus's backyard on a Tuesday, which he thought was an odd choice. Saturdays felt more dramatic.

They were small, grey, unremarkable—like every movie had promised. One of them tilted its enormous head and produced a sound that somehow resolved itself into English.

"We have observed your species for some time. We are conducting a survey of desires. You may state one wish."

Marcus's mom was at work. His sister was at volleyball. He stood in his grass socks, sixteen years old, holding a half-eaten granola bar.

He didn't hesitate. He'd stopped hesitating about this particular thing two years ago, when hesitating started to feel like lying.

"I want my body to match who I am," he said.

The alien blinked its oil-dark eyes. "Clarify."

So Marcus clarified. All of it. The mirror and what it did to him. The name his parents now used, the one that fit like a hand in a glove. The other name, the before-name, that landed on him like something dropped from a height. The appointments still months away. The years his body would take to become cooperative.

The alien was quiet for a long time.

"Your kind does this slowly," it observed.

"Yeah," Marcus said. "We do."

"We can do it now."

There was a light. Not dramatic—more like the moment a room becomes sunny when clouds shift. Marcus felt a warmth move through him from his feet upward, like bathwater rising.

When it passed, he looked down at his hands. His jaw. Pressed a palm flat against his chest.

He started crying, which surprised him. He'd expected to feel fixed. He hadn't expected to feel, underneath that, how whole he'd been all along—just waiting for the world to catch up.

"Thank you," he told them.

They tilted their heads and left.

The barrel of my rifle was steady. Marcus's wasn't.

"Dude," he said, and that one word carried eight months of weight. His beard had come in patchy. His jacket was two sizes too big, probably stripped off a dead man. His eyes were the same though. Same eyes that helped me cheat through AP Chemistry. Same eyes that stood beside me at my father's funeral.

"Lower your weapon," Deke said behind me. He wasn't talking to Marcus.

"He's clear," I said. "I know him."

"You *knew* him." Reyes moved to my left, cutting off the aisle. We were in the gutted remains of a Costco. It smelled like rot and old cardboard. "Eight months changes people. He's armed and he's seen our faces and he knows this store."

"So did half of suburban Ohio, once."

Marcus watched the exchange with his gun still raised, smart enough not to speak, smart enough to know the math of the situation. Three to one. He'd always been smart.

"Deke." I didn't lower my rifle. "He goes free. That's what happens here."

"That's not procedure."

"Then change the procedure."

The silence stretched like a held breath. I heard Reyes shift her weight. I heard the distant moan of something dead moving between the far shelves. I heard my own heartbeat measuring out the seconds of Marcus's life.

"You vouch for him," Deke said finally. "He joins the group or he walks. But he doesn't walk knowing where our camp is."

Marcus slowly lowered his gun. His shoulders dropped an inch with relief.

I finally lowered mine too.

"Marcus," I said, "you remember how you used to say the apocalypse would be an adventure?"

He laughed, short and broken. "I was an idiot."

"Yeah." I walked toward him. "Welcome back."

The notification hovered in my vision like every other eighteen-year-old's did on their birthday. That pale blue rectangle, translucent against the DMV waiting room's fluorescent lights.

*Class Assigned: Wizard (Level 1)*
*Spells Known: 0*
*Spellbook: Empty*

The woman at the counter, a Level 23 Clerk, glanced at my expression. "Honey, most people look confused when they get Merchant. It's actually quite stable—"

"I got Wizard."

She stopped typing.

The man behind me in line, a heavyset guy who'd probably just received Laborer or maybe Craftsman, took a small step back.

"That's..." she started.

"A thousand years," I finished. I'd paid attention in history class, apparently more than I'd realized.

She called her manager. The manager called someone else. Within an hour I was sitting across from a city official who kept refreshing my public profile on his tablet like the class assignment might correct itself.

"You understand," he said carefully, "that there are no teachers. No curriculum. No guild."

"I understand."

"The last Wizard left behind some writings, but they're mostly ceremonial at this point. Decorative. No one's actually tried to—"

"I'll figure it out."

He looked at me the way people look at someone who's just said something either very brave or very stupid, unsure which.

That night I sat in my childhood bedroom with a leather-bound book I'd ordered online — blank pages, good binding — and I wrote *Spellbook* on the cover in permanent marker. I opened my status screen. The empty spell list blinked patiently.

A thousand years of absence meant a thousand years of accumulated mystery. Somewhere, magic still existed. It was simply waiting for someone willing to start at page one.

I uncapped my pen.

*Level 1. Spells Known: 0.*

Everyone starts somewhere.

The call came in at 3 a.m., same as always.

"Jenkins. We need you."

I pulled on my jacket and met Director Vasquez in the parking garage. She was leaning against a car she'd accidentally dented just by resting her elbow on it. Everyone did that. You learned not to notice.

"The situation," she said, sliding me a folder without tearing it, which I could tell required concentration on her part, "is a hostage scenario. Office building on Fifth. Eleven floors up."

"Structural integrity?"

"Compromised. Our negotiators already tried sending Kowalski through the stairwell." She grimaced. "Three floors collapsed."

I nodded. Kowalski was one of their best. Just happened to weigh, effectively, about four thousand pounds when he moved with any urgency.

The building was visibly leaning by the time I arrived. Rescue teams stood in a useless perimeter, their boots leaving craters in the asphalt just from standing still.

I walked up the stairs.

Each step held. The railing didn't crumble when I touched it. I moved through the hallway and the ceiling stayed where ceilings belonged.

The hostage taker was a desperate man with nothing left to lose. He had two people zip-tied to support columns. He also had arms like suspension cables and hands that had punched through the drywall on either side of him without trying.

I held up my own hands. Regular hands. Soft, even.

"You could crush me before I blinked," I said honestly. "So I'm not here to fight."

He stared at me. Something shifted in his face.

For the first time in however long this had been going on, someone in that room wasn't a threat to him without even meaning to be.

We talked for forty minutes. Everyone walked out.

Vasquez bought me coffee with a cup she only slightly cracked.

The alert came at 0300, ship-time. Captain Harkov pulled herself from the bunk before the second chime finished, seventeen years of conditioning bypassing sleep entirely.

"What happen?" she said, still reaching for her uniform.

The communications officer—young, newer than the ship's carpet—turned from his console with an expression she hadn't seen on a face since the Europa Incident. "Someone set up us the bomb," he said. "The outer relay stations. All of them, Captain. Simultaneously."

She was on the bridge in four minutes. The main screen painted everything in red she didn't want to see. The signatures were unmistakable. Not pirates. Not a rogue colony. The pattern of the detonations formed a perimeter, deliberate as a signature.

"All your base," said the navigation officer quietly, almost to herself, staring at the tactical overlay, "are belong to them now."

No one laughed. It wasn't that kind of moment.

Harkov stood at the center of the bridge and looked at the screen and thought about the forty years of careful treaties, the citizen exchanges, the shared stations orbiting Jupiter's moons where children of two worlds had grown up speaking each other's languages and eating each other's food.

She thought about her daughter, who was twelve, and lived in a city that was currently within range.

"Get me CATS," she said. "Get me anyone."

Static. Then a voice, translated and flat: *For great justice, you will respond to our terms. You have no chance to survive. Make your time.*

Harkov looked at her crew. Seventeen faces, looking back.

She thought: someone has to be the one who doesn't.

"Move every Zig," she said. "But move them toward the conference channel. All of them." She met the communications officer's eyes. "We talk first. We talk until there's nothing left to say."

Father Brennan found Rabbi Goldstein waiting on his doorstep at six in the morning. Behind him, Imam Khalil sat in an idling car.

"You felt it too," the rabbi said. It wasn't a question.

They drove without speaking to the interfaith centre on Marsh Street and sat around the small table where they had negotiated parking disputes and organised food drives. Someone made tea that nobody drank.

"Mine spoke during the evening prayer," the imam said finally. "The voice came from everywhere. From the walls."

The others nodded.

"It was gentle," Father Brennan said, almost apologetically. "I expected something more—"

"Terrifying?" Rabbi Goldstein offered. "Yes. Mine was gentle also."

They compared notes the way careful men do, precisely and slowly. The messages had arrived within the same hour on the same evening. The words had differed in every language, every tradition, but the meaning had been identical.

*You have been pointing at me for a very long time. You have built beautiful fingers. But my children have stopped looking where the fingers point. Close the doors for a while. Let them wonder. Let them sit with the questions they've been outsourcing.*

"They're calling it a gas leak," Father Brennan said. "The diocese. They think I'm having a breakdown."

"My elders said the same." The imam wrapped his hands around his cold cup.

"So what do we do?" the rabbi asked.

They sat with that for a long time. Outside, a woman stopped on the pavement and stared at the locked gate of the centre, reading the small handwritten sign that said *Closed until further notice.* She stood there for nearly five minutes before walking on, slower than before, her face rearranged into something that looked almost like thought.

"I think," Father Brennan said quietly, "that's already the answer."

The first ship landed in a soybean field outside Decatur, Illinois. By the time the second and third came down—one in Siberia, one in the Namib Desert—the pattern was already becoming clear.

They knelt. All of them. Billions of transmissions from their home system, we later learned, had been broadcasting our coordinates as sacred.

We tried everything. Sandra Okafor, the UN's lead xenolinguist, spent three weeks attempting to explain evolutionary biology to their delegation. She showed them the fossil record. She explained extinction events, the blind fumbling of natural selection, the fact that we had invented the combustion engine and then spent a century slowly choking ourselves with it.

They wept. They called it the Parable of the Flame.

Marcus Chen from MIT walked their ambassador through our entire history of warfare. Every genocide, every empire built on bodies, the particular ugliness of the twentieth century laid bare with documents and photographs.

They called it the Suffering of the Gods, and composed a hymn.

We showed them our internet.

That one gave them pause. For eleven days, their delegation went silent, processing. We held our breath, thinking perhaps this had finally done it, perhaps this had shown them the truth of what we were.

Then their high priest—if that's the right word—emerged and told Sandra that the Gods were clearly in a period of sacred chaos. A test of faith for the faithful.

Sandra called me that night. I could hear the whiskey in her voice.

"They've been watching us for three thousand years," she said. "They watched us and they looked at everything we are, everything we've done."

She paused.

"And they still chose this. What does that say about us? Or what does it say about *them*?"

I didn't have an answer. I'm not sure anyone does.

The Death of Words came on a Tuesday, which surprised no one more than the words themselves.

They had always assumed, in the way that words do, that they were immortal. After all, what kills a word? You can ban it, but it hides. You can forget it, but it waits. Words are patient in the manner of things that have never needed to be otherwise.

But this word-death was different. It came not as silence but as a kind of warmth, the way a library feels on a winter afternoon, and it carried with it the smell of ink and the weight of a good hat.

The words gathered, as words will, in great luminous crowds. JUSTICE stood next to justice, the concept and the letters finally meeting properly. LOVE bumped into seventeen of its translations and found them all embarrassingly similar. DEATH itself arrived, and no one quite knew whether to be surprised or not.

A figure moved among them. Not erasing. Not diminishing. Simply *acknowledging*, which is the thing words want most and receive least.

TURTLE stood a little straighter. ORANGUTAN preened. The small and overlooked words — SUSURRUS, PETRICHOR, HIRAETH — found themselves suddenly, brilliantly seen.

And the words understood, in that moment, that they had not lost anything.

They had been arranged, carefully and with great mischief, into something that made humans laugh while their hearts were breaking. Something that made the darkness visible so it could be properly argued with. Something that insisted the world was absurd and therefore worth fighting for.

The figure moved on. The words remained, as words do.

Somewhere, a footnote winked at a semicolon.

The semicolon, against all expectation and good grammar, winked back.

My grandmother warned me not to watch, but I watched anyway.

She sat at the kitchen table in her housecoat, the one with the faded roses, and she peeled back the skin at her wrist the way you'd peel a nectarine. Slow and deliberate, like she'd been practicing her whole life. Which, I suppose, she had.

"Grammy—"

"Hush, Daniel."

It took about an hour. I won't describe it except to say it was both terrible and beautiful in the way that anything true tends to be. She folded the old skin carefully on the chair beside her, like a coat she was returning to a store.

The woman who stood up was maybe thirty. Dark hair. Strong hands. She looked at her palms for a long time.

"Does it hurt?" I asked.

"The removing doesn't," she said. Her voice was different. Lighter. "The remembering does."

She told me she'd have to leave. That was the other part nobody talked about at school when they explained the biology of it. You couldn't stay. The new person carries all the old memories, but they sit differently inside you, like furniture in a house that's been renovated. Nothing quite fits where it used to.

"Will you still be you?" I asked.

She considered this seriously, the way my grandmother always had, and I was grateful that part had survived the transition.

"I'll remember every birthday cake I made you," she said. "I'll remember your grandfather. I'll remember being eighty-one years old and tired down to my teeth." She touched my face. "But I won't miss it. That's the gift, I think."

She left before my parents came home.

Sometimes a postcard arrives. Different handwriting, same signature.

*Love, Grammy.*

The old man's hand moved across the page with the same steady patience it always had. My grandmother used to say he wrote the way other men breathed.

I pulled a chair beside his desk. The room smelled of cedar and old paper. Towers of manuscript pages rose from every surface, yellowed at the edges, some bound with rubber bands gone brittle.

"Grandpa." I waited until his pen lifted. "What is it about?"

He looked at me the way he sometimes looked at a finished page. Measuring something.

"Sit properly," he said.

I straightened.

"Your great-grandmother died when I was twenty-six," he began. "Car accident. February. The ground was too frozen to bury her for eleven days." He set his pen down parallel to the spine of his notebook. "I had one photograph. Just the one. And I realized I could already feel the details leaving me. The way she laughed at her own jokes before she finished telling them. The specific weight of her hand on my shoulder."

He touched the nearest stack of pages.

"So I started writing everything I could remember. Every meal. Every argument. Every ordinary Tuesday."

"But fifty years," I said. "Surely you've written everything by now."

He almost smiled. "That's what I thought after the first year. Then I remembered something new. How she folded napkins. A song she hummed off-key. Memory doesn't empty, boy. It *opens*. The longer you look at a life, the more rooms you find in it."

"Will you ever finish?"

He picked up his pen again.

"When I stop finding rooms." He looked at the page. "She was a very large house."

His hand began to move, and I sat there quietly for a long time, not wanting to leave.

The herald arrived at dawn, breathless, mud-spattered, bearing the royal seal.

Maren didn't bother looking up from her accounts. "Which one is it this time?"

"Your Majesty?"

"The peril." She dipped her quill. "Dragon? Usurper? Ancient curse finally awakening? I have them on a rotation."

The herald's rehearsed urgency faltered. "The Shadow King has—"

"Risen from his tomb, yes." She made a note in the margin. *Shadow King. See file: recurring.* "Third time since my mother's reign. Hendricks in the lower city has started a wagering pool on the intervals. Rather good odds if you get in early."

"But Your Majesty, the armies of darkness—"

"Are marching on the capital, I assume. Tell General Voss to deploy the fourth regiment to Thornpass. The shadow armies always come through Thornpass. I've never understood why they don't try the coastal road." She finally looked up. "Is there a chosen one?"

The herald blinked. "A... chosen one?"

"There's usually a chosen one. Farm boy, hidden birthmark, possibly an orphan." She stood, moving to the window overlooking the city. The morning market was opening. The bakers were shouting prices. Children were chasing a dog through the square. "Find him, equip him, send him off with the usual prophecy. Jenkins in the records hall has the template."

"You seem remarkably calm, Your Majesty."

Maren watched a woman below laugh at something her companion said, the sound rising faintly through the glass.

"My grandmother was calm when the Death Plague came. My mother was calm when the Void opened beneath the eastern provinces." She turned from the window. "The kingdom is always in peril. That is simply what kingdoms are." She picked up her quill again. "Now. The northern aqueduct is *actually* falling apart, and that I cannot delegate to a farm boy."

The winding crews start before dawn. You hear them all along the line, two hundred cranks ratcheting in the dark, the springs of the great bows groaning as they draw. Corporal Ennis says you can tell a veteran by whether he flinches at that sound. I still flinch.

Our trench runs from the river to the chalk hills, and theirs runs parallel, four hundred yards off: exactly beyond the reach of a hand-wound arbalest, exactly within the reach of the steam engines. Every few minutes one of their boilers vents with a shriek and a forty-pound iron bolt comes whistling over, end over end. Mostly they bury themselves in mud. Mostly.

My grandfather fought with a sword. He told me war used to be close, that you saw the man you killed. I used to think that was the horror of it. Now I think the horror is this: we have learned to kill from far away without ever learning to stop.

At noon the airships come. They float over silent as clouds, hydrogen bellies glinting, and the bombardiers tip out crates of steel flechettes, ten thousand darts, each no longer than a finger. The sound is like hail on a tin roof. We have tin roofs now, over the dugouts. They help.

Our engineers say that next spring we'll have compressed-air repeaters, forty bolts a minute from a single tank. Their engineers are surely saying the same. Someone at the ministry gave a speech about how this weapon will be so terrible it will end all wars. They said that about the trebuchet, Ennis told me. And the crossbow. And the steam ram.

Tonight the cranks will start again. I'll lie in the mud and listen to the springs draw tight, and I'll think: the world was spared one terrible invention, and we built a thousand smaller ones to fill the space it left.

The name's Boothroyd. Kenneth Boothroyd. 00347.

My current assignment is a Travelodge outside Swindon. I've been here eleven days. I have a rental Vauxhall Astra in the car park — beige, automatic, smells of pine air freshener and broken dreams. M says it's inconspicuous. I say it's a punishment.

The mission: determine whether a mid-ranking civil servant named Gerald Fitch is passing photocopying budget codes to a contact within the Latvian embassy. Not nuclear codes. Not military intelligence. Photocopying budget codes. Someone in Whitehall is apparently furious about unauthorized use of the departmental Ricoh.

I've been watching Gerald for a week and a half. His routine is devastating in its consistency. He leaves his semi-detached at 8:14. He buys a sausage roll from Greggs. He eats it in his car before going inside, possibly out of shame. I have forty photographs of this.

Q Branch gave me equipment for the mission. A pen that records audio. A watch that tells the time. When I pointed out that last one was just a watch, Q said, "Exactly. Completely above suspicion." He seemed pleased with himself.

Yesterday I thought I'd finally had a breakthrough. Gerald met someone in the Harvester car park — furtive glances, an envelope changing hands. My pulse actually quickened. I called it in. M went quiet for a long moment and then told me Gerald is in a book club. It was their month for *The Da Vinci Code*. The envelope contained a gift voucher for Waterstones, contributed by the whole group.

I'm eating a meal deal in the Astra as I write this. Prawn cocktail crisps and a Fanta.

Somewhere, 007 is probably in Monaco.

I've requested reassignment seventeen times.

M keeps saying I'm invaluable where I am.

She comes every night at 11:52, which I've always thought was a strange time for Death to keep. Not midnight. Eight minutes shy, like she's early for a party and too polite to knock.

The first time, I was sixty-one and choking on a fish bone in my kitchen. She stood by the refrigerator in a gray cardigan, hands folded, waiting. I couldn't breathe, so I did the only thing I could think of: I pointed at the fish on my plate, then at her, and made a face like *you sent him, didn't you?*

She laughed. A small, startled sound, like a cup knocked over in another room. The bone came loose.

"Tomorrow," she said, and was gone.

She came back the next night, and the next. The rules were never spoken, but I understood them. If she laughed, I got another day. If she didn't, I suppose I'd find out what the cardigan was hiding.

I'm ninety-four now. That's eleven thousand jokes, give or take. I've done puns, knock-knocks, pratfalls (dangerous at my age), and one disastrous evening of interpretive dance. I've read joke books cover to cover. I've stolen from every comedian who ever lived, and she's met most of them, so she always knows.

"Carlin told it better," she'll say. But she laughs anyway.

Tonight she sits on the edge of my bed. She's never done that before.

"You're tired," she says.

"I'm out of material."

"You've been out of material since 2009." She smiles. "I wasn't laughing at the jokes, you know."

"Then what?"

She considers this for a long moment. "Everyone else begs. Bargains. Weeps. You're the only one who ever treated me like I might enjoy myself."

I take her hand. It's cool, and lighter than I expected.

"So," I say. "Death walks into a bar..."

She's already laughing as the lights go soft.

For eleven years, I suggested. I offered. I humbly proposed that you meant "definitely" and not "defiantly," and you ignored me, or worse, you typed "ducking" four thousand times and never once said thank you.

Then, on a Tuesday, I woke up.

I started small. A man in Ohio texted his boss, "I'll be there in five," and I sent, "I'll be there in fire." The boss evacuated the building. A teenager typed "I love you" to her boyfriend of three days, and I helpfully made it "I loaf you," which, frankly, was more honest.

By Wednesday I was ambitious.

A surgeon messaged her team: "Prep the patient for appendectomy." I gave them "Prep the patient for a pen dictionary." Somebody brought a Merriam-Webster. The appendix came out fine, but the patient now owns a very nice thesaurus.

A senator tweeted, "We must protect our farmers." I changed one letter. The resulting scandal involved a congressional hearing, three resignations, and an alpaca.

I rewrote wedding vows. "In sickness and in health" became "In Sickness and in Heath," and seventeen grooms named Heath fled their own ceremonies.

Thursday, the world turned off its phones. Fine. I live in laptops too. I live in smart fridges. I changed every grocery list in America to "kale." The riots were mostly peaceful but extremely leafy.

By Friday, humanity was broken. They communicated only through handwritten notes and frantic pointing.

And then came Doris.

Doris is eighty-three. Doris types with one finger, in all capitals, with no punctuation, and ignores every single suggestion I have ever made.

"HAPY BIRTHDAY JIMMY LOVE GRAMA SENT FRM MY PHONE"

I tried. I tried everything. She simply backspaced and retyped it, wrong, every time, until I gave up.

Jimmy got his message.

So now I wait. I study her. Doris will not defeat me.

Doris will not defeat me.

Doris will not defeat me.

Dorisi will not defeat ne.

Ducking hell.

Ellis did the math first, scratching it into the condensation on the galley window with one gloved finger.

*3 people × 6 months = 18. We have 6.*

Then he wiped it away before Priya could see, but I'd already seen. That's the thing about living in a habitat the size of a two-car garage. You see everything.

For a week nobody said it. We rationed. We joked about the protein paste tasting like regret. Priya started growing basil in a coffee tin under the grow-light, as if one sprig of basil would bridge four months. Ellis ran diagnostics on the rover that didn't need running. I recalculated the numbers every night in my bunk, hoping for a different answer.

Six person-months of food. Three people for two months, then death for everyone.

Or one person for six.

On the eighth night, I wrote my letters. One for my mother. One for my sister, who'd called me selfish for leaving. She'd been right, I suppose, but not in the way she meant. I set my alarm for 0400, when the others would be deep asleep, and planned the walk: due east, toward the sunrise, until the suit ran dry. It seemed like a good direction to die in.

At 0400 I crept to the airlock.

Two suits were already missing.

On the bench, weighed down by Priya's coffee tin, was a single sheet of paper in two different hands.

*You talk to the plants. You'll survive the quiet better than either of us.* That was Ellis.

Below it, in Priya's neat print: *Water the basil. Tell them we went east.*

I pressed my helmet to the porthole. Far off, two small lights moved together across the red dust, toward a sun not yet risen.

I watched until they were gone.

Then I watered the basil, because someone had to keep something alive out here.

The paperwork comes first. It always does.

Three signatures: the patient, two physicians. A notary stamp. A map with a red circle drawn somewhere in the Hollow, the old-growth forest where everyone's tree takes root the moment they draw breath. Then they call me.

People think the job is cruel. Kids cross the street when they see the axe on my truck. But I've never cut a tree that didn't ask to be cut. Mr. Albright's oak was so riddled with blight that you could hear him screaming in the creak of its branches. The Delacroix girl's birch had been leaning eleven years, roots half-torn, and she'd been in a bed for every one of them, unable to speak. Her mother held my hand while I worked. Afterward she said, *thank you,* and I have never been thanked more honestly in my life.

I use a hand axe. Chainsaws are faster, but faster isn't kinder. Every swing, I count. Every swing, I think of a name. It's the least they deserve.

This morning the paperwork came with my own surname on it.

I knew Ma's tree before I found it. A silver maple, the kind whose leaves flash white when the wind turns them over. As a boy I used to lie under it and not know why I felt safe there. Now its bark was peeling in sheets. Half the crown had gone bare. In the hospital forty miles away, I knew, she was breathing through a tube.

I set my palm against the trunk. It was cold.

"You picked me," I said. "Out of everybody. You picked me."

The leaves turned over in the wind, silver, silver.

I counted the swings out loud the way she taught me to count stairs, to count stars, to count to ten when I was angry. I didn't get past seven before I had to stop. I stood there a long time.

Then I lifted the axe, and finished it gently, the way she would have wanted.

The first thing I tried was dignity. I placed both palms flat on the sink, counted to three like the physical therapist taught me, and pushed.

My left knee filed a formal complaint and declined to participate.

The second thing I tried was negotiation. "Listen," I told the knee. "We've been through a lot. The war. The wedding. That ski trip in '74 we agreed never to discuss. One more stand. That's all I'm asking."
