The knee said nothing, which is how I knew it was serious.

My phone, of course, was on the kitchen counter, where I had left it so it wouldn't fall in. Margaret used to laugh at that. "Who's calling you, Harold? The Pope?" Six years she's been gone, and I still put the phone where she'd tease me about it.

Biscuit wandered in around noon. She sat in the doorway and regarded me with the open contempt cats reserve for anything that isn't feeding them.

"Go get help," I said.

She licked her own back foot, which I took as a no.

By two o'clock I had read the shampoo bottle eleven times. I now know more about argan oil than any man should. I sang every verse of "Danny Boy" I could remember, then invented several more. Biscuit left during the third invented verse. Critics.

Around four, the light through the frosted window turned the color of weak tea, and I got quiet. It occurred to me that this was, more or less, what old age was going to be: a small room, a stubborn body, and a lot of time to think about who wasn't there.

Then the front door opened.

"Grandpa? You didn't answer your phone, so Mom made me—"

Emily stopped in the hallway. Seventeen, all elbows and eyeliner, staring at me.

"Don't," I said.

She was already laughing. So was I.

She helped me up anyway. She's got Margaret's grip.

The first time I counted my future lives, there were eleven of them, strung ahead of me like lanterns on a dark road. A baker in Lagos. A hydroponics engineer on the Ceres shelf. A girl who would die at nine but laugh more in those years than I have in thirty-four.

The second time, there were still eleven. But they were wrong.

The baker was thinner. The engineer slept alone in a bunk built for two and didn't know why she kept leaving room. The nine-year-old didn't laugh at all.

It took me weeks to name what was missing: *her*. In every life I had glimpsed, there had been someone. A sister, a husband, a stranger on a train who stayed. Different faces, same eyes, grey as wet slate. She was the thread, and somewhere behind me I had cut it.

So I went backward.

I stood in a Roman kiln-yard and watched a potter cough out his lungs. Fine. I walked the paper-choked halls of a Ming tax office. Fine. I sat in a Kentish tavern in 1720 with a drunk who'd been me and listened to him curse the king. Fine, fine, fine.

Then Brittany, 1643. A fisherman named Yann, mending nets by lamplight.

I remembered him. He had been my first visit, before I understood the rules, when I still thought this was a gift. That night a storm was coming, and I had felt his death sitting in my own chest like a stone. I had leaned close, the way you do with sleepers, and whispered: *Don't go out tonight.*

He hadn't. He lived to sixty-one.

And on the rocks below the harbor, a girl with slate-grey eyes clung to the wreck of her father's boat until dawn, waiting for a stranger in a skiff who never came.

I stand behind Yann now. The wind is rising. His lamp gutters.

He has fourteen good years left if I stay quiet.

I lean in close.

*Go,* I tell him. *She's waiting.*

On the night my father died, I stopped for gas at a Shell station off Route 9. The hospital was ninety minutes from my apartment, and the fuel light had been on since Thursday.

It was 2:14 a.m. I know because I kept checking the time, as if it might eventually tell me something. The nurse had written 11:52 p.m. on a form. For two hours and twenty-two minutes the world had been a place without him in it, and nothing about the gas station knew.

The pump wouldn't take my card, so I went inside. A man ahead of me was buying scratch tickets and working them at the counter with a quarter, one after another, unhurried. I wanted to scream at him. Then I noticed his hands shook, and that he still wore a hospital wristband, the same white plastic as my father's.

He lost on every one. He said "Well," to nobody, and held the door for me on his way out.

I bought a coffee I didn't drink. The cashier, a teenager with chipped green nail polish, said, "Long night?" I said yes. She said, "Me too. My mom's kicking me out Sunday," then looked horrified that she'd said it. I told her I was sorry. She told me she was sorry too, though she didn't know for what. We were both right.

I sat in the car for twenty minutes. A woman in a minivan pulled in, laughing into her phone, and I hated her. Then I heard her say, "No, Mom, *twins*," and she started crying too.

I think about them still: the man with the wristband, the girl with the green nails, the mother of twins.

If you were at that Shell, I was the woman in the blue Corolla with the engine running. You probably didn't notice me. That's all right. I was just someone in your way at a gas station.

You were in mine.

"Daddy, are we the bad guys?"

The Dark Lord set down his knitting. Through the tower window, a column of torches wound up the mountain pass like a burning thread. Somewhere at its head rode the boy with the prophesied sword, the one the songs called the Dawnbringer.

"What makes you ask, sweetheart?"

Mira pressed her nose to the glass. "The cook says they're coming to kill us. She says we burned the harvest in Edrin."

"We did."

"And the bridge at Vell."

"Also true."

She turned, eyes wide. "Then why?"

He patted the cushion beside him, and she climbed up, small and serious. He'd always liked that about her: she asked the question underneath the question.

"Seven years ago," he said, "the five kingdoms were at war with each other. Every season, more graves. Then a terrible sorcerer rose in the north." He wiggled his fingers spookily, and she almost smiled. "Suddenly the kingdoms had someone worse to hate than each other. They signed treaties. Built roads to move armies against me. Married their princes to each other's princesses. Do you know how many people have died fighting me?"

"How many?"

"Four hundred and twelve. Do you know how many died in the war before me, every year?"

She shook her head.

"Thirty thousand."

Mira was quiet for a long time. Below, a horn sounded, closer now.

"The bridge at Vell was empty," he added. "I checked. And Edrin had grain stores the king didn't tell anyone about. Nobody starved. They just had to share."

"So you're the good guy."

"No. I'm the bad guy. That's the job. Somebody has to be." He kissed the top of her head. "Tonight the Dawnbringer wins, and the kingdoms will have a hero to rally around. That'll hold them for a generation, maybe two."

"And then?"

He picked his knitting back up. It was a small black cloak, nearly finished, sized for someone who would grow.

"And then," he said gently, "they'll need someone new to hate."

Dr. Amara Okafor had spent eleven months calculating the end of the world, and she had gotten very good at it.

Diameter: fourteen kilometers. Velocity: twenty-two kilometers per second. Impact: March 9th, somewhere in the South Pacific. The math left no room for hope. She had stopped checking it twice.

So when the numbers changed, she assumed she'd made a mistake.

"It's slowing down," said Pell, her graduate student, at 3 a.m. on a Tuesday. He said it the way people describe a dream they don't quite believe.

Asteroids do not slow down. Amara checked the data herself, then had Mauna Kea check it, then Atacama. The object was decelerating at a steady, deliberate rate, like a car easing toward a stop sign.

By February, the big telescopes could resolve its surface. It wasn't rock. It was something like rock, grown rather than formed, and it was covered in grooves. Patterns. Pell was the one who recognized them.

"That's the Chicxulub crater," he whispered, tracing a spiral with his finger. "And that's the Permian one. Siberian Traps. And that one..." He trailed off.

There were five marks. Five mass extinctions. Each one etched into the surface like tally marks on a prison wall.

Except it wasn't a prison. Amara understood it slowly, the way you understand grief. It was a gardener's notebook.

The thing had come before. It had come when the trilobites ruled, when the great reptiles ruled. It had looked at what Earth had grown, found it lacking, and cleared the soil for something new.

Only this time, it was slowing down. This time, it was looking first.

On March 8th, it stopped just beyond the Moon's orbit and hung there, silent, for nine hours.

Then every radio telescope on Earth received the same transmission. Translation took the world's best linguists four days, though the meaning had been obvious from the first hour.

It was a single question.

*Show me why.*

The sky over Metropolis was the color of a bruise, and the ships kept coming.

Clark Kent ran down Fifth Street with his tie flapping and his glasses askew, looking for anywhere private. The alleys were full of fleeing people. The phone booths had all been ripped out years ago. He'd written a column about it, actually, a nostalgic little piece Perry had cut to four hundred words.

So when he saw the blue box standing in the middle of the road, POLICE PUBLIC CALL BOX glowing above the door, he didn't question it. He stepped inside and started unbuttoning his shirt.

Then he looked up.

The room went on. And on. Coral-colored struts curved toward a ceiling he couldn't see the end of. In the center, at a hexagonal console humming like a living thing, stood a thin man in a long coat, staring at him.

"Ah," said the man. "Hello. You're undressing."

"I... this is a phone booth," Clark said, which even he knew was a weak argument.

"It's really not." The man squinted, then produced a buzzing silver tube and waved it at Clark's chest, where the red S was half-visible. The device whined in confusion. "Oh, that's *brilliant*. Kryptonian. Last of, I'd wager. Don't suppose you know anything about the Sontarans parked over your city?"

"Sontarans?"

"Potato-headed. Militaristic. Very rude." He pulled a lever. "Thing is, their ships run on a field your yellow sun overcharges. Bit like you, actually. Someone fast enough could fly straight through the core array and pop the lot."

Clark finished pulling off his shirt. "Someone fast enough."

"Mm. I'd do it myself, but I'm more of a pressing-buttons sort." The man grinned. "Pair of lonely aliens, you and me. Fancy a team-up?"

Clark straightened his cape. Through the door, he could hear the city screaming.

"Open it," he said.

The Doctor did, and Superman went up like a promise.

The first thing Harold Pike noticed was that the ceiling was made of wood.

He had expected chrome. Holograms, maybe. A soothing artificial voice welcoming him to the year whatever-it-was. He had paid two hundred thousand dollars in 2019 for the promise of chrome.

Instead, a woman with gray braids and dirt under her fingernails leaned over him and said, very slowly, "Can... you... understand... me?"

"Yes," Harold croaked.

She burst into tears. Behind her, a dozen people in rough wool clothing began to cheer, hugging each other, someone banging a pot with a spoon.

It took three days before Harold could walk, and another two before anyone would answer his questions properly. The woman's name was Ama. She brought him soup and watched him eat it like he was a miracle.

"What year is it?"

"3016."

"And the company? CryoNova?"

Ama frowned. "That name is on the old plaques. We don't know what it meant."

Harold set down his spoon. "Then who's been maintaining the tanks?"

"We have." She said it simply, as if it were obvious. "My mother, and her father, back and back. Forty generations. We learned to patch the cooling lines. We learned to make the power. Some years were very hard."

"But why? Did you know how to revive us?"

"No. We only learned this last decade. We weren't sure it would work." She looked at her hands. "We weren't sure any of you were still... you."

"Then why keep going? For a thousand years?"

Ama was quiet for a long time.

"There was a sign on the door," she said finally. "From before. It said, *We will wake you.* Someone promised. And whoever they were, they were gone, and couldn't keep it."

She shrugged, embarrassed.

"We didn't want them to be a liar."

Harold Pemberton had been seventy-nine for six years.

Officially, of course, he was twenty-three. His papers said so, and so did his skinny jeans, which he'd been sewn into in 2011 and had not removed since. The beanie hid his liver spots. The oversized sunglasses hid everything else. And when anyone looked too closely, Harold had the most powerful weapon of the age: he took out his phone, held it at arm's length, and made a duck face.

Nobody questioned a man taking a selfie. Nobody looked past it.

The Department of Actuarial Efficiency had tried. Their agents prowled the coffee shops of Portland with clipboards, sniffing for the telltale signs: a newspaper, a landline, a fondness for Perry Como. Last spring an agent had cornered Harold in a Starbucks and asked his opinion of the music playing.

"It's a banger," Harold said, though it sounded to him like a garbage truck reversing into a kazoo factory.

The agent narrowed his eyes. "And what do you call a pair of sneakers?"

"Kicks," Harold said. "Fresh ones."

The agent left. Harold went into the bathroom and shook for twenty minutes.

He had rules. Never say "in my day." Never complain about your knees. When your back gives out, call it planking. When you fall asleep at 8 p.m., post about "self-care." Always pay with an app, never a checkbook, even though the app frightened him in a way the Korean War hadn't.

Tonight there was a knock at the door. Harold peered through the peephole and saw an agent he recognized: Inspector Dunn, the best they had, young and relentless.

"Open up, Pemberton. I know what you are."

Harold opened the door. Dunn stepped inside, glanced around, and then slowly peeled back the edge of his own hairline. Underneath was a wisp of pure white.

"Eighty-four," Dunn whispered. "Tell me, son. Where do you get those jeans?"

My mother's mask was porcelain-white, with a painted smile that never changed. My father's was plainer, a smooth oval with two dark eye-holes. My teachers, the baker, the boy who pushed me into the creek when I was seven: all white, all blank.

Only I went bare.

"Why?" I asked once, touching my cheek.

"Because you're a child," Mother said. Later, when I was no longer a child, she said, "Because you haven't been chosen yet."

So I grew up with my face hanging out like laundry. Everyone could see when I was jealous, when I was lying, when I liked someone. The boy from the creek saw me blush at sixteen and laughed behind his mask, and I never knew whether he was laughing *at* me or just laughing. That was the worst of it: I was a book anyone could read, and I lived in a library of locked covers.

Then came Ellis. Ellis, whose mask was chipped at the chin, who never laughed when I blushed, who sat beside me on the church steps every evening for a year and said little. I learned Ellis by voice and hands. By the tilt of a head. By patience.

We married in spring. That night, in our small rented room, Ellis's fingers found the ribbon behind the mask and hesitated.

"Everyone's been able to see you," Ellis said quietly. "Your whole life. Every fear. Every hope. I watched you hope about *me* for months before you ever said a word."

My face burned. Of course it did.

"That's not fair," I whispered.

"No. It isn't. That's why we do this."

The ribbon slipped. The mask fell into Ellis's lap.

The face beneath was ordinary. Freckled. Wet-eyed. Terrified.

And there it was, written plainly, the thing I'd shown the whole world for twenty years and never once been shown back.

"Now," Ellis said, voice shaking, "we're even."

"Forty-three," I'd told them at the gas station when Marisol asked my count. I said it the way you'd say your shoe size: bored, slightly put upon.

Now there was one shambling across the parking lot toward us, and everyone had stepped back to give me room.

"Go on," said Dev. "Show us the thing. The skull thing."

I had described "the skull thing" in some detail over canned peaches. It involved a pivot.

The zombie was a middle-aged man in a fleece vest. He still had his lanyard on. It said HI, I'M GARY.

"Hi, Gary," I said, before I could stop myself.

Behind me, someone exhaled slowly through their nose.

I raised the crowbar. I'd been holding it like a baseball bat all week, which is apparently wrong. Marisol leaned over and gently rotated it in my hands, the way you'd fix a child's grip on a fork.

Gary moaned. I moaned back, which I want to stress was not on purpose.

"Are you... waiting for it to consent?" Dev asked.

"I'm reading him," I said. "Every one's different."

"It's Gary," said Marisol. "Gary is not complicated."

Gary lunged. I screamed, a high, clear note that was honestly impressive, and swung. The crowbar missed Gary entirely, struck the metal cart corral, and rang out like a church bell. Every zombie within half a mile turned its head.

Gary, startled, tripped over his own feet and lay on the asphalt, gnawing at the air near my sneaker.

I looked down at him. He looked up at me. We were both, I think, new at this.

Old Pete sighed, stepped forward, and did the skull thing. It did involve a pivot. I'd been right about that much.

"Forty-four," Marisol said flatly, and handed me the peaches.

Then the groaning started from every direction at once, and we ran.

I've never studied for a test in my life. Why would I? Priya Raman, front row, thinks in perfect bullet points. Marcus behind me hums the quadratic formula like a lullaby. Even when they're wrong, they're wrong together, and the average of thirty anxious brains is a solid B-plus.

So when Mr. Halloway's replacement walked in, a small woman with gray braids and an oatmeal-colored cardigan, I didn't look up. I was already drifting through the room, sampling. Priya: *mitochondria, mitochondria.* Marcus: *should've eaten breakfast.*

Then a voice like a dropped piano.

**NO CHEATING IN MY CLASSROOM.**

I clutched my desk. Nobody else flinched. The woman (Ms. Ferro, the board said) was writing the date, back turned, chalk tapping.

*Yes, you,* she thought, quieter now, almost amused. *Third row, hoodie, trying very hard to look innocent. You think loud, dear. Like a radio left on in an empty house.*

I tried to shut my mind. It was like closing a door I'd never noticed was there.

*Don't strain. You'll give yourself a nosebleed. Stay after the bell.*

When the room emptied, she sat on the edge of her desk and studied me with eyes that had seen the inside of a lot of heads.

"How long?" she asked aloud.

"Since I was nine."

"And you've used it to copy biology answers." She sighed. "There are maybe forty of us worldwide. The brightest one I've found in a decade is using it to pass tenth-grade cell division."

"So I'm in trouble."

"Oh, enormously." She slid a blank sheet toward me. "Starting tomorrow, you'll learn how to keep people out. Then you'll learn how to listen for the ones who are hiding."

"Hiding from what?"

She smiled, and for the first time I couldn't hear a single thing she was thinking.

"Study hard," she said. "This is one test you can't cheat on."

My grandfather kept the newspaper framed above the mantel: PIG ASCENDS AT LEYSDOWN, AVIATOR DECLARES "FIRST LIVESTOCK PASSENGER." The photograph shows a small pig in a wicker basket lashed to a biplane strut, looking mildly inconvenienced by history.

Nobody noticed at first. Then a Chicago bartender swore the Cubs would win another World Series "when pigs fly," and they won in 1910, and 1911, and every October since. One hundred and seven consecutive championships. The other teams still show up, the way you'd still show up to a funeral.

After that, people noticed.

A senator said he'd balance the budget when pigs fly. The national debt has been zero since 1931. A Belfast man said there'd be peace in Ireland when pigs fly, and a man in Jerusalem said the same about his own city, and both of them lived long enough to be bored by it. Every politician who ever sneered "when pigs fly" at a campaign promise discovered that the promise had quietly kept itself.

It got smaller and stranger, too. Somewhere in Ohio, a woman's ex-husband has called her every Sunday since 1952, apologizing. He died in 1979. The calls still come.

Teenagers learned fastest. My sister said she'd clean her room when pigs fly, and for the rest of her adolescence she couldn't leave a sock on the floor without it folding itself into a drawer. She has never forgiven the pig.

By the sixties, the phrase was regulated. You need a license now, like for explosives. Schools teach "when hell freezes over" instead, which is how we lost Norway.

But mostly the world is just kinder than it has any right to be, built out of a century of sarcasm taken at its word.

Every morning, a V of Berkshires passes over my house, heading south for the winter, honking softly. My son waves at them.

He once asked me what we did before.

"We doubted things," I said.

He didn't understand, and I didn't explain.

Daniel Whitmore sat across from me with the hollow look of a man who'd read his own name in the paper.

"I didn't kill those women," he said.

"I know," I told him, and I meant it more than he could imagine.

The trick to losing a case is that no one can ever see you lose it. Juries smell indifference, and so do bar associations. So for eleven weeks I was magnificent. I dismantled the fiber analyst on cross until she apologized to the court. I made the lead detective admit he'd decided on Daniel before the second body was cold. The *Ledger* called it the defense of the decade. Partners at three firms sent flowers.

But every defense has a load-bearing wall, and Daniel's was his alibi. He'd been home alone, streaming a film, on the night of the third murder. I built everything on that. I subpoenaed the streaming company's logs myself and showed the jury the timestamps: playback began at 8:52 p.m.

What I didn't put on a slide was page 311 of the log, which showed the film paused at 9:14 and never resumed.

Daniel had simply fallen asleep on his couch. I believed him. I had excellent reason to.

Discovery rules required me to turn the full log over to the prosecution, so I did, buried in four hundred pages of server data, exactly as the law demanded. A junior ADA with good eyes found it on day forty-one. I objected, sputtered, and requested a recess. I looked, by every account, blindsided.

The jury was out for six hours.

Afterward, on the courthouse steps, reporters asked whether I'd appeal. I said yes, of course, with the tired dignity of a man who'd given everything. Daniel clasped my hand through the cuffs and thanked me for believing in him.

At 9:14 that night, three years ago, I'd been washing my hands.

I always remember the time.

Tommy Kowalczyk knocks at 9:15 every morning, three times, hard enough to rattle the chain.

"Danny. You know what day it is."

It isn't. It hasn't been for six years. But for Tommy it's always March 3rd, 2019, the day my eight hundred dollars was due to Vinnie Russo. It's also the day Tommy stepped off my curb, still cracking his knuckles at me, and met a city bus.

The first week, I paid him. I didn't know what else to do. He'd take the envelope, nod, and leave, and the next morning he'd be back, looking at me like I'd never seen a dollar in my life. By Friday I'd emptied my savings and he'd delivered four thousand dollars to a man who, it turned out, had been arrested on March 4th.

So I made the tape.

Now when Tommy knocks, I open the door and hand him the remote before he can grab my collar. He frowns, because he's a professional, but he sits on my couch and presses play.

*Hi, Tommy. It's me, Danny. It's not 2019. You got hurt. Vinnie's in Danbury doing twenty years. You don't work for anybody anymore. Your mother is fine. She's at Sunnyvale and she likes the pudding. You like your eggs over medium. You're my friend.*

He always cries at the Vinnie part. I've never understood that.

Then I make him eggs, over medium, and we play chess, and he beats me, because whatever the bus took, it left the Sicilian Defense intact. My daughter calls him Uncle Tom-Tom. He taught her to throw a punch, thumb outside the fist.

This morning, while I was clearing his plate, he watched the tape a second time. He doesn't usually.

"Danny," he said. "Thing never actually says whether you paid."

I set down the plate.

"Doesn't it?"

He looked at me a long moment. Then he smiled, and moved his knight.

"Check."

"Shut the dog up."

Papa didn't shout it. He breathed it, the words barely louder than the boots crunching across the frost above us. In the dark of the root cellar I could feel his hand groping toward me, toward Bruno, and I knew what that hand meant. I had seen him with the chickens.

Bruno kept growling, low and steady, a sound like a motor deep in his chest. He didn't understand. He thought the men upstairs were the danger, and that he was supposed to stop them, the way he'd stopped the fox last spring.

"Mila." Mama this time, pleading. "Please."

Upstairs, a drawer crashed to the floor. Someone laughed. A flashlight beam slid across the gaps in the floorboards, painting stripes on Mama's face, on the baby asleep against her shoulder, on the potatoes we'd stored for a winter we might not see.

Bruno's growl rose toward a bark.

I found Papa's wrist in the dark and pushed it away. Then I did the only other thing I could think of. I crawled to the coal chute at the back of the cellar, the one that opened onto the slope behind the barn, and I lifted the iron flap just enough.

"Go," I whispered into Bruno's ear. "Go get the fox."

He went like water. A second later his barking exploded outside, wild and joyful, racing up the hill toward the treeline.

The boots stopped. Voices argued. Then the whole house shook as they ran, out the door, after the noise, the way men will chase anything that runs.

We listened to Bruno bark until dawn, the sound growing smaller and smaller among the pines, never once stopping.

There was no gunshot. I have chosen, for seventy years, to believe that means something.

Every dog I've owned since, I have let bark as long as it likes.

The waiter set down the plate, and the universe held its breath.

"Enjoy your meal," he said.

Gerald had trained for this moment his entire life. Thirty-four years of birthdays, funerals and dental appointments had each been a rehearsal for this single exchange. His mouth opened. Somewhere, a violin began to weep.

"You too."

The words left him like doves released at a wedding, and then, horribly, like doves flying into a ceiling fan.

The waiter would not be enjoying a meal. The waiter was *working*. The waiter would be standing for six more hours, carrying the meals of others, enjoying nothing.

Time slowed. Gerald saw the waiter's eyebrow twitch a single millimeter, a seismic event. Across the restaurant, a child dropped a fork, and the clatter echoed like cathedral bells announcing the death of a king. His wife, Linda, closed her eyes. She had married him. She had *chosen* this.

"Haha," Gerald said. "I mean—"

But there was no "I mean." There was only the abyss, and the abyss was garnished with a sprig of parsley.

He thought of his mother, who had taught him manners. He thought of his grandfather, who had stormed a beach in Normandy so that his descendants might live free, and here was that freedom, squandered on a catastrophe within reach of a breadstick. He thought of the waiter's future children, who would one day ask, "Daddy, what's the strangest thing a customer ever said to you?" The waiter would stare into the dying embers of the fireplace and whisper, "There was a man. In a fleece vest."

"No worries," said the waiter, already walking away.

*No worries.* Two words. Were they mercy, or the cruelest dismissal ever spoken by human lips? Gerald would never know. Empires had fallen with less ambiguity.

He lifted his fork with trembling hands, as a knight lifts a sword he no longer believes in. He took a bite.

The salmon was fine.

He would think about it every night until he died.

The paramedic told me later that I was gone for four minutes. She said it like it was good news, like four minutes was nothing, a commercial break.

It wasn't nothing.

I don't remember the truck, or the windshield, or the road coming up to meet me. I remember warmth, and a field of tall grass that moved like breathing, and a light that didn't hurt to look at. I remember feeling *finished*, the way you feel when you set down a heavy bag you'd forgotten you were carrying.

And I remember the girl.

She was maybe seven. Barefoot, grass-stained knees, a gap where her front tooth should have been. She had Emma's eyes, that exact gray-green I fell in love with across a crowded bar eleven years ago. She took my hand like she'd done it a thousand times.

"You can't stay," she said.

"Who are you?"

She laughed, and it was my laugh, the embarrassing one, the honk. "You haven't met me yet. That's the whole point. Go on."

Then she pushed me, hard, both hands against my chest, and I was screaming on asphalt with someone's palms pumping my sternum and the taste of copper in my mouth.

Now I'm in a hospital bed, and Emma is holding the hand the girl held. She's been crying. She keeps almost saying something and then stopping.

Finally she does.

"I was going to tell you this weekend. I wanted it to be special." She presses my fingers against her stomach. "Eight weeks. Isn't that crazy?"

I smile. I cry. I tell her it's the best news of my life, and it is.

But I can't stop thinking about the field.

About how happy that little girl looked, how at home.

About how she was already *there*, waiting on the other side.

And how she pushed me back alone.

Walter said it about everything.

When the Cubs won the Series: "Stranger things have happened." When the dog learned to open the fridge: "Stranger things have happened." When the doctor said *pancreatic* and *months* in the same sentence, Walter patted my hand and said it again, softer, like a prayer he didn't quite believe.

He'd been gone four years when the dead came back.

Not zombies. Nothing gruesome. At 2:07 on a Tuesday afternoon, every person who had ever died simply appeared, clean and whole and looking slightly embarrassed, standing in kitchens and cornfields and the middle of the Atlantic, where they did not sink. The news said they'd counted a hundred and seven billion before the counters gave up. Cleopatra was on CNN. Someone's great-great-grandfather was stuck in a Walmart, terrified of the automatic doors.

They stayed exactly one afternoon. Nobody knows why. Nobody knows who allowed it. The theologians are still yelling at each other.

Walter appeared by the bird feeder, holding the same chipped mug he'd died holding. He looked at the yard, at the new fence, at me in my gardening gloves with my mouth hanging open.

"Margie," he said. "You let the roses go."

I threw a trowel at him. Then I held him for three hours, and we said the things. The real things, the ones the hospital didn't leave time for. He told me where he'd hidden the good bourbon. I told him I'd sold his truck and was sorry, and he said he wasn't.

At 6:58, he began to fade at the edges, like a photograph left in a window.

He smiled that crooked smile and squeezed my hand.

"Well," he said. "Stranger things have—"

"No, Walter," I said, crying and laughing at once. "They haven't."

He thought about it. Then he nodded.

"No," he agreed. "I suppose they haven't."

And then the yard was empty, and the bird feeder swung gently in the evening air.

He first came in on a Tuesday in March, sleeves rolled, forearm already crowded with ink. Four vertical lines and a diagonal slash, over and over, marching from wrist toward elbow like fence posts.

"One more," he said. "Same as the others."

It took me ninety seconds. He paid in cash, tipped twenty, and left.

Two weeks later, he was back. Then again. Then again. Sometimes it was ten days, sometimes nineteen, but he always came, always sat in the same chair, always said the same thing. *One more.* By autumn, the marks had wrapped around his forearm and started climbing the bicep.

You hear things in this business. I'd decided he was counting bodies, or prison years, or drinks he hadn't had. I didn't ask. People who want to be asked usually tell you first.

In December, though, his hand shook while I worked, and I said, "You okay?"

He watched the needle a long moment. "My wife has Alzheimer's," he said. "I visit every day. Some days she knows me. Most days she doesn't." He nodded at the arm. "Those are the days she knows me."

I looked at all those little gates of ink. Hundreds of them. I thought about how many days must have gone *unmarked* between them.

"Why not write them down?"

"Paper gets lost." He smiled a little. "She used to say I'd forget my own head. Figured I'd keep it somewhere I couldn't."

He didn't come back in January. Or February. I told myself it meant nothing.

In March, a year to the day, the bell over the door rang. He looked thinner. He sat in the chair and rolled up his sleeve, and for a while he didn't say anything at all.

"She passed," he finally said. "Sunday."

"I'm so sorry."

"She knew me." His voice cracked on it. "At the end. She said my name."

I picked up the needle, and for the first time I didn't wait for him to ask.

The dreambook arrived with Mira the way a name does: handed over by the midwife, pressed into my arms on top of her. Cream pages, a clasp no one locks because no one needs to. Reading another person's dreams simply isn't done.

I told myself I was checking for nightmares. She was four and had stopped sleeping through the night.

I expected crayon logic: purple dogs, teeth falling out, a staircase made of soup. Instead I found a sentence so clean it stopped my breath. *The lighthouse keeper's daughter learned to speak in the language of ships, which is mostly silence and occasionally fire.*

Two hundred pages. Chapters. A plot that turned like a key.

We owed eleven months on the house. I typed it out at the kitchen table, changed nothing, and sent it under my mother's maiden name. The advance paid the mortgage. The second book paid for the car. By the third, critics were calling me luminous, and Mira was sleeping eleven hours a night, smiling into her pillow while I waited in the hallway for the pages to fill.

The fourth book was different.

A man finds a well in his garden that answers questions. He lowers a bucket every evening and draws up gold, and every morning the well is a little shallower. His daughter grows quieter. She stops drawing. She stops singing in the bath. The man notices, the way you notice weather, and lowers the bucket anyway.

I read it at 3 a.m. with the hall light humming.

The last chapter was only a page. The well is dry. The man looks down and sees, at the very bottom, his daughter's face looking up, not angry, just patient, the way children are patient with adults who haven't figured something out yet.

*He could have asked,* the final line read. *She would have given it to him.*

In the morning Mira ate her cereal and hummed. I put the book on her nightstand and, for the first time, locked the clasp.

Then I sat down beside her and asked her to tell me a story.

The forestry office called it Plot 4471, but everyone in town knew it as Walter's tree.

Most souls settled into something dignified. Oaks were popular. The mayor's grandfather had become a sequoia so enormous they'd rerouted the highway around him. Ellen's sister was a weeping willow by the river, which surprised no one.

Walter had come back as a crabapple. A small, crooked, stubborn crabapple that grew sideways out of the hill behind the hardware store, dropping sour fruit on customers' windshields every September.

"Of course he did," Ellen had said at the planting, and the whole congregation laughed, because they'd known him.

She visited on Sundays. She brought a thermos and a folding chair and read him the paper, mostly the sports section, mostly the parts that would annoy him. Sometimes the branches shifted when the wind wasn't blowing. Sometimes a single blossom dropped into her lap in the middle of a box score, and she chose to believe it was commentary.

The arborist came in her eleventh spring of widowhood. He had a clipboard and a kind face, which made it worse.

"Root rot," he said. "Crabapples don't live long. Thirty years, maybe forty. He's had a good run."

"What happens when it dies?"

The arborist hesitated. "Nobody knows. The theologians say they move on. Somewhere further."

Ellen looked at the twisted trunk, at the bark worn smooth where she'd rested her hand a thousand times.

"Further," she repeated.

That evening she went to the county office and filled out the forms. Species selection, she wrote, then crossed it out. She'd always assumed she would choose a maple, something with good fall color, something people would photograph.

Instead she wrote *crabapple*, and under location, *as close as legally permitted*.

Roots travel, after all. Roots find each other in the dark.

She figured she'd catch him before he got too far.

The first time I noticed, I was nine. I wanted the last slice of birthday cake, and my cousin Danny, reaching for it, sneezed so hard he knocked it into my lap. Frosting side up.

By twelve, I'd stopped losing anything: coin tosses, spelling bees, the race to the ice cream truck. Other kids around me fell off bikes and lost homework. My neighborhood had the highest rate of broken arms in the county. I didn't connect it until my mother, sitting beside me at bingo, watched her card go blank for six straight hours while mine filled itself like magic.

Dad figured it out first. He was smarter than me and greedier than both of us. He took me to the track and had me point at horses. I pointed. He bet. The horse won by four lengths, and my father dropped dead in the parking lot with the ticket still in his fist. The coroner called it an aneurysm, one in a million.

I've tried to be careful since. My girlfriend in college asked me to help her study for the bar. She passed with the highest score in state history, and the next morning her apartment building burned down with her license framed on the wall. She lived. She doesn't speak to me.

So now I live at the end of a gravel road in Montana, eleven miles from the nearest person. My neighbors' cattle stay healthy. The diner in town stays open. I order groceries by mail, and the driver leaves them at the gate without stopping the engine.

There's one indulgence. A retired teacher in Ohio and I play chess by post. Every move, I try with everything I have to lose.

I've won forty-one straight games.

His last letter said: *Your sacrifices are the strangest I've ever seen. They keep working. Same time next week?*

He's never once asked me for anything. I think that's why he's still alive.

The DNA site matched me with Daniel Kessler on a Tuesday. By Thursday I'd found his Instagram, his Yelp reviews, and the restraining order.

He had my face. He used it to sneer at waitresses.

I watched him for a month. He parked in disabled spots. He fired a receptionist by text on her wedding day. He kicked a pigeon. Actually kicked it. Somewhere back in 1989, an overworked adoption agency had split us up, and I'd spent thirty-four years wondering what I was missing. Now I knew: a man who reviewed a children's hospital gift shop at one star.

I could have introduced myself. Instead, I bought his exact jacket.

The first time, I went to the diner where he'd made a teenager cry over cold eggs. I tipped her two hundred dollars and apologized, sincerely, for being a monster. She hugged me. The next morning, when Daniel came in, she smiled at him with such warmth that he sent his food back three times out of sheer confusion.

I returned his neighbor's leaf blower, which he had stolen. I volunteered at the animal shelter under his name, and now they call him every week asking when he's coming back to walk Biscuit. I called his ex-wife and told her she deserved better, which she did, and that I was proud of her, which made her cry and then text him "thank you" at two in the morning.

He began to unravel. People waved at him. Strangers thanked him. His boss praised his "remarkable personal growth" in front of the entire board and promoted him to lead the company's new charity initiative, which he now has to run, publicly, with a smile.

Last week I saw him alone in his car, gripping the wheel, staring into the rearview mirror like he didn't recognize the man looking back.

Good. That's the idea.

Tomorrow I'm donating a kidney. The hospital has his name on the paperwork.

The name is written in a slanted, careful hand along the inside of my forearm: *Lila Marchetti.*

I notice it before I notice anything else. Before the hospital ceiling, before the tubes, before the dull, enormous ache radiating from my right shoulder. The ink isn't ink. It's under the skin, the way they always are, the color of an old bruise.

I have never heard of Lila Marchetti. I'm sure of it. I'm an accountant. I coach my nephew's soccer team. Last thing I remember is the forklift at the warehouse tipping, the crush of the pallet, someone screaming my name.

A nurse comes in and sees me staring at it. Her face does something complicated.

"Mr. Dunn. You're awake. I'll get Dr. Okafor."

"Who is she?" I ask. My voice is gravel. "Who's Lila Marchetti?"

The nurse leaves without answering.

Dr. Okafor arrives with a woman in a gray blazer who doesn't introduce herself as a doctor. Dr. Okafor talks first. He explains about the accident, about how my arm couldn't be saved. He explains about the donor program, about how lucky I was that a match came through so quickly, about nerve regrowth and physical therapy and how I may not have full sensation for a year.

I look down at my right arm. At the knuckles that aren't mine. At the faint tan line where someone else wore a watch.

The woman in the blazer pulls a chair close.

"The donor was killed in a traffic stop four days ago," she says. "We didn't know about the name. It was covered by a tattoo sleeve. The surgical team found it during prep. By then, you were already open."

"So he—"

"Lila disappeared in 2019. We never found her." She leans forward. "Mr. Dunn, we're going to need you to tell us if you ever feel anything strange. Anything at all."

The fingers of my new hand curl, slowly, into a fist.

I didn't tell them to.

The number on my forearm is wrong. Everyone assumes it's a joke, or a prison thing, or a lottery pick. It's none of those. It's Danielle's phone number, except it isn't, because I was nineteen and drunk on cheap tequila in a Tijuana parlor and I said "four" when I meant "nine."

Danielle left me two weeks later anyway, so it didn't matter much. Still, about a year after that, lonely and stupid on a Tuesday night, I dialed the number on my arm just to see who'd answer.

"Hello?" An old woman. Brisk voice.

I panicked. "Is Danielle there?"

"No, honey, but I'm Margaret, and I'm awake. What's wrong?"

I don't know why I told her. Maybe because she was a stranger, or because she didn't hang up. I told her about Danielle, about the tattoo, about dropping out of community college. She laughed so hard at the tattoo part she started coughing.

"Well," she said, "you'll have to call me again. You're wearing my number for life. Seems only fair."

So I did. Every Tuesday for eleven years.

She told me about her husband, Ray, who'd died of something slow. She told me to go back to school, and I did. When I got engaged, she made me describe the ring three times. When my daughter was born, I held the phone to her tiny face so Margaret could hear her breathe.

We never met. She said she was "too old and too ugly for in-person," and I let her keep that.

Last spring, a man answered. Her nephew. He'd found my name written on her kitchen calendar, every Tuesday, in blue ink, going back years.

People ask if I regret the tattoo.

I tell them it's the only thing I've ever gotten exactly right.

My god is the god of lost things, which is a hard sell.

"So he finds my keys?" the first man asked me, outside a laundromat in Toledo.

"Sometimes," I said. "Mostly he just knows how it feels."

That man became convert number one. That night I found a quarter wedged between the floorboards of my apartment. I hadn't dropped it. It was simply *mine to find*.

That's how the power works. Every soul that turns toward him, he turns a little more toward me.

At fifty converts I could find any set of car keys within a city block. At three hundred, I found a wedding ring at the bottom of Lake Erie and handed it back to a weeping widow, who knelt right there on the pier. At two thousand, I found a runaway girl in Denver before the wrong people did.

The god of war has millions, and his emissaries can level hills. The god of money has more. Mine has the grieving, the forgetful, the people who check their pockets three times before leaving the house. We're not glamorous. We're loyal.

At ten thousand converts, I could find anything. A forgotten name. A misplaced afternoon. The exact moment a marriage started going wrong. People lined up outside my door holding photographs.

At ten thousand and one, he finally spoke to me directly.

His voice was small, like something heard through a wall.

*Will you find me?*

I didn't understand. I'd prayed to him every day for six years.

*Not where I am,* he said. *Who I was. I was big once. Before the others. Back when losing something meant losing everything, and people begged me for every lamb and every child. I've forgotten what I looked like.*

So I closed my eyes and looked.

It took three days. I found him in a cave painting in France, in a lullaby in Mali, in the way my grandmother used to touch the doorframe before leaving.

I brought him back.

He wept, the way the widow had.

Then he asked me to keep going.

The neurologist used words like "brainstem" and "respiratory drive," and then admitted she had no name for what was wrong with him. To Martin, it sounded like a ship that had gone down with all hands.

"Your body forgets to breathe," she said. "Awake, you remember for it. Asleep, nobody does."

There was a machine that could help, eventually, once the insurance cleared and the surgeon came back from Lisbon. Three weeks. Until then: stimulants, alarms, a nephew paid to poke him.

The first night was easy. He'd stayed up before, for exams, for colic, for the bad year after Ruth died. He made coffee at two and drank it on the porch and listened to the freight trains he'd slept through for thirty years.

By the fifth night he had learned the town's secret population. The woman who walked her greyhound at 3:40, always the same loop. The bakery lights coming on at four, a radio playing mariachi. The boy at the gas station who was studying for something with flashcards and who, by the second week, started holding up cards for Martin to guess. "Mitochondria," Martin said, and the boy grinned like he'd won.

Exhaustion did strange things. Colors went loud. He cried at a cereal commercial. Twice he caught himself mid-nod and felt his chest go still, quietly, like a clock someone had put a finger on. Both times he gasped awake with his heart slamming.

On the nineteenth night he sat on the porch and realized he wasn't afraid of the dark anymore. He'd spent his whole life closing his eyes on it, missing half of everything.

The surgeon came back. The machine went in. The doctor said he could sleep now, safely, as long as he liked.

Martin thanked her, went home, and set his alarm for 3:30.

The greyhound would be coming by soon, and he still hadn't learned its name.

Ama forgot the basket.

That was the whole of it, really. Twelve thousand years of historians would build towers of theory: climate shifts, population pressure, the slow genius of the human mind bending toward permanence. But on the actual day, Ama set down a reed basket of wild barley beside the rock shelter, turned to scold her youngest for poking the fire with a bone, and walked off with the rest of the band toward the river. The basket stayed behind.

It rained for four days.

When they came back, the shelter smelled wrong. Sour, warm, faintly like overripe figs. The barley had swollen and split, and the bottom of the basket held a cloudy, bubbling mush. Ama's mate, Dorr, who would eat anything, scooped a handful into his mouth before she could stop him.

He made a face. Then he made a different face. Then he took another handful.

By nightfall the whole band had tried it. By moonrise, old Hesk, who had not spoken a kind word since the last mammoth, was singing. The two brothers who'd been feuding over a flint knife wept and embraced. Someone invented a dance. Someone else fell into the fire, though not badly.

In the morning, everyone's heads hurt. Everyone also wanted more.

But the wild barley grew only in scattered patches, and the band moved too often to find it at the right time. So Ama, practical and grumbling, pressed a few spare grains into the mud by the shelter and told everyone they were staying put until those came up.

They came up. The band stayed. Then they needed walls to guard the barley, and counting marks to track it, and a chief to settle arguments over it, and gods to thank for it.

Ama, very old now, watched the first village rise around her.

"I only wanted a drink," she muttered.

The coffee is the important part. Not for her. For him.

Marisol pours it into the travel mug, black, two sugars, the way the newspaper said Daniel Okafor liked it, and sets it on the bench at the trailhead before she starts stretching. By the time she's finished her calves, the mug is cold and he is sitting beside it.

"Morning," he says. "You know what time it is?"

"Six-fifteen."

"Huh. Thought I'd be later." He always thinks he'll be later.

They run. He's faster than her, or was. He wears a gray Boston '09 shirt and shoes that went out of production a decade ago, and he talks the whole first mile about his daughter's science fair project, a volcano, which he is sure will win. Marisol has looked it up. It didn't. It came in third. She doesn't tell him.

At mile two, his breathing starts to catch. At mile three, he presses a hand to his chest and laughs it off. At mile four, by the split oak with the plaque bolted to it, he stops.

Every morning, he stops.

He looks at the oak like it's a wall. Then he looks at her, confused, and is gone, and she finishes the loop alone.

That was two years ago, the first time. She has tried everything since. Running faster. Running slower. Talking to him about anything except his chest. Once, she grabbed his hand at the oak and felt nothing but October air.

This morning she doesn't pass him at mile three. She drops back, matches his stride exactly, breath for breath.

"You okay?" he asks.

"Tired," she lies. "Pace me in?"

He grins, the grin of a man who has never once been asked to carry anyone. "Come on. Stay on my shoulder."

The oak comes up. He doesn't look at it. He's looking back at her.

They pass it together.

At mile five he's laughing. At mile six, he's just light.

The first time, I stubbed my toe on the coffee table at two in the morning, said "Oh my God," and a voice from the couch said, "Yes?"

He was wearing a bathrobe. His beard went on longer than the room did. I screamed, and He waited politely for me to finish.

"Sorry," I said. "It's just an expression."

"I know," He said. "I come anyway. It's a policy."

After that, I learned how often I said it.

I said it when the barista spelled my name wrong, and He appeared behind the counter, apologizing on her behalf. I said it on a first date when she told me she'd never seen *The Godfather*, and He pulled up a chair and agreed it was a tragedy. I said it during the second date, later, in a context I will not describe, and He materialized at the foot of the bed, looked at us both, and said, "Ah. My mistake," which did not help.

I tried substitutes. "Oh my gosh." "Good grief." "Jeez." That last one brought His Son, who was nicer about it but stayed for dinner.

At my job interview, the manager asked where I saw myself in five years, and I muttered "God, I don't know," and He answered for me. In detail. With dates. I didn't get the job, mostly because of what He said about the manager's marriage.

Eventually I got careful. Weeks passed. I swore in other languages. I sighed instead.

Then, one night in the hospital, waiting outside a room I wasn't allowed into, I said it again. Not as an expression. Just His name, quietly, the way you'd knock on a door you weren't sure was there.

He sat down beside me. No bathrobe this time.

"You know," He said, "this is the one I always hope for."

He didn't promise anything. He just stayed.

It was still terribly inconvenient. It was also the only thing that helped.

Walt hadn't held a rifle in fifty-three years, and the thing Tyler pressed into his hands was neon green and weighed nothing.

"Just stay behind the hay bales, Grandpa," Tyler said. "You'll be fine."

Across the field, another old man was being fitted for a mask by a girl in braces. He was small and wiry, with a cane he leaned on like an afterthought. He looked over. Walt looked back. Neither waved.

The whistle blew. Kids scattered, shrieking. Walt crouched, knees popping, and watched the old man not move at all. That was the first thing. Everyone moves. The old man just sank into the tall grass along the tree line and was gone.

Walt's skin went cold. He knew that kind of stillness. He'd spent a wet season in the Quang Tri highlands learning to fear it.

So he waited. He'd learned that too. Twenty minutes passed while children eliminated each other in bursts of pink and orange. Then he saw it: a single fern trembling against the wind. He'd seen the same tremble once, through rain, a moment before a bullet took the radio off Danny Kowalski's back.

Walt fired. Missed. A paintball cracked against the bale an inch from his ear, exactly where a man's head would be if he hadn't flinched left. In 1968, he had flinched left.

The fern parted. The old man stood, mask up, staring.

"Hill 881," the man said slowly. "The tall one with the radio friend. You moved left."

"You always fired low," Walt said. "Lucky for me."

They regarded each other across a field of shrieking grandchildren, and the years settled on them both, heavy as wet wool.

Then a blue paintball smacked the old man square in the chest. The girl in braces whooped. Another splattered Walt's thigh. Tyler, grinning.

The old man laughed first, a dry, astonished sound. After a moment, Walt joined him.

"Lunch?" the man asked, wiping blue from his shirt. "I think we have much to talk about."

"Yeah," Walt said. "Yeah, we do."

The birds were the first part of the work.

She fed them all winter on seed and suet until they trusted her, and then she taught them to follow the paths that wound in from the villages. Children dropped things when they were led into the woods. Pebbles, sometimes. More often bread, because the parents who brought them out here had nothing else left to give.

The birds ate every crumb. There must be no way back to a house where someone had decided you were one mouth too many.

The roof was the second part. A frightened child will run from a stranger, run from a lantern, run from a kind voice calling through the trees. But no child alive has ever run from sugar. So she baked, and she iced, and every spring she patched the gingerbread where the rain had softened it, and she waited.

Tonight there were two. A boy and his sister, gray with hunger, breaking off pieces of her windowsill with shaking hands.

"Nibble, nibble, little mouse," she called, softly, the way you'd speak to a deer. "Who's that nibbling at my house?"

They froze. She saw herself as they must see her: bent, hooked, squinting through cataracts. She had long stopped minding.

Inside, she fed them pancakes and milk and apples, and put them to bed under clean linen. In the morning she took the boy's wrist between her fingers, because her eyes were too poor to trust, and her heart broke a little at how thin it was. *Weeks*, she thought. *Weeks before he's well.*

The girl watched her the whole time. Clever girl. Suspicious. Good. That would keep her alive.

The old woman stoked the oven high and began to knead the dough. She had a great deal of bread to make.

She did not see the girl edging closer behind her.

The light came through Eli's bedroom window at 3:14 a.m., which he knew because he'd been staring at his phone, rereading the same text from his dad: *Still not calling you that.*

Then the phone was gone, and so was the bedroom.

The room he stood in had no corners. Something stood in front of him, though "stood" was generous. It looked like a heat shimmer that had learned to be patient.

"You are distressed," it said, in a voice like a held note. "We have been surveying your species. Your distress is loud. Yours is among the loudest."

"Cool," Eli said, because his heart was going too fast for anything smarter. "Sorry?"

"Do not apologize. We wish to understand. We perceive you directly. The pattern of you." It flickered. "You are a boy."

Eli's throat closed. Nobody had ever said it like that. Not as a concession, not with a sigh, not *if that's what you want.* Just a fact, like gravity.

"Yeah," he whispered. "I am."

"Then we do not understand. Why does your shell disagree with you? Why do the others argue with something so obvious?"

"I don't know," he said, and laughed, and was horrified to find he was crying. "I've been asking that for like four years."

The shimmer considered this. "This is a small error. We may correct it. Do you wish it?"

He thought of binders and blood tests, waitlists and paperwork and his dad's face.

"Yes," he said. "God, yes."

---

He woke up in his own bed. Sunlight. His phone on the floor.

He didn't go to the mirror right away. He lay there and breathed, and his chest rose flat and easy beneath his T-shirt. He said "good morning" to the ceiling, and his voice cracked low, rough, unmistakable.

Downstairs, his father looked up from the coffee pot and went very still.

"Eli?" he said.

It was the first time.

Somewhere far above the atmosphere, something patient made a note: *Small error. Corrected. The others will take longer.*

In A.D. 2101, war was beginning, and Ensign Priya Okonkwo was the only person on the bridge who knew it didn't have to.

The transmission had come in eleven minutes earlier, a dense braid of harmonics from the ship hanging off Jupiter's shoulder like a black tooth. The translation matrix had chewed on it for nine of those minutes and spat out a single line, which now glowed on the main screen in letters three feet high:

ALL YOUR BASE ARE BELONG TO US.

The captain had gone pale, then red. Somebody near the weapons station had said, quite clearly, "Somebody set up us the bomb," which made no sense, but nobody was making sense anymore.

Priya stared at the raw harmonics on her own console. The matrix was a cheap contract job, rushed into service when the first signals arrived. It flattened tone. It ignored the rising seventh that ran beneath the whole message like a held breath.

In every fragment she'd studied for two years, that rising seventh meant *offered*. Not taken. Given.

*All that you stand upon, we will stand upon with you.*

It wasn't a threat. It was a vow. The Cats, as the tabloids had insisted on calling them, weren't claiming Earth. They were asking to join it.

"Captain," she said.

"Not now, Ensign."

"Sir, the translation is wrong."

He turned. Every face on the bridge turned. The weapons officer's hand hovered over the panel, and Priya understood with sudden clarity that history was a matter of who spoke first and who was believed.

"Explain," the captain said. "Quickly."

She did. She talked faster than she ever had, about harmonic modality and tonal inversion and a seventh that meant everything. When she finished, the silence lasted long enough that she could hear the hum of the reactor.

Then the captain exhaled. "Open a channel," he said. "Tell them we accept."

Priya's hands shook as she composed the reply. She checked it three times.

For great justice, she thought, and sent it.

The first sign was the alarm clock. I slapped it like always, and my hand just bounced off. Then I noticed the clock was bolted to a steel slab, the slab was bolted to the floor, and the floor had fist-shaped dents in it like a hailstorm had hit it from above.

By noon I'd figured it out. Everyone here could bench-press a minivan. Doors were vault doors. Forks were titanium. Eggs came in reinforced cartons labeled *DO NOT GRIP*, and most people just bought them pre-scrambled.

By Tuesday, I was famous.

"You opened a jar of pickles," the government agent whispered, staring at me like I'd parted the sea. "And the jar is still *intact.*"

They called me the Gentle. I got a costume, soft gray with a feather on the chest. My first mission was defusing a bomb, because the last bomb squad had snipped a wire and accidentally cut through the bomb, the table, and part of Ohio. After that I rescued a cat from a tree without uprooting the tree. I signed a treaty without punching through the desk. I carried a Ming vase across a museum while a crowd of four hundred held its breath so hard the windows bowed.

Then, one night, they called me to a hospital.

A woman lay in a bed made of steel cable, her breathing shallow, ninety-four years old. Her family stood pressed against the far wall, hands jammed in their pockets, fists clenched white.

"She wants someone to hold her hand," her grandson said, voice cracking. "We've never... none of us have ever been able to."

I sat beside her. Her fingers were thin as paper. I wrapped mine around them, barely any pressure at all.

She smiled. "Oh," she breathed. "So *that's* what it feels like."

Her grandson cried without making a sound, careful even with that.

I've defused eleven bombs since then. That's still the mission I'm proudest of.

The clerk at the Department of Classification had a stamp for everything. Merchant, in sensible brown. Guard, in navy. Healer, in a soothing green. She'd once had to dig Bard out of the bottom drawer, and she told me this proudly, the way people tell you about the time they saw a celebrity.

Then she looked at my card and stopped talking.

"Wizard," she said finally.

"Is that bad?"

"It's not in the system." She typed, frowned, typed again. "The dropdown ends at Woodcutter."

My stats, once she printed them by hand, were not inspiring. Intelligence 14. Strength 6. Mana: 3/3. One spell.

*Light: Produces a small flame at the fingertip. Cost: 1 mana. Duration: 4 seconds.*

Twelve seconds of fire a day. My cousin Derek, a level 3 Fighter, could already deadlift a pony.

The news vans came the next morning, and with them a historian from the university, a thin man who kept touching my sleeve like I might evaporate. The last Wizard, he said, was a man named Aldous Venn, one thousand and fourteen years ago.

"What level did he reach?"

"Ninety-nine."

"What did he *do*?"

The historian smiled. "The records say he 'unmade the war.' They don't say which war. That's rather the point, I think."

Nobody could tell me how Wizards leveled. Fighters fight. Merchants sell. I tried everything. I meditated. I chanted. I waved a stick at the cat until she bit me.

Then, at two in the morning, bored and miserable, I finished a library book on tidal patterns, and a soft chime sounded behind my eyes.

*+2 XP.*

I read another. *+2 XP.* A textbook on soil chemistry. *+5 XP.*

It took four hundred pages to reach level 2. My Light spell now lasts five seconds.

That's fine. I hold it under the blanket and turn the page.

Aldous had time. So do I.

Deke spots him first, through the shattered window of a Walgreens: a shape crouched behind the pharmacy counter, rifle across his knees.

"Scav," Deke says, and the word does what it always does. Marta drifts left. Boone thumbs off his safety.

Rules are rules. Armed strangers don't get conversations. They get the first bullet, because the alternative is that they give it.

Then the shape lifts its head and I see the chipped front tooth. Owen. Owen, who broke that tooth on my parents' diving board when we were eleven. Owen, who drove four hours to sit with me in the hospital after Dad. Owen, who I'd assumed was dead, because everyone was dead.

He sees me. His mouth opens.

"Vote," Boone says. It's a formality. Three hands go up. Boone looks at me.

"I know him," I say.

"Knew," Marta corrects. "Eight months, Cal. You don't know what he's done to still be breathing."

She's right. But I don't know what *I've* done either, not in any way I'd say out loud. The things that kept me fed. The family on Route 9.

Owen sets the rifle on the counter, slow. Raises his hands. "Cal," he says, voice cracking. "Cal, it's me."

Boone presses his pistol into my palm. That's the other rule: you know them, you handle it. You prove where your loyalty sits.

The gun is heavy. Owen is crying now, and I'm thinking about the diving board, the wet click his tooth made on the concrete, how he laughed with blood on his lip and said *don't tell your mom.*

I raise the pistol.

I turn.

Boone first, because he's fastest. Then Deke. Marta gets one shot off that punches through a box of Cheerios before I put her down.

Then it's quiet, and Owen is staring at me like I'm the thing that crawled in from the street.

"Pick up your rifle," I tell him. "We've got maybe ten minutes before the noise brings them."

Grandpa shed on a Tuesday, which seemed wrong to me. Something that big should happen on a Sunday.

He did it in the bathroom, the way most people do, with the door locked and the fan running so nobody would have to hear. When he came out, he was twenty-six, tall, with a jaw like a shovel blade and hair so black it looked wet. He was holding the old skin over his arm like a coat he'd forgotten to hang up.

"Well," he said, in a voice I'd never heard before. "That's done."

Grandma took the skin from him without a word. She folded it carefully at the shoulders and the knees, the way she folded flags at the Legion hall, and she carried it upstairs to the cedar chest.

The new Grandpa remembered everything. He remembered teaching me to bait a hook, and the name of my first dog, and the exact amount of pepper Grandma liked in her eggs. He fixed the gutters in an afternoon. He laughed more. His knees didn't click on the stairs.

But Grandma started sleeping in the guest room.

"He's still him," I told her one night, because I was fifteen and thought I understood things. "It's the same person."

She was sitting on the floor beside the open cedar chest, one hand resting on the folded skin. Her own hands were spotted and thin, the knuckles swollen like knots in old rope.

"I know he is," she said. "But this is the face that cried when your mother was born. These are the hands that held mine at the hospital. I spent fifty-one years learning every line of this." She smoothed a crease. "I'm not ready to start over with a stranger who knows all my secrets."

"Will you shed someday?"

She closed the chest gently.

"No, honey. Somebody has to remember what we looked like."

The prosecutor had built her case on a single fact: Elias Marrow could not lie.

Everyone knew it. His coworkers, his ex-wife, the barista who'd once asked if he liked her haircut and received a careful, devastating answer. Eleven years of verbal honesty so total it had become a local curiosity.

So when Detective Royce found the bloody scarf in Marrow's car, when the fibers matched, when the timeline fit, the District Attorney did something unprecedented. She put the defendant on the stand herself.

"Mr. Marrow," she said, smiling at the jury. "Did you kill Margaret Hale?"

The courtroom leaned forward.

Elias folded his hands. He had known this question was coming for three weeks. He had spent those weeks in a quiet cell, smiling at the ceiling.

"No," he said.

Silence. Then murmurs, then chaos. The prosecutor's smile faltered.

"Mr. Marrow, you understand you're under oath."

"I always am."

"Then explain the scarf in your car."

"I can't. I didn't put it there."

She tried for an hour. She asked where he'd been that night. Home, reading Dostoevsky. She asked if he'd known the victim. Never met her. She asked, desperate, if he had ever harmed anyone at all.

"Objection," said his attorney. "Relevance."

"Sustained."

The jury deliberated for forty minutes. Everyone knew Elias Marrow could not lie.

On the courthouse steps, cameras flashing, he spotted Detective Royce leaning against a pillar, jaw tight, hands shoved deep in his coat pockets.

Elias walked over.

"Ten years," Royce muttered. "Ten years I've known what you are. I just needed one to stick."

"You chose poorly," Elias said. "Forty-three, and you planted evidence for the one I didn't do."

Royce paled.

"Which raises an interesting question, Detective. Where did you get her scarf?"

Royce said nothing.

Elias buttoned his coat against the wind and smiled.

"I never lie," he said. "So believe me when I tell you: I'll be seeing you soon."

The first one knelt in a parking lot in Duluth, in front of a woman named Marcy Kowalski who was loading groceries into her Corolla.

By the end of the week there were eleven thousand of them, kneeling on every continent. They didn't kneel to presidents or popes. They knelt to whoever happened to be nearest: a bus driver in Lagos, a teenager in Osaka, a man selling churros outside a stadium in Monterrey.

Marcy, as the first, got the translator.

"Why?" she asked it. The question had been asked a million times by then, by smarter people with better microphones, but the creature had waited for her.

It made a sound like wind through tall grass. The translator, after a long pause, said: *We do not end.*

They had no death, it explained. Their bodies repaired themselves, their memories were perfect, their stars were young. Nothing they made was ever lost, because they never left it. They had lived a billion years and had never once built anything they wouldn't be around to see finished.

Then they found our signals. Old ones, drifting outward. Lullabies. A man reading a eulogy for his brother. Construction footage of a cathedral that took six hundred years to complete, every mason who laid its first stone long dead before the last.

*You plant trees whose shade you will not sit in,* the translator said. *You teach children to remember you, knowing they will forget. You love what you cannot keep. Every one of you. Every day.*

Marcy thought about her father, who had spent his last summer rebuilding a boat he knew he'd never sail. She'd thought it was sad, then. She'd thought it was stubbornness.

*Where we come from,* the creature said, *only a god would do something so impossible.*

Marcy looked down at her groceries: the milk that would spoil, the bread that would go stale, the flowers she'd bought for no reason at all.

She handed it a daisy.

It wept.

Every year, on the twelfth of March, the tall customer came into the shop.

Margaret had owned Second Chapter Books for thirty-one years, and she had learned not to look at him too directly. It wasn't that he was frightening, exactly. It was more that her eyes kept sliding off him, the way they slid off a word you'd read so many times it stopped meaning anything.

He always went to the same shelf. Fantasy, P. He always ran a bony finger along the spines, slowly, with the air of a man visiting a grave.

"Looking for anything in particular?" she asked, the first year.

JUST SEEING WHAT'S IN, he said. His voice arrived without passing through the air.

He always bought one. A battered paperback, cracked spine, someone's bus ticket still tucked inside as a bookmark. He paid in old coins that she never quite managed to examine before they were simply ordinary money in her till.

This year, curiosity won.

"What do you do with them?" she asked. "You must have a whole shelf by now."

He considered this.

I LEAVE THEM, he said. HOSPITAL WAITING ROOMS. TRAIN STATIONS AT TWO IN THE MORNING. ON THE BEDSIDE TABLES OF CHILDREN WHO HAVE BEEN TOLD THEY ARE TOO MUCH.

"Why?"

He held the book up to the light, as if checking it for watermarks.

HE WROTE ME KINDER THAN I AM, he said. AND THEN, SOMEHOW, I WAS.

Margaret didn't know what to say to that, so she bagged the book, and he took it, and the little bell above the door rang as he left, though she never saw the door open.

Outside, the wind carried the sound of somewhere far away: a click-clack of shutters on a tower that wasn't there, passing a message that never quite arrived, because it was never meant to.

GNU, it said.

The tall customer paused, and listened, and smiled.

The signs went up on a Tuesday. Same wording on every door, from St. Brendan's to the Al-Noor mosque to Temple Beth Shalom:

*CLOSED UNTIL FURTHER NOTICE. PLEASE PRAY AT HOME. QUIETLY, IF YOU CAN.*

By Thursday, the town was furious. Weddings were postponed. Funerals were moved to the Elks Lodge. My editor wanted answers, so I spent a week getting doors shut in my face by every clergyman in the county.

Father Delgado just shook his head. Imam Rashid smiled apologetically. Pastor Lynn told me, very kindly, to go home and hug my kids.

It was Rabbi Feldman who finally cracked, mostly because I caught him at two in the morning, carrying a thermos of soup up the synagogue steps.

"You'll print it," he said.

"Probably."

He studied me for a long moment. Then he sighed and unlocked the door.

Inside, every pew was empty except the very last one. Sitting there, hunched over, was an old man in a coat too thin for October. He wasn't glowing. He wasn't anything. He looked like someone who'd been awake for a very, very long time.

The rabbi set the soup beside him. The old man nodded his thanks without looking up.

"He walked into St. Brendan's first," Feldman whispered as we stepped back outside. "Then the mosque. Then here. Same thing every time. Sat down in the back and asked if he could have one week. Just one, where nobody asked him for anything."

I stared at the door. "That's... that's who I think it is?"

"We had a meeting. All of us. Decided it was the least we could do, after everything."

"People deserve to know."

"People," the rabbi said gently, "would line up around the block. With lists."

I thought about my own list. My mother's diagnosis. The mortgage. My daughter.

I went home. I didn't write the story.

That night, I hugged my kids, and for the first time in my life, I prayed without asking for a single thing.

The dragon came on Tuesday, which was inconvenient, because the lich had been booked for Tuesday.

Wenna Holloway, Undersecretary of the Royal Office of Imminent Doom, stared at the scheduling ledger while the castle shook around her. Plaster sifted into her tea. Somewhere above, a trumpet blew the three short notes that meant *peril, considerable*.

"It's early," said Corvin, her clerk, peering out the arrow-slit. "It's a full week early. And it's brought friends."

"Wyverns aren't friends. They're opportunists." She ran her finger down the page. The prophecy of the Seventh Son was due Thursday. The Sundering of the Northern Ward was penciled in for the solstice. The farm boy with the mysterious birthmark had arrived yesterday and was already asking where he might find a wise old mentor.

The Kingdom of Aldermere had been in peril for three hundred and twelve consecutive years. Wenna knew because she had the records. Every so often some bright young courtier suggested that perhaps, just once, they might try being *not* in peril, and every so often the Office let them. The last attempt had lasted nine days. Taverns emptied. Blacksmiths went bankrupt. The bards, with nothing to sing about, began composing ballads about crop rotation, and the people nearly rioted.

Peril, it turned out, was the kingdom's chief export. Heroes came from every corner of the world to be tested here. They bought swords, maps, and rounds for the house. They married local girls and settled down to bore their grandchildren with stories.

"What do we do?" Corvin asked.

Wenna dipped her quill and drew a neat arrow, moving the lich to Friday.

"Send the farm boy," she said. "Tell him the dragon killed his uncle."

"He doesn't have an uncle."

"Then he'll have a very confusing character arc." She sipped her plaster-flecked tea. "Ring the bells, Corvin. The kingdom needs saving."

She smiled. It always would.

Grandpa's typewriter had been clacking since before I was born. It was the sound of every summer I spent at his house: the steady rhythm through the wall, the ding of the carriage return, the occasional pause while he lit his pipe. Fifty years, Grandma used to say, rolling her eyes. Fifty years and never a word of it shown to anyone.

I was nineteen before I finally asked.

He didn't look up. He finished his sentence, pulled the page free, and set it face-down on a stack taller than my forearm. Then he nodded at the shelves behind him. I'd always assumed they held old tax records. Forty-some binders, each labeled with a year.

"Go on," he said.

I pulled down the first one. The opening page was dated the day my father was born.

*Today the milk cost thirty cents. Your mother laughed at a dog chasing its own tail outside the hospital window. The Hendersons painted their fence green, which everyone agrees was a mistake.*

I flipped forward. A page for every day. The weather. Songs on the radio. What the neighbors argued about. What my dad said at breakfast when he was four, and nine, and sixteen.

"I wanted him to know what the world was like," Grandpa said. "Not the history-book version. The real one. The small things nobody writes down."

The binders kept going past 1998, past the accident. I opened one at random. *Today your son lost his first tooth. He looks more like you every day.*

My throat went tight. "You kept writing to him."

"Didn't know how to stop." He rolled a fresh sheet into the machine, then hesitated, hands hovering over the keys.

Slowly, he stood and pulled out the chair.

"My fingers aren't what they were," he said. "And somebody ought to tell him about today."

I sat down. The keys were cool and worn smooth.

*Today,* I typed, *I finally asked.*

Gerald Pinch was Double-O Fourteen, which meant he held a license to audit.

Not to kill. That was Seven, down the hall, whose door Gerald passed every morning on his way to the room with the broken radiator. Seven's door had a brass plaque. Gerald's had a Post-it note, curling at the corners, that read *00-14 (EXPENSES) - KNOCK LOUDLY, HEATER IS ON.*

His car was a 2006 Vauxhall Astra from the motor pool. It had no ejector seat, though the passenger door did occasionally eject itself on roundabouts. His gadgets, issued personally by Q Branch, consisted of a calculator with a paper roll and a stapler that Q had described, with visible boredom, as "fairly robust."

"Tuesday," M said, sliding a folder across the desk. "Montenegro."

Gerald's heart lifted. "A mission, ma'am?"

"In a sense. Seven was there last month." She tapped the folder. "Casino chips, four point two million. One Aston Martin, submerged. A hotel suite, partially exploded. And a line item that says only, and I quote, 'Martinis, various.'"

Gerald opened the folder. The receipts were stained with what he hoped was champagne.

"The Treasury wants it reconciled by Friday," M said. "Or they cut our budget by a third."
