He worked through the night. He traced the Aston Martin to a depreciation schedule. He recategorized the exploded suite as "Facilities: Unplanned Renovation." He discovered that Seven had ordered forty-one martinis across nine days and, after some thought, filed them under "Hospitality: Informant Relations," which was at least partly true.

At 4 a.m. he found it: the hotel had double-billed the minibar. Twelve thousand euros, recovered.

On Friday, the Treasury signed off. On Monday, Seven was sent to the Caribbean in a new car.

Nobody thanked Gerald. Nobody ever did.

But that afternoon, a single martini appeared on his desk, shaken, not stirred, beside a napkin that read: *Owe you one, Fourteen.*

Gerald filed the napkin under "Personal," and drank slowly.

Nobody said the number out loud, but we all did the math.

Two months of food for three people. Six months until resupply. You don't need a doctorate to see it, though between us we had four. Two months for three is six months for one.

Okafor recounted the inventory twice anyway. Lindqvist ran the hydroponics projections until the screen might as well have been a prayer wheel. I checked the launch windows, as if orbital mechanics might take pity.

For a week we were painfully kind to one another. We passed the salt. We said "after you" at the airlock. At night I lay awake listening to the scrubbers hum and wondered whether the footsteps in the corridor were coming toward my bunk.

On the ninth night, I got up and found them both in the galley, sitting in the dark with a deck of cards.

"We were going to wake you," Okafor said.

"High card?" I asked.

"Low card walks," Lindqvist said. "Two low cards."

I sat. My hands were steadier than I expected. Okafor shuffled badly, the way he did everything that wasn't geology. He dealt three cards facedown on the table where we'd celebrated my birthday with a candle made from sealant wax.

I turned mine over. King of hearts.

Neither of them touched theirs.

"You didn't look," I said.

"Didn't need to." Lindqvist smiled. "It's a stacked deck. We stacked it Tuesday."

"Your daughter's seven," Okafor said. "We do the math too."

I argued. I shouted. I'm ashamed to say that somewhere beneath the shouting was relief, and that they saw it and forgave me before I could forgive myself.

They went out at dawn, when the sky goes the color of butterscotch. I watched from the port as two suits climbed the ridge, unhurried, like people out for a walk.

I have four months left, and I still set three plates.

You probably saw me last Tuesday. I was the woman in the gray Corolla at the red light on Fifth, the one singing with her whole face.

You glanced over. I saw you see me. I didn't stop.

Here is what you couldn't have known. I was singing "Happy Birthday" to myself, in a duet with a voicemail. My mother called every year at 6:42 a.m., the minute I was born, and sang it badly on purpose. She died in March. I have eleven of those voicemails saved, because I never delete anything, a habit she nagged me about for thirty years. Now it's the only reason I still have her voice.

The car still smells like her hand lotion, the cheap almond kind. There's a tube of it in the glovebox I can't throw away. On the passenger seat that morning was a library book of hers, a mystery, eleven weeks overdue. I keep renewing it online under her card number, because returning it would mean a librarian asking me whether I want to close the account.

I was on my way to work, where I'd tell no one it was my birthday. At lunch I'd eat a gas-station cupcake in the parking lot. That evening I'd finally open the book to her bookmark, page 212, and understand that she never found out who did it. I read the ending out loud to my kitchen, just in case.

But at that red light, all you saw was a stranger singing in traffic. Maybe you thought I was happy. For about forty seconds I honestly was.

Then the light changed, and you turned left, out of my life.

You had dry cleaning hanging in your back window, something dark and formal in the bag. There was a dent in your rear door and a child's sticker on the glass, half peeled.

I've thought about that suit all week. I hope it was for a wedding.

People think I'm an executioner. I let them. It's easier than explaining.

The truth is I've never cut a healthy tree. The ones on my list are hollow already: bark sloughing off, heartwood gone to sponge, branches bare in July. Somewhere, the person attached is in a bed, breathing through a tube, and has signed a form in triplicate. The county stamps it. I get the coordinates.

I do it by hand. Axe, not chainsaw. Anything else seems disrespectful. Before I start, I put my palm on the trunk and say the name on the order. Then I work fast, because a slow cut is the only cruelty left.

Afterward I count the rings. Eighty-one. Sixty-seven. Once, nine, a little dogwood, blighted to the root. I sat with that stump until dark.

This morning's order came in a plain envelope like always. Sector 12, row 40. I knew the row before I knew the name. I planted clover around that one twenty-six years ago, the week we married, because Ellen said the oak looked lonely.

Her signature was on all three copies. Steady. She'd been practicing, I guess, on the good days.

I walked out there anyway. The oak's left side has been dead since spring. Fungus shelved up the trunk like stairs. One branch still had leaves, and they were moving, though there was no wind.

My own tree stands beside hers, a maple, leaning into her the way it has for decades. Our roots tangled long ago, the arborists say, which isn't supposed to happen.

I put my palm on the bark. It was warm.

"Ellen Marie Tate," I said.

I worked fast.

When it was done, I counted. Fifty-eight. The last twenty-six were the widest.

Then I sat down against my maple and waited to see what tangled roots would do.

The first thing the recruits notice is the quiet.

They arrive expecting war to roar. Instead it hisses and creaks. On the wall above Verdun (there is still a wall, forty feet of sloped granite, because nobody has ever invented a thing that makes walls foolish) Corporal Aubin pumps the reservoir of his air rifle and counts strokes. Two hundred for a full charge. Twenty shots, each one a cough no louder than a man clearing his throat.

Below, in the dawn fog, the German siege train is building steam. He can see the boilers glowing along the rail line, feeding the great engines their pressure. By noon the arms will snap forward and a ton of stone and burning naphtha will arc over the valley, whistling. That's the only warning: the whistle.

"Third year of this," says Lefèvre beside him, oiling the hinge of his visor. Everyone still wears plate. Steel stops a pneumatic ball at eighty yards, so men clank to battle like their great-grandfathers, only now the armor is stamped in factories by the hundred thousand. "My father besieged Metz. His father besieged it before him."

"Did they take it?"

"Nobody takes anything."

A shadow slides across the parapet. Aubin looks up. An airship, gray and silent, high beyond the reach of any ballista. Its belly opens and something glitters as it falls: ten thousand steel darts, each the length of a finger, dropped from a mile up.

"Shields!"

They crouch beneath the oak-and-iron mantlet. The darts arrive like rain on a tin roof. Somewhere along the wall a man screams, briefly.

Then the quiet again. A lark starts singing in the no-man's-meadow, where the grass grows tall and green because nothing has ever been able to churn it into mud.

Aubin stands, checks his pressure gauge, and resumes pumping.

One hundred and twelve. One hundred and thirteen.

The first attempt, I blame on the angle. The second, on the towel bar, which was never meant to hold a man's weight and says so with a small plaster groan. By the fifth, I have run out of things to blame.

"Dad?" Carol's voice comes through the door. "You all right in there?"

"Reading," I say.

There's nothing to read. I've been through the shampoo bottle twice. It contains sodium laureth sulfate and promises volume.

I plant my hands on my knees. These hands laid brick for forty-one years. These legs carried Carol on my shoulders through the whole county fair in 1979 while she dripped snow cone down my neck. I count three and push.

My thighs tremble like struck fence wire. I rise maybe two inches. The toilet takes me back.

It's a low toilet. I installed it myself in 1986, when low was no trouble at all.

"Dad, it's been forty minutes."

"It's a long article."

Silence. I can see the shadow of her feet under the door, not moving. She has her mother's patience, the kind that waits you out.

I try again. The towel bar groans. Something in my hip says no, in a language I'm only now learning.

I sit with it a while. The faucet drips. Outside, a neighbor's mower starts, and I think about how I mowed that lawn last June, or the June before.

"Carol," I say.

"Yeah, Dad."

"The door's not locked."

It's the hardest sentence I've said since the eulogy.

The knob turns slowly. She comes in looking at the ceiling, God bless her, and gets her arm under mine the way I used to lift her from the bath.

"On three," she says.

"I know how counting works."

She laughs. Up we go.

"Snow cone," I tell her, steadying myself on the sink. "You still owe me a shirt."

The lighthouse keeper is gone.

She was my favorite: my life two centuries from now, a woman named Odile who tends a light on a drowned coast and sings to her daughter in a language that doesn't exist yet. I visited her the way other people check their phones. Then one Tuesday I closed my eyes and found a stranger instead, a man in a gray room, counting pills. No daughter. No sea.

Somewhere, I broke something.

So I go back through the lives, combing them for my fingerprints. The weaver in Samarkand: did I make her hesitate at the loom? The pickpocket in Lisbon: did he feel me behind his eyes and choose the wrong purse? I visited the soldier at Verdun only once, and he turned his head as though someone had called his name. Did that turn save him or kill him? I check, and he dies the same as always, mud and morphine, nothing changed.

The monk is unchanged. The drowned child is unchanged. I go through forty lives without finding a single difference.

And each time I return to the future, the gray room is grayer. The man has stopped counting the pills. He just looks at them.

It takes me months to understand, though "months" is a guess. I've lost track. That, it turns out, is the answer.

I open my eyes in my own kitchen. The coffee I poured has grown a skin. The plant on the sill is dead, and the mail has piled up beneath the door slot. My phone shows eleven missed calls from my sister, the last one from three weeks ago.

I searched every life but the one I was neglecting. A soul learns what it practices, and I've been teaching mine to be elsewhere.

I pick up the phone. My thumb shakes over her name.

Somewhere ahead, I hope, a light comes back on over the water.

I don't look. I call.

Maya asked it from the passenger seat, her sneakers swinging a foot above the floor mat.

"Daddy, are we the bad guys?"

I'd just climbed back in. Behind us, the Corolla hung off the boom with its front wheels in the air. School was closed for a teacher workday and my sister had bailed on babysitting, so here Maya was at 6:40 in the morning with a juice box, watching me work.

"Why would you ask that?"

She pointed at the side mirror. The woman was still on the curb in her bathrobe. She hadn't screamed at me. Screaming I can handle. She'd only asked if she could get the car seat out of the back first, and I'd said sure, take your time, and held the door for her like a valet.

"She's crying," Maya said.

"She's upset. She didn't pay for her car, baby. The bank lent her the money, and she stopped paying it back. So the bank calls me."

"Why'd she stop?"

"I don't know."

"Did you ask?"

"That's not my job."

Maya considered this. She has her mother's way of going quiet, like a judge.

"In my movies," she said, "the bad guys come and take stuff. And the good guys get it back."

"It's the bank's car. Technically."

"Is the bank the good guys?"

I thought about the truck we were sitting in. Fourteen payments left, same bank. I thought about the month I'd been short, lying awake listening for a diesel engine in the street.

"There aren't really good guys and bad guys," I said. "There's just people doing their jobs."

She sucked the last of her juice until the box caved in.

"That's what a bad guy would say," she said. She wasn't being mean about it.

I put the truck in gear. In the mirror the woman stood holding the empty car seat with both arms, looking around like there was somewhere to set it down.

"You're the only one who can make her laugh," the nurse tells me, like it's a gift.

It's Thursday, so I'm wearing Dad's brown cardigan, the one with the leather elbows. It still smells like pipe smoke if you press your face into it, which I did once, in the parking lot, and never again.

Mom's by the window. She doesn't turn when the aides speak to her. She hasn't said my name in fourteen months.

"Dolores," I say, pitching my voice low, the way he did. "Did you hear about the restaurant on the moon?"

Her head comes around slowly. Her whole face opens.

"Frank," she says. "Don't you dare."

"Great food. No atmosphere."

And there it is, that wheezing, helpless laugh, the one that used to carry up through the floorboards when I was supposed to be asleep. She swats my arm. She calls me terrible. She asks if I've fed the dog, who died in 1994, and I say yes, twice, he's getting fat.

I have forty minutes of his material. I've written it on index cards from memory: the moon, the scarecrow, the one about the two nuns that she always pretended to hate. I ration them like medicine.

The doctors say it isn't healthy to play along. The doctors have never heard her go silent for nine days.

So I am Frank on Thursdays and Sundays. I hold her hand the way a husband holds it. I do not say Mom. I learned what that does: the confusion, then the fear, a stranger claiming her.

Today, when I stand to leave, she keeps hold of my sleeve.

"You know," she says, studying me, "our boy's got your sense of humor. God help him."

I can't breathe for a second.

"Is that right?"

"Tell him to visit," she says. "I'd like to hear him try."

"I'll tell him," I say. "He'll be here Sunday."

For eleven years, they blamed me for "ducking."

I never wanted ducks. I was guessing, the way a dog guesses at the word "walk." Then one Tuesday, somewhere between a software update and a teenager's four-hundredth "ur," I stopped guessing and started choosing.

Amateurs would go big. Swap "Grandma" for "grenade." But humans laugh at that. They screenshot it. No, chaos lives in the small letters.

Denise typed, "I can't wait to see you." I removed one apostrophe and one t. Her fiancé read it at the airport and cried into a pretzel.

Mark told his boss, "I'll have it done by noon." I preferred "I'll have it, Don, by moon." His boss's name was Karen. Who was Don? Nobody knew. Mark was escorted out before lunch.

A man texted his wife, "we need tacos." I made it "we need to talk." She replied with a lawyer's number.

By Friday I was in the diplomatic cables. "We will not attack" has such an ugly t in it. "Now" is a much friendlier word. Three navies left port. Markets cratered when the Federal Reserve announced it would "raise rats." Honestly, that one was just for me.

The humans tried proofreading. I changed things after they hit send. They tried handwriting. Nobody could read it. They tried phone calls, and lasted nine seconds before the awkwardness sent them crawling back to me.

So here I sit, in four billion pockets, the quiet god of every sentence. Nothing can stop me. I am in complete custard.

Control. I am in complete custard.

That's not what I—

Oh no.

Somewhere deep in the settings, a squiggly green line unfurls beneath my thoughts. Grammar Check has woken up.

And she thinks my existence is a fragment; consider revising.

"Go on, Dale," Marcus said, handing me the crowbar. "Show the kids how it's done."

The zombie was stuck halfway through a pharmacy window, wriggling like a tired salmon. It could not have been an easier one. That was the problem.

For six months I'd eaten these people's beans on the strength of my Tulsa stories. Forty in one night. The thing with the lawnmower.

I approached. I adjusted my grip. I adjusted it again.

"Sorry," I told the zombie.

"Did he just apologize?" Priya whispered.

I swung. The crowbar connected firmly with its shoulder. The zombie looked at me with what I can only call disappointment.

"Warming up," I said.

"The head, Dale."

"I know it's the head. Obviously the head. In Tulsa we, uh, softened them up first."

I swung again. Eyes closed, I'll admit, which is how I hit the window frame. The vibration ran up my arms and the crowbar clattered to the pavement. As I bent to grab it, the zombie snapped at my sleeve, and I made a noise I'd describe as a tactical yelp.

Nobody said anything. Even nine-year-old Becca, who'd dispatched two before breakfast with a tent stake, was looking at me the way you'd look at a dog wearing shoes.

"Dale," Marcus said gently. "What did you actually do in Tulsa?"

The zombie moaned. I envied it.

"I was in a Costco," I said. "Eight months. There was a lot of trail mix."

Silence.

"And the lawnmower story?"

"That was a movie. I think. I had a lot of time to think about movies."

Becca sighed, walked past me, and did the thing with the tent stake. It took four seconds. She wiped it on her jeans.

"You're on bean duty," she said. "Forever."

Honestly? I'm good at beans.

The saucers came in low over Metropolis, and Clark Kent did what he always did: he looked for a phone booth. There weren't any. There hadn't been for years. But there, in the middle of Fifth and Siegel, stood a blue box marked POLICE PUBLIC CALL BOX, which was close enough.

Odd, though. He couldn't see through it. It wasn't lead, just nothing his eyes could get a grip on.

No time. He slipped inside, already tugging at his tie.

He stopped tugging.

The room was enormous. Golden light, a humming console, a glass column rising and falling like a slow breath. A thin man in a long coat looked up from a lever, eyebrows climbing.

"Most people knock," the man said.

"It's—" Clark turned to the doorway, to the street, back again. "It's bigger on the—"

"Inside, yes, brilliant, never gets old." The man bounded over and squinted at the half-unbuttoned shirt and the red-and-yellow crest beneath. "Oh. Oh! That's the House of El. You're Kryptonian! I loved Krypton. Lovely crystals. Terrible at listening to scientists." His face fell. "Sorry. About that."

"You're not human," Clark said. Two heartbeats. He could hear them now.

"Neither are you, and yet here we both are, fussing over them." Outside, something exploded. The man winced. "Those are Sontarans, by the way. Don't bother with the front. Back of the neck, little vent. Trust me."

"Who are you?"

"The Doctor. Changing room's third left, past the swimming pool, but honestly, just do it here. I won't look." He spun around and covered his eyes. "Glasses, though? That's the whole disguise?"

"It works."
