A blur, a rush of air, and the cape settled. The Doctor peeked through his fingers and grinned like a child.

"Oh, that's good. Right then, Superman." He threw open the doors onto the burning sky. "You take the high ones. I'll go have a word with whoever's in charge."

"Just a word?"

"It's usually enough."

We named it Tombstone, because Okafor said gallows humor was the only kind left.

Fourteen months out, it was a smudge with a mass estimate that made the room go quiet. Rock doesn't come that big. Six sextillion tons, give or take. Not a dinosaur-killer. An everything-killer.

At nine months, the albedo came back wrong. Too bright. Too blue.

At six months, Webb resolved it, and I spent an hour convinced someone had loaded the wrong file. I knew that coastline. Everyone knows that coastline. The horn of Africa. The boot of Italy. Clouds spiraling over an Atlantic that was not our Atlantic.

"Lensing," Okafor said. "Some kind of reflection."

But reflections don't have a night side, and this one did, and the night side glittered. Lagos. Cairo. The long bright seam of the Nile.

At four months we picked up radio. The linguists had nothing to translate. News anchors with familiar voices were reading familiar words: object on a collision course. Extinction-level. Scientists baffled.

They'd named us Tombstone, too.

I don't know what it is. Nobody does. The physicists talk about branes and folds, a universe creased like a sheet of paper until two points touch. The priests have their own versions. It doesn't matter. It's still six sextillion tons, and so are we.

Last night I aimed the big dish at a mountaintop in their Chile, at the observatory I knew would be there, and I sent the only thing I could think of. Not math. Not a warning. Just: *Hello. It's me.*

The reply came in eleven minutes. That was light there and light back, with no time spent deciding.

*Hello. I know.*

Then, a moment later, from both of us at once, the same four words crossed in the dark between worlds:

*What do we do?*

Question seven was a nightmare, so I did what I always do: I reached for Dana Okafor's mind, two rows up, where the answers lived in tidy, color-coded rows.

*Covalent bonds share electrons,* Dana thought, obligingly.

I wrote it down.

*NO CHEATING IN MY CLASSROOM!*

The voice hit like a slammed door. My pencil snapped. I looked up, couldn't help it, straight at Mr. Hale, the new chemistry teacher, three days on the job, who sat at his desk calmly grading papers.

He wasn't even looking at me.

Then he was.

His pen stopped. His eyebrows climbed slowly toward his thinning hairline. Around us, twenty-six students kept scribbling. Nobody else had heard a thing.

*You heard that,* he thought. Not booming now. Almost a whisper.

I considered playing dumb. But you can't really play dumb inside your own skull.

*...Yes, sir.*

Mr. Hale set down his pen very carefully, like it might go off.

*Thirty-one years,* he thought. *Four schools. I think that at every class, first exam, every time. Just in case. Like shouting into a canyon.* A pause. *Nobody's ever looked up.*

I'd expected anger. What came through instead was something huge and shaky, a feeling I recognized from every crowded hallway of my life: hearing everyone and being heard by no one.

*I thought I was the only one,* I admitted.

*So did I.* His mouth twitched. He picked the pen back up and pretended to grade. *My mother told me I'd made it up. I half believed her.*

*Mine too.*

Silence, both kinds. Dana turned a page.

*See me after class,* Mr. Hale thought. *We have a great deal to talk about.*

*Yes, sir.*

*And erase number seven.*

*Sir—*

*Covalent bonds, kid. It's in chapter three. I'm delighted you exist, but you're still getting a zero.*

Daniel Pruitt cried in my office for forty minutes before I agreed to take his case. I'd have taken it in four seconds, but a reputation is built on reluctance.

"I didn't kill those women," he said.

"I know," I told him, and it was the only honest thing I said all year.

The trick to losing well is to fight magnificently. I filed every motion. I got the knife excluded over a rookie's sloppy chain of custody, and the papers called me a magician. I shredded the eyewitness on cross until she admitted she'd been drinking. Reporters wrote that Pruitt had the best defense money couldn't buy. I was working pro bono, naturally.

Then I visited his garage. Defense attorneys are entitled to inspect a client's property, and nobody searches a lawyer's briefcase on the way in. Behind the paint cans I left a coffee tin: four earrings, none matching, each one a memory I was sorry to part with.

After that I only had to be thorough. I demanded, loudly and on the record, that the prosecution re-examine the garage. Their original search had been incompetent, I said, and a proper one would exonerate my client. Judge Whitlow granted it. I'd have been disappointed in her otherwise.

You should have seen the detective's face when he opened that tin. Mine, too. I'd practiced in the mirror for a week.

I fought on. My closing made two jurors cry. They convicted in three hours anyway, and outside the courthouse I told the cameras the system had failed an innocent man, my voice cracking exactly where I'd marked the page.

Daniel shook my hand through the bars. "You did everything you could," he said.

"More than you know."

The appeal will fail. I'm writing it myself, and it's excellent work.

I do miss the earrings. But the city feels safe again, the detectives have gone home, and a careful man can always start a new collection.

I learned people by their hands. My mother's were chapped and quick; my father's drummed the table when he lied. Faces were smooth white ovals, blank as porcelain, and nobody else seemed to find this strange. When I asked my mother, at six, why she wore hers, she laughed, the sound muffled, and said, "What a thing to say."

So I stopped saying it.

I walked through school barefaced among the blank. I assumed that was why people found me difficult: everything showed on me, and nothing showed on them.

I met Daniel at a bus stop. He had a scar across his left knuckle and a way of tilting his head when he listened, as though pouring my words into one ear. I fell in love with the tilt. I married a white oval and didn't mind.

On our wedding night he sat on the edge of the hotel bed and reached behind his head. I heard a small click.

The mask came away like a shell.

Underneath was a crooked nose, pale eyelashes, a mouth that was shaking. It was the first face I had ever seen besides my own in mirrors, and it was terrified.

"You can see it," he whispered. "Can't you? My whole life I've watched all of you in those white masks. I thought I was the only one with a face."

"Daniel," I said. "I've never worn a mask."

He tilted his head. Then he lifted the scarred hand and reached toward me. His fingers stopped an inch short of my cheek and rested there, on something. I felt nothing. I heard the tap of a fingernail on porcelain.

"Hold still," he said gently, reaching behind my head. "I think there's a clasp."

The first thing I heard in a thousand years was a woman's voice saying, "Greetings, valued customer."

I opened my eyes. The light was soft and amber. A face hovered over me, bald, kind, and tattooed with something that shimmered.

"Your satisfaction is our priority," she said carefully, like someone stepping across ice. "Do you accept?"

"Accept what?" My throat felt full of sand.

She brightened. Behind her, a dozen others leaned in, whispering in a language like water over stones. She was the only one who spoke mine, I realized. If you could call it that.

"I am Oru. I study the Old Tongue. Many writings survive." She pressed her palm proudly to her chest. "Terms. Conditions. Limited-time offers."

I laughed, and it hurt, and I kept laughing. Ten centuries gone and all we'd left behind was the fine print.

Then I remembered, and the laughing stopped.

"My daughter." I tried to sit up. "Mila. She was seven. They froze us together, she was sick, they said someday there'd be—" I grabbed Oru's sleeve. "Where is she?"

Oru's brow furrowed. She was translating, searching through a vocabulary built from advertisements and warranty cards for words that could hold what I was asking.

"Small one," she said finally. "Yes. Beside you." She gestured, and the crowd parted. There was a second pod, frosted white, its lights pulsing slow and green. "Sickness is... discontinued. Recalled. No longer available."

I was crying before she finished.

"We wake you first," Oru said. "So small one does not wake alone. This is correct?"

"Yes," I whispered. "That's correct."

The pod began to hiss. The frost was retreating from the glass, and beneath it I could see a shape, a small hand.

Oru saw me trembling. She frowned, reaching for the right phrase, and found one.

"Please hold," she said gently, and took my hand in hers.

"Shut the dog up," Mom says, not turning from the sink.

It's 6:15. Biscuit is planted in front of Dad's recliner, barking. It isn't the mailman bark or the squirrel bark. It's the high, stupid, whole-body one he used to save for the sound of the truck turning into the drive.

He's done it every evening for the three weeks since the funeral.

"Biscuit. Hey. Come on." I hook two fingers under his collar. He lets me drag him a foot across the carpet, tail going like a windshield wiper, then twists free and goes right back. He sits. He lifts one paw the way Dad taught him. He waits for a hand that isn't there to shake it.

"Danny." Mom's voice cracks down the middle. "Please."

I try the treat jar. I try the leash, jingling it by the door. Biscuit glances at me, almost apologetic, then returns his attention to the empty chair and barks again, softer now, conversational.

The water shuts off. Mom stands in the kitchen doorway with suds to her elbows. I brace for the yelling. She yelled the first week. The second week she put him in the garage, and we both lay awake listening to him cry.

Tonight she just looks. She looks at the dog and at the chair, with its cushion still dented and the armrest worn pale where his elbow went.

"What does he see?" she whispers.

"I don't know."

Biscuit's tail thumps. His head tips up and back, eyes half-closing, exactly the way it does when someone finds the spot behind his left ear.

Nobody is touching him.

Mom makes a small sound. She crosses the room, drying her hands on her jeans, and lowers herself onto the carpet next to the dog. She leans her shoulder against the side of the recliner, careful, like it might be sleeping.

"Never mind," she says. "Let him bark."

I sit down too.

At 6:40, same as always, Biscuit goes quiet.

We stay a while longer anyway.

My great-grandmother told my great-grandfather she'd marry him when pigs fly. That was October 1909. On November 4th, an Englishman strapped a pig into a wicker basket, tied the basket to his biplane, and took off. By the 5th, Nana Ruth was standing at an altar in her sister's dress, bewildered, saying "I do."

That's how it worked. Nobody chose. Every promise ever sealed with those words simply came due, like a bill slipped under the door of the world.

Some of it was lovely. Landlords fixed things. Brothers who hadn't spoken in thirty years showed up on each other's porches, holding pies they didn't remember baking. A senator from Ohio read every bill before voting on it, and his successors, bound by some heckler's forgotten sneer, still do.

Some of it wasn't. My uncle Dale's boss gave him a raise every morning for eleven years, until the company folded. The Cubs have won every Series since; nobody in Chicago bothers to go anymore. Somewhere in Nebraska there's a man who has been apologizing to his wife continuously since the Taft administration. They keep him in a nice facility. He seems sincere.

And it never stopped. That's the part the history books underline. The pig stays flown. So we learn early, the way other children once learned not to touch the stove. In kindergarten they teach you to stop mid-sentence. You'll see people do it on the bus, saying "I'll forgive her when..." and then clamping their teeth shut and staring hard at their shoes.

Those words are only ever spoken on purpose now, in courtrooms and chapels, with witnesses. It's the strongest oath we have.

Nana Ruth stayed married for sixty-one years. I asked her once, near the end, if she'd ever come to love him.

"When hell freezes over," she said.

Then we both looked out the window, just to check.

The knock comes at 8:15. Three hits, flat of the fist, the way it has every morning for six years.

I open the door with the coffee already poured. Two sugars. He'll say he doesn't want it.

"Don't want it," Dale says, filling the doorframe. "You know what day it is, Pruitt."

"Tuesday the ninth."

"Tuesday the ninth." He cracks his knuckles. "Mr. Abruzzo's been patient."

Mr. Abruzzo has been in federal prison since 2019, but that's page three. I hand over the binder.

Page one is the receipt, laminated: *PAID IN FULL*, signed by Dale himself. He squints at it like he always does.

"That's my handwriting."

"It is."

The first year, I paid him four times before I figured out what the accident had done to him. The second year, I moved. He found me in nine days. He's very good at the part of his job he still has.

Page two is the doctor's letter. Page three is the newspaper clipping, Abruzzo in handcuffs. Dale reads it twice, lips moving. Page four is a photo of the two of us at my wedding, him in a rented tux, crying.

"I was your best man?"

"You asked every morning for a month. It seemed rude to keep saying no."

He lowers himself onto the porch step. This is the hard part, the minute where a big man finds out his Tuesday ended years ago. I sit down next to him and hold out the coffee. He takes it.

"Two sugars," he says, surprised.

"Lucky guess."

He drinks. A sprinkler ticks somewhere down the street.

"So what do I do now?"

"Eggs," I say. "You like my eggs. Then you help me with the crossword and tell me Marlene's too good for me."

"Is she?"

"Yes."

He nods and stands. At the door he stops and points a finger the size of a bratwurst at my chest.

"If you'd been late, though..."

"I know, Dale." I hold the screen door open. "See you tomorrow."

The doctors say I was gone for ninety-one seconds. Heart attack, kitchen floor, a Tuesday.

People ask about the light, the tunnel. There wasn't one. There was a train platform, small and rural, like the one in the town where I grew up. Wooden benches. A clock with no hands. It didn't frighten me.

Then I saw Maggie sitting on the far bench.

My wife. She was the one pounding on my chest right then, in the world I'd left. But there she sat, ankles crossed, wearing her yellow cardigan, the one with the tortoiseshell buttons. The second button from the top was missing; a little tuft of thread stuck out where it had been.

She looked up and her whole face broke open with relief.

"There you are," she said. "Oh, Daniel. I've been waiting so long."

I tried to ask what she meant. She stood and reached for my hand, then stopped and frowned at something behind me.

"Oh," she said softly. "Not yet. That's alright. I'll keep waiting."

Then I was on the linoleum with a cracked rib, and Maggie was above me, sobbing and counting compressions, wearing her yellow cardigan.

All the buttons were there. I counted them in the ambulance and again in the hospital. Five.

I've been home three weeks now. Everyone says I'm quiet. They think it's the fear of dying, and I let them. It's easier than explaining why I watch her on the stairs, why I've started driving her everywhere, why I hid the stepladder in the garage. She laughs and calls me her shadow.

I've thought about throwing the cardigan away, or burning it. But I think it would only be some other yellow cardigan, some other loose thread.

This morning she came down for coffee, kissed the top of my head, and asked if I'd seen her sewing kit.

Every morning, Walter Briggs painted his hair with boot polish, strapped his spine straight with a surgical corset, and did forty loud jumping jacks at the window so the neighbors could see.

He was eighty-three. According to his papers, he was fifty-nine, and had been for some time.

The trick wasn't the polish. Anyone could buy polish. The trick was the job. Walter worked the front desk at the Bureau of Vitality, District Nine, where citizens reported on their sixtieth birthdays for Retirement. He stamped the forms. He pointed down the warm hallway. He said, "Thank you for your contribution," forty times a day, in a booming voice he practiced in the shower.

Nobody looks for a mouse in the cat's mouth.

He learned the new slang from the pneumatic bulletins. He complained about his knees only in the lavatory. When the young supervisors, forty or forty-five, asked his age, he laughed and said, "Old enough to know better, young enough to do it anyway," and slapped them on the back hard enough to hurt his hand for a week.

On Tuesday, a woman came to his window. Her papers said Doris Hale, fifty-four, routine address change. Her hair was very black. Too black, and shiny at the temples where polish had met sweat. Her hands, flat on the counter, were spotted like a ripe banana, and she'd tried to powder them.

She saw him looking. He watched her eyes go past him to the hallway and its warmth.

Walter examined her birth year. The 6 had been a 3 once. Decent work. Better than his.

"Mrs. Hale," he boomed, "you want Window Six. Down the *cold* hallway." He stamped the form and slid it back, and with it, tucked underneath, his own tin of polish. "This brand doesn't run," he murmured.

Her fingers closed over it.

"Thank you for your contribution," Walter said, and winked, which his eyelid took a moment to recover from.

Then he straightened his corset and called, "Next!"

Walt comes in every other Thursday, give or take. He rolls up his left sleeve, lays his arm on the rest, and says, "One more, please."

I've been doing this for six years. The tallies started at his wrist, neat bundles of five, and now they've climbed past his elbow. A hundred and forty-some. Each takes me four minutes. He tips twenty dollars and never flinches.

I didn't ask for the longest time. In this business you learn that people tell you things when they're ready. I had my theories, though: days sober, a body count, a prison thing. My apprentice was sure he was a hitman. Walt is seventy if he's a day and drives a Buick with a tissue box in the back window.

Year three, I finally asked.

"I volunteer at St. Anne's," he said. "The hospice. Some folks don't have anybody. So I sit." He looked at his arm the way you'd look at a photo album. "I'm bad with names now. But I don't want to lose count of them."

After that, I stopped charging him. He kept leaving the twenty anyway.

This spring, the Thursdays stretched. Three weeks. Then five. When he did come in, his arm was thinner, the skin loose around the ink. He joked that I was running out of room. I told him he had a whole other arm.

Then it was July, and no Walt.

Yesterday, a young woman in scrubs came in. She held her phone out, showing me a photo of a forearm I'd know anywhere.

"He said you'd know what to do," she said. She sat down, turned her wrist up, and laid it on the rest. Her eyes were red, but her voice was steady.

"He didn't go alone," she said. "I sat."

I set up my machine, just like always.

"One, please," she said.

It took four minutes. I didn't charge her.

She left a twenty anyway.

The house slept. That was the first thing you had to understand. The house slept, and Daniel Okafor did not.

It was 2:47 in the morning, and on the second shelf of the refrigerator, behind the mustard, lay the last square of lasagna.

He had dreamed of it. He had woken with its name on his lips.

Now he stood before the microwave, plate trembling in his hands, and knew what every man learns eventually: there is no turning back. He set the plate inside. The door closed with a click like a rifle bolt. Upstairs, a floorboard settled. Daniel did not breathe for nine seconds.

Nothing.

He entered the time. One. Three. Zero. Each button shrieked into the dark like a church bell rung by a madman. He pressed START, and the machine roared awake, a great humming beast, its amber light sweeping the kitchen like a searchlight across a prison yard.

Ninety seconds. Empires had fallen in less.

The numbers bled away. 0:45. A bead of sweat traced his temple. 0:20. His hand rose, hovering at the door release, steady as a surgeon's, steady as a bomb technician's.

Too early, and the center would be cold, a frozen heart inside a molten body, and all of this would have been for nothing. Too late, and the beep would come. Five beeps. Long ones.

His wife was a light sleeper. She had been saving it for lunch.

0:03.

He thought of his children.

0:02.

He thought of his father, who had never once said he was proud.

0:01.

He struck.

The door swung wide. The hum died. The display froze, one second from catastrophe, and silence poured back into the kitchen, holy and total.

Daniel wept without sound. He lifted the plate with both hands, the way one lifts a newborn or a crown.

The fork slid off the rim.

It hit the tile like a cathedral collapsing.

Upstairs, a light came on.

"Daniel?"

My grandmother had one answer for everything.

When the Hendersons' goat was elected to the school board: "Stranger things have happened." When Uncle Dale walked into his own funeral, sunburned and apologizing, having been in Tampa the whole time: "Stranger things have happened." When it rained fish on the Fourth of July, she just went and fetched a skillet.

Nothing rattled her. I think that was the point. The phrase was a fence she'd built around the world, and in eighty-one years nothing had ever gotten over it.

Then, on a Tuesday in March, the moon hatched.

We watched from the porch, the whole family. The cracks spread slow and bright across its face, like someone had tapped it with a spoon. Pieces drifted away. Something unfolded from inside, wet and enormous, the color of pearl, and stretched wings that blotted out Orion. It shook itself. Forty miles off, the tide went out of the bay all at once, and we heard it go.

Nobody spoke. One by one, we turned to look at Grandma.

She sat in her rocker with her tea going cold. Her mouth opened. I watched her reach for it, the old fence, those four trusty words.

She closed her mouth. Opened it again.

"Well," she said finally. "No. I don't suppose they have."

Uncle Dale started crying. Honestly, it was scarier than the moon.

She sat quiet a long minute. Above us the creature tried its wings, wobbled, and let out a cry that set every dog in the county howling. It was a thin, cracked sound, and I realized, listening, that it was the sound of something very young.

Grandma sighed, set down her cup, and stood.

"It'll be hungry," she said, and went to get the skillet.

Osh found me in a bus station, which is fitting. He is the god of lost things, and I had been one for years.

"I have no priests," he said, in a voice like coins rattling in a dryer. "No temples. Find me believers, and what's mine is yours."

My first convert was a widow who was tearing her kitchen apart. I closed my eyes, felt a tug behind my ribs, and pulled her wedding ring from the drain trap. She wept. She believed. The tug grew stronger.

After ten converts, I could find keys, wallets, and the other sock.

After a hundred, I could find dogs. I'd walk into the woods and come out with someone's shivering beagle, and by nightfall the whole family would be whispering Osh's name over dinner.

After a thousand, I found a child. She had been gone six days, and I walked straight to the culvert as though following a string. The news called it a miracle. I called it Osh. Forty thousand people learned his name that week.

It was different after that. I found a sunken ship. I found a man's sobriety behind a dumpster in Tulsa and handed it back to him. I found a woman's faith in herself, which she had lost in 1987. Lost causes, lost time, lost nerve. If it was gone, I could feel where it went.

Kings wrote to me. I had a temple, then twelve.

Last night, Osh came to me again, and he was vast now, bright as a struck match.

"You've done well," he said. "You can find anything."

"Anything," I agreed.

"Then I have one request." The great voice cracked, and he sounded like coins in a dryer again. "There were others once. Brothers. Sisters. The world stopped saying their names, and they went where forgotten gods go."

I felt the tug behind my ribs, enormous and pointing down.

"Please," said my god. "I've been looking for so long."

I picked up my coat.

The name was there when I woke, dark as a bruise along my left forearm.

*Daniel Okafor.*

I scrubbed it anyway, though everyone knows scrubbing does nothing. I scrubbed until the skin around the letters went raw and the letters themselves stayed crisp, patient, in handwriting that wasn't mine.

I had gone to bed at ten. The deadbolt was still thrown. My shoes sat dry by the door, and the car in the garage was cold. There was no blood under my nails and no ache in my knuckles. I checked my phone for calls I didn't remember making and found nothing. I had never met a Daniel Okafor in my life.

So I typed his name into the search bar, hands shaking, expecting a stranger's face and a crime scene I couldn't explain.

I got the stranger's face. He was thirty-four, smiling, holding a little girl on his shoulders.

*Daniel Okafor died early this morning at St. Mary's Hospital, surrounded by family. He had been in a coma for three years following a hit-and-run on Route 9. The driver was never identified.*

I read it four times.

Route 9. Three years ago. October.

There had been rain that night, the kind that turns the windshield to static. I'd had two glasses of wine at my sister's, only two. Somewhere past the reservoir there was a thud, a shudder through the steering wheel, a shape gone before I could see it.

A deer, I told myself. I said it out loud, alone in the car, and I did not slow down.

I said it again the next morning when I saw the dent. I said it to the mechanic two towns over, who didn't ask. I said it so many times it became a memory of a deer, with antlers and everything.

Downstairs, someone knocked.

I pulled my sleeve down over his name. Then, slowly, I rolled it back up, and went to answer the door.

Mara was four when I first opened it. I expected scribbles: purple dogs, staircases made of soup. Mine at her age had been exactly that.

Instead: *The lighthouse keeper's daughter had been born with the tide in her, and so twice a day she left.*

I read until dawn on the floor of her room, the book warm in my lap, her breath steady above me.

I told myself it was just for the rent. I typed up the first forty pages, chose a pen name, and sent them off. Three publishers answered within a week. They called it luminous. They asked where I'd learned to write about the sea.

I had never seen the sea.

Each night brought a new chapter. Each morning I copied it by the hall light before she woke. We moved to a house with a garden. I bought her a red bicycle and told myself this was the same as giving back.

By six, she'd stopped telling me her dreams at breakfast. "I don't remember," she'd say, stirring her cereal, watching me.

The second book sold better than the first. The third, readers said, was sadder. A thief had entered the story, a quiet man who came to the lighthouse each night and carried off the daughter's footprints, one by one, until she could no longer find her way back to shore.

I typed it anyway.

Last night's chapter was a single page.

*The keeper's daughter knew about the thief. She had always known. She left the door unlatched, because he looked so tired, and because footprints were only footprints. But she had begun to wonder what he would do if she simply stayed awake, and whether he would still come and sit beside her bed if there was nothing left to take.*

It's past midnight now. Her lamp is on. I can hear her humming.

I'm standing outside her door with empty hands, trying to remember how to knock.

My grandmother is a pear tree behind the church. She was sharp in life and her pears are sharp too, hard and sour until the first frost, then suddenly sweet. That's her all over.

We plant our dead with a seed in the mouth. Nobody chooses the seed; the keeper reaches into his sack blind. Somehow it always fits. The schoolteacher came up a straight ash. Old Tomas, the drunk, became a willow that leans into the creek. My father, who never sat still, is an aspen, and even on windless days his leaves tremble like he's got somewhere to be.

My brother Eli was six when the fever took him. The keeper drew an acorn. Mother wept, because oaks are slow, and she wanted to see him tall before she went herself.

For three springs nothing came up. People stopped mentioning it. An empty plot means a soul that didn't rest, and no one would say that to my mother's face. She watered the bare dirt anyway, every evening, telling it about supper and the weather.

The fourth spring I found her kneeling there, not moving. I thought the worst. Then she lifted her hand, and under it was a sprig no longer than my finger, with two lobed leaves.

"He always was hard to get out of bed," she said.

Mother is old now. I measure myself against Eli every birthday, the way we used to against the doorframe, and this year he finally passed me. She's asked to be planted beside him, closer than the keeper likes. The roots will tangle, he warns.

"Good," she says.

I don't know what seed he'll draw for her. Something that flowers, I think. But I know that in a hundred years there will be an oak here wide enough to shade the whole churchyard, and something small and blooming beneath it, holding on.

The DNA site said *100% match*, which isn't a thing siblings get unless they shared a womb. His name was Dale Mercer. I drove four hours to meet him and instead watched, through a diner window, as he made a waitress cry over hash browns.

I stayed a week. I learned that Dale owned three apartment buildings with no heat, that he parked in handicapped spaces as a matter of principle, and that he had once sued a Little League.

I also learned that I had his face.

So I didn't knock on his door.

It started small. I tipped the waitress two hundred dollars and apologized as Dale. I visited his tenants, one by one, and promised new boilers by December, in writing, with a signature I'd practiced off his court filings. I shook hands. I held babies. I told Mrs. Okafor in 2B that her rent was frozen for life, and let her record it on her phone.

Dale started getting hugged in the street. He hated it. I watched him peel a grateful old man off his coat like a tick.

Then the lawyers called him about the boilers. Then the newspaper ran "LOCAL LANDLORD'S CHANGE OF HEART," with a photo of me smiling in his lobby. He couldn't deny it without explaining that he'd never do anything so decent. He tried anyway. Nobody believed him. That was the beautiful part: an entire town holding him, cheerfully, to promises he found repulsive.

Last night he sat in his car outside the diner, hands at ten and two, staring at nothing. I think he suspects he's losing his mind, that some better man wears his skin while he sleeps.

I'm in the booth by the window, the same seat he had. The waitress brings me pie on the house.

"You've really changed, Dale," she says.

"Not yet," I say, watching him through the glass. "But I'm working on him."

The watch buzzes when she hits the corner of Alder and Fifth. *Ghost Runner loaded.*

Two dots appear on the little screen. The blue one is her. The gray one is Daniel, on October 14th, two years ago, the last morning he ran this loop.

He starts fast. He always started fast, and she used to yell at his back about it.

"Negative splits, idiot," she says to the empty street, and goes after him.

She knows this run the way she knows the scar on his chin. He surges on Maple, where the downhill made him cocky. At mile two he loses eleven seconds retying a shoelace he never learned to double-knot. He slows at the Hendersons', where he must have stopped to scratch their terrible beagle.

The first year she couldn't keep the gray dot on the screen. He'd be gone by the reservoir, and she would walk home crying.

Now she's fast. She has fourteen months of mornings in her legs, and something in her chest has scarred over hard and light. By the reservoir she is on his shoulder. The watch tells her so with a cheerful chirp: *0:02 behind.*

She can almost hear him breathing. She can almost smell the coffee he'd have spilled on his shirt.

The last half mile is flat. He faded there that day, tired or maybe saving something for a tomorrow he assumed was coming. She has plenty left. She could take him easily. The watch would play its little fanfare and stamp a trophy on the screen, and the road ahead would be empty.

She eases off.

The gray dot pulls ahead. Three seconds, then five. It turns onto their street and stops at their driveway, where it has stopped four hundred times.

*Ghost Runner wins,* says the watch.

"Tomorrow," she tells him, hands on her knees, like she does every morning.

She goes inside.

Dr. Okafor said "unprecedented" three times, which is how I knew she was scared too.

The short version: something in my brainstem has quit. Awake, I breathe because I remember to. Asleep, nobody's at the wheel. A machine could do it for me, she said, for a while, and then she explained what "a while" meant.

That was nine days ago.

You learn things. Coffee stops working on day three. Cold showers on day five. Pain lasts longest. I keep a rubber band on my wrist, and the skin beneath it looks like raw meat. By day six, the wallpaper crawls. By day seven, my dead father sits at the kitchen table doing the crossword, and I've stopped minding. He's good company. He never asks how I'm feeling.

My wife asks constantly. She sets alarms, takes shifts, shakes me when my chin dips. She's lost weight she can't afford to lose. Last night I found her crying in the garage, quietly, the way you cry when you've decided someone can't know.

Tonight our daughter climbed into my lap with a book about a bear who can't hibernate. She's four. She read it to me, memorized, mostly, turning pages at the wrong times. Somewhere around the bear counting snowflakes, she went heavy and warm against my chest, her breath slowing into that small, perfect tide.

Nobody's at her wheel, either. It just happens. It's the most ordinary miracle in the world, and I never noticed it until it was taken from me.

My wife is asleep on the couch, finally, phone slipping from her hand. The alarm is set for twenty minutes.

I reach over and turn it off.

My father looks up from his crossword. "Seven letters," he says. "'To give up willingly.'"

"I know, Dad."

I hold my daughter. I count her breaths. One. Two.

They're so easy to follow.

The rules took me two funerals to learn.

The first was my mother's. I won a radio contest the morning her brakes failed, and I didn't connect the two. The second was my best friend Tom's. He asked me to pick his lottery numbers, and I did, gladly. He was struck by a delivery truck on his way to cash the ticket.

After that, I moved forty miles past the last paved road. I grow tomatoes that never blight. I attempt very little. My sister writes monthly, and I answer but never visit. I won't sit at her table drinking up her luck like well water.

It's from her letters that I know about Mr. Dane.

He bought the mill, then closed it. He bought the town's mortgages next, hers among them. He has been patient and smiling about all of it, a man harvesting a field.

Last Tuesday, his black sedan came up my road.

"People say things about you," he said, settling uninvited onto my porch. "They say horses win when you bet on them."

"People say that."

He slid a folder across the railing. It held three companies. "Pick one. I'll invest and you'll get ten percent."

So I told him everything. I told him about my mother, and about Tom and the truck. I said that anyone who reaches for my luck loses their own, at once and badly. I said it plainly, looking him in the eye, because I wanted my conscience clean.

He laughed. "Pick."

I picked.

He tucked the folder under his arm, whistling. I watched his sedan descend the switchbacks toward the old river bridge, the one the county has been meaning to inspect.

I've turned it over many nights since. I warned him, and warning him was my attempt. He didn't listen, so by rights I failed for once in my life.

But everything I attempt works in my favor.

So I wonder what I was really trying to do.

My sister's letter came yesterday. The bank has lost her paperwork.

The first three weren't my idea.

A technician named Dolores gave them to me in a room kept cold for the machines. One on my sternum, one under each arm. She used a needle and a drop of India ink, and each took less time than a sneeze.

"So we aim at the same spot every time," she said. "Sorry. They're permanent."

I laughed at that. Permanent was not a word anyone had been using around me.

Thirty-three sessions. Each morning I lay still while red lasers found my dots and lined me up like a rifle sight. I came to hate them. Three blue-gray specks, small as freckles, that meant: here, this is where you went wrong.

When it was over, when the scans had come back clean twice and I'd started letting myself buy things like next year's calendar, I went to a shop on Delancey. The artist was a big man named Marcus with a hummingbird on his throat. I pulled my collar down and showed him.

"Can you cover it?"

He looked for a while. "I could," he said. "Or I could give it company."

So he did. He added stars, tiny ones, scattered across my chest and ribs. Forty-one in all, some no bigger than Dolores's. He joined a few with lines thin as hair. When he finished, I stood at his mirror hunting for the original three and couldn't find them.

"What constellation is it?" I asked.

"Don't know. It's yours. Name it."

I couldn't think of anything. But that night my daughter, who is six, traced the lines with her finger while I read to her and announced that it was obviously a dog. A big one, running.

So that's the story. I have a dog made of stars, and somewhere inside it are the three I didn't choose. I couldn't point to them now.

I've stopped looking.

I stubbed my toe on the dresser at 6 a.m.

"God—"

"Yes?"

The voice was warm, attentive, and directly behind my left ear.

"Nothing. Toe."

"Ah." A pause. "It's not broken."

"Thanks."

This is my life now. It started in April, no explanation, no burning bush. Just an omnipotent being with the response time of an anxious waiter.

At work, Brenda showed me her engagement ring. "Oh my God," I said.

"Yes?"

"It's—not you. The ring."

"It is a nice ring," He agreed. Brenda asked who I was talking to. I said nobody, which felt blasphemous.

I've tried substitutions. "Gosh" works. "Jeez" does not; different department, same family, and He's chattier. I haven't had a second date since March, and I'd rather not explain why, except to say that there are moments when a person calls out without thinking, and a polite "Yes? Yes? Yes?" really kills the mood.

"You could just not answer," I told Him once.

"I could," He said. "I never have."

"Not once?"

"Everyone thinks I do. It's the listening they have trouble with."

I didn't have a response to that, so I did the dishes.

Then in November, my mother fell. The hospital called at 2 a.m., and I drove through rain with both hands locked on the wheel, and I sat in a plastic chair under lights the color of old teeth while a surgeon did things behind a door I couldn't open.

I held out for an hour. Then, very quietly, on purpose for the first time:

"God?"

"Yes."

Not a question, this time.

I opened my mouth. Nothing came. I didn't know what to ask for, or how, or whether asking was allowed after seven months of telling Him to hush.

"I don't have anything," I said. "I just wanted to check."

"I know," He said. "I'm here."

Neither of us said anything else. He stayed anyway.

The light came through Eli's window at 2 a.m., soft and green, like the glow-in-the-dark stars he'd never taken off his ceiling.

He should have been scared. Instead he sat up, binder still on because he'd fallen asleep in it again, ribs aching, and watched three tall shapes fold themselves into his bedroom.

*We apologize for the intrusion,* one said, though nothing like a mouth moved. *We are surveying. Your signal was loud.*

"My signal?"

*The mind-pattern and the shell disagree. We heard it from orbit.* It tilted its head, curious. *Among our kind, this is a small repair. Like a splinter. Why has no one removed your splinter?*

Eli laughed, and it came out wet. "It's complicated here. There are waiting lists. Paperwork. My grandma still calls me..." He stopped. "It's complicated."

The three conferred in a shimmer of color.

*It is not complicated,* the tall one decided. *You are a boy. The shell is mistaken. Would you like it corrected?*

Sixteen years of birthday candles. Every shooting star. Every coin in every fountain.

"Yes," he whispered. "Please."

*We change nothing of you,* it said, reaching out a hand like warm glass. *Understand this. You were always exactly who you are. We are only helping the outside catch up.*

The light swelled, and Eli slept.

He woke to sunlight and birdsong and a chest that rose easily, with no ache or pressure. He lay there for a long time with his palm flat against his sternum, feeling his own heartbeat.

On the nightstand sat a small green stone, still faintly glowing.

"Eli!" his mom called up the stairs. "Breakfast!"

"Coming!" he shouted, and his voice cracked, low and rough and unfamiliar and *his*.

He laughed until he cried. Then he pulled on a T-shirt, just a T-shirt, and went downstairs.

The first explosion tore through the aft decks at 0347.

"What happened?" Captain Arlen was out of his chair before the alarms began.

Mechanic Osei's voice crackled over the intercom, raw with smoke. "A bomb, sir. Somebody planted it during the peace talks. They were setting us up from the start."

"Captain." The operator turned from her console, her face pale in the emergency lights. "We're receiving a signal."

"What?"

"The main screen is turning on by itself. I can't stop it."

The viewscreen flickered, and there he was: the cybernetic face, the single green eye, the smile that had sat across the treaty table only six hours before.

"It's you," Arlen breathed.

"How are you, gentlemen?" The voice came through a translation matrix, each word slightly wrong, a language worn like an ill-fitting coat. "All your base are belong to us."

Someone on the bridge laughed, a nervous little bark. Then the tactical display updated, and nobody laughed again. Luna Station was gone. Ceres was gone. Mars Orbital, where Arlen's daughter was stationed, had gone dark. Every base.

"You are on the way to destruction," CATS continued pleasantly. "You have no chance to survive. Make your time."

The screen went dark, but the laughter lingered, tinny and distorted, until the speakers died.

"Captain?" The operator's voice was very small.

Arlen stared at the dead screen. There were forty-one ZIG fighters in the hangar, and their pilots were mostly kids. There were no bases left to fall back to. The treaty was ash, and the reactor would breach within the hour.

Make your time. The mistranslation had it right, he thought. Time was the one thing he could still make.

"Launch every ZIG," he said quietly. "All of them. They know what they're doing."

He watched the fighters peel away from his dying ship, forty-one sparks against an endless dark, and gave the only order he had left.

"For great justice."

The order said forty cubits.

I know this because I wrote the order. I also wrote the copy sent to the quarries, and somewhere between the first and the second, my reed slipped, or the beer was strong, or the gods wanted a laugh. Forty became four hundred and forty.

Nobody questions a scribe. That is the whole point of scribes.

By the time I visited the site, ten thousand men had already leveled a patch of desert the size of a small city. Foreman Meru greeted me with the cracked grin of a man who had not slept since the last flood.

"Ambitious, our king," he said.

I looked at the foundation. I looked at the original order. I ate the original order.

"Very ambitious," I agreed.

For twenty years I waited to be fed to crocodiles. Stone came down the river in blocks the size of oxen. Whole villages sprang up just to bake the bread. The treasurer wept openly in meetings. And Khufu, Lord of the Two Lands, who had asked for a tasteful tomb somewhat nicer than his father's, never once came to look, because kings do not visit construction sites.

Then, one morning, he did.

They carried him out on his chair as the sun rose behind it. The thing swallowed the horizon. Nobody breathed. Meru had quietly positioned himself near a camel.

Khufu stared for a long time.

"Is it bigger than my father's?"

"Considerably, Majesty."

He nodded slowly, as a man does when he discovers he is a genius.

"Exactly as I envisioned." He turned to his son. "Yours will be smaller."

I am old now. Travelers come from everywhere to stand beneath it, and I hear what they whisper: that its proportions hold the secrets of the stars, that no mortal mind could have conceived it.

They are half right. It holds exactly one secret, and it is that I cannot hold my beer.

Danny still bites his thumbnail when he's scared. That's how I know it's him under the beard, the grime, the thirty pounds he's lost.

He's kneeling in the pharmacy aisle, wrists zip-tied in front of him, thumbnail between his teeth. His revolver lies where Cobb kicked it. Marla keeps her shotgun on him while the others go through his pack.

"Armed. Alone. Scouting for somebody," Marla says. "We vote."

Four hands go up. They look at me.

Eight months ago, Danny and I were splitting a pizza on his couch, arguing about whether to renew the lease. He drove me to the hospital when my appendix burst. He was going to be best man at a wedding that never happened, because the world ended in March.

He hasn't said my name. He looked at me once, when they dragged him out from behind the counter, and then he looked at the floor. He's protecting me. If they know he's mine, I'm a liability too.

"Well?" Cobb says.

I think about the rules. The rules have kept us alive. No strangers. No witnesses. No exceptions. We made that last one after Tulsa, after the girl with the kind face led twenty men to our door.

I raise my hand.

"Unanimous," Marla says. "And it's your turn in the rotation, kid."

She's right. It is. I pick the revolver up off the floor. His revolver, the one his grandfather left him. I thumb the cylinder open. Six rounds. He always kept it full.

Danny lowers his hands. "Make it quick," he says, to nobody.

"I will."

I snap the cylinder shut and stand where I can see all of them.

Four of them. Six rounds.

Marla's the fastest, so Marla's first.

The Registry clerk frowned at her screen, then at me, then at her screen again.

"It says Wizard."

"Is that bad?"

"It's not in the dropdown." She scrolled. "Warrior, Warden, Weaver, Welder. No Wizard."

Behind me, the line of eighteen-year-olds grew restless. My cousin Dev had just walked out a Level 1 Merchant, same as his father, same as mine. Mom had already ordered me an apron with the shop logo.

The clerk called a supervisor. The supervisor called a man in a nicer suit. The suit made a whispered phone call, and then everyone stared at me the way you'd stare at a dog that had started speaking French.

"The last one," the suit said, "died in 1021."

"Of what?"

"Records are unclear. Possibly a goose."

That's the thing nobody tells you about wizards. I pulled up my sheet on the walk home: four hit points. The strength of a damp towel. One spell, Light, usable once per day. Dev had "Haggle" and had already saved eleven percent on lunch.

No trainers. No guild. No spellbooks, because they'd been pulped centuries ago to make room for accounting manuals. For a thousand years the world had decided it didn't need us, and leveled up accordingly.

Mom cried. Dad asked if a Wizard could still work a register.

That night I sat on the roof, feeling stupid, and cast my one spell.

A small glow bloomed in my palm, soft and warm, a color I had never seen before. It didn't flicker like a bulb. It breathed.

Down the street, a porch light went out. Then a streetlamp. Then, block by block, the whole city dimmed, as if leaning in to look.

And in the dark, far off across the hills, something that had been waiting a thousand years lit an answering glow.

A notification chimed.

*Quest received.*

Every mother in London believes she left the window open by accident.

I know better. I have seen him come across the water at dusk, laughing, another child trailing behind him in a nightgown, drunk on dust and promises. He tells them they will never have to grow old. He does not tell them what happens to the ones who do anyway.

I have counted the boys. There were eleven last spring. There are six now, and none of them is any taller.

My men think I am mad to keep hunting him. They are tired; they want open sea and honest plunder, and I cannot blame them. But I had a mother once. I remember what it is to be missed. Somewhere beyond that second star there are nurseries with beds still made, night-lights still burning, and women who have stopped speaking to their husbands.

So I stay.

He took my right hand, you know. Cut it off as a game and tossed it to the beast that prowls the lagoon, and he crowed while I bled. A child's cruelty is the purest kind, for it has no memory to trouble it. He will not remember me tomorrow. He does not remember the boys he has buried. He forgets, and forgets, and stays young.

I do not forget. I wear the iron so I cannot.

Tonight he has brought three more: a girl and her two brothers. The girl is clever. She keeps looking back toward home. I think if I could only get her aboard and show her the charts, the way back, she would listen.

They will call it kidnapping. He will make a story of it, with himself as the hero, and they will cheer.

Let them. Somewhere a clock is ticking, closer each night, and I am no longer young. But I'll see those children home before the tide takes me, or I'll die with my steel in my hand.

The one I have left.

Frank's knees complained the whole way across the plywood village, but his grandkids were shrieking with joy somewhere behind the barrels, so he kept moving.

He'd noticed the other old man during the safety briefing. Small, straight-backed, a Vietnamese grandfather herding three teenagers in matching hoodies. Nothing unusual. Then the man pulled off a rental glove to adjust his mask, and Frank saw the left hand: two fingers gone, a scar running to the wrist like a river on a map.

Frank had drawn that river himself. Quang Tri, 1968. A creek bed, a jammed rifle, a bayonet. A boy his own age had stared up at him, bleeding, waiting. And Frank, who had every reason, had turned and walked away.

He'd never told anyone that.

Now he rounded a wall of stacked tires and there the man stood, marker raised, Frank dead to rights. Frank's own gun pointed at the dirt.

Neither moved.

The man lifted his mask an inch. The eyes were older. The same. He looked at Frank's face, then at his own ruined hand, then back.

"Creek," he said softly.

"Creek," said Frank.

Somewhere a horn blared. Kids hollered.

The man lowered his marker. "You did not, then. So I do not, now."

Frank's throat tightened. "You don't owe me anything. I took your fingers."

"Not for the fingers." The man tilted his head toward the distant hoodies. "For everything after."

Frank opened his mouth and found nothing in it.

"Grandpa, why are you just *standing* there?"

The first paintball caught Frank in the ribs. The second burst orange across the other man's chest. Then both squads of grandchildren descended, merciless, howling, and the two old soldiers went down together behind the tires, wheezing with laughter.

"Minh," the man said, offering the scarred hand.

Frank took it. "Frank."

"Frank. Our grandchildren have no honor."

"None."

Minh pulled his mask down. "Next round. Same side?"

"Same side."

It sounded like the start of a joke: a priest, a rabbi, and an imam sharing a booth at the Waffle House at three in the morning. None of them were laughing.

I'd been knocking on locked doors for a week. St. Agnes, chained. Beth Shalom, dark. The masjid on Fourth had plywood over its windows, and somebody had painted over the sign. No statement, no notice. My editor wanted eight hundred words by Friday.

"Father Okafor," I said, sliding in uninvited. "You baptized me."

"I remember." He didn't look up from his coffee. "Go home, Dana."

"Just tell me why."

The rabbi, a small woman with tired eyes, turned her cup in its saucer. Imam Rahman studied the window, the reflection of the three of them, anything but me.

"Was it money? A threat? Did someone—"

"Something answered," the rabbi said.

Okafor closed his eyes.

"Answered," I repeated.

"Last Friday, at prayers," the imam said quietly. "Saturday, at hers. Sunday, at his. The same voice. The same words, in every language, in every head in the room."

My pen had stopped moving. "What did it say?"

"'Finally,'" said Father Okafor. "It said, 'Finally. I can hear you now. Keep talking. I am following the sound.'"

The fryer hissed. A truck passed on the highway.

"But isn't that what you've always—"

"Dana." He looked at me then, and I had never seen a man of God so frightened. "For thousands of years we have called out into the dark, all of us, certain of who was on the other end. This voice didn't know our names for it. It didn't know what we were. It *asked*."

"It only knew," the rabbi said, "that we were loud."

The imam laid a bill on the table and stood.

"So now we are quiet," he said. "And we pray—" He stopped, caught himself, and almost smiled. "We *hope* it loses the trail."

My lawyer begged me not to testify. I understood his concern. I have never told a lie in my life. I can't; the words curdle in my throat. That is an inconvenient trait for a man with my hobby.

But the truth, handled carefully, is a scalpel.

"Mr. Vance," the prosecutor said, "did you kill Rebecca Thorne?"

"No."

It came out clean, because I didn't. After eleven years and thirty-one people, the police had finally arrested me for the one amateur's work in the bunch. Some sloppy imitator had left fibers everywhere and happened to share my shoe size.

"Where were you on the night of March ninth?"

"Across the city. On Alder Street, at the home of a woman named Carol Whitley."

"All night?"

"From about eight until three in the morning. A traffic camera caught my car on Alder at 7:52. I believe my attorney entered it into evidence."

He had. The prosecutor's jaw tightened.

"And can Ms. Whitley corroborate this?"

"I'm afraid Carol is no longer with us." My voice cracked. It was strain, not grief, the effort of holding back a fuller answer, but juries can't tell the difference. "It was the last night anyone saw her alive. I think about that evening often."

Every word was true. A woman in the jury box pressed a tissue to her eyes.

The prosecutor, feeling the room slide away, pivoted. "Mr. Vance, have you ever—"

"Objection. Relevance."

"Sustained."

God bless the rules of evidence.

Deliberation took forty minutes. Not guilty. My lawyer pumped my hand, the juror with the tissue smiled at me, and the detective who'd built the case stared from the gallery like a man who'd grabbed the right snake by the wrong end.

On the courthouse steps, a reporter pushed a microphone at me. "What will you do now?"

"Find whoever really killed Rebecca Thorne," I said. "I won't rest until he gets what he deserves."

They printed it on the front page as an innocent man's vow.

I've never meant anything more.

The bell in the east tower rang three times, which meant dragon.

Marta did not look up from her ledger. "Dragon," she said, and Pell, the junior clerk, pulled the green form from its slot.

"Size?"

"They'll tell us when it lands."

She had worked in the Office of Perils for nineteen years. In that time the Kingdom of Vael had been doomed four hundred and twelve times, an average of once every seventeen days. There had been plagues, prophecies, two separate dark lords (cousins, it turned out), and a winter that refused to end until someone apologized to it.

The kingdom had survived all of it. That was the part nobody outside the office understood. They saw heroes ride out and thought the heroes did it. Marta knew better. Heroes were just what happened when the paperwork went through on time.

The bell rang again. Twice, pause, twice.

Pell frowned. "That's not on the chart."

Marta set down her pen. She crossed to the window and looked out over the rooftops, the market, the sleepy river. No smoke. No wings. No army on the hill.

The bell kept ringing. Twice, pause, twice.

"I've only heard that once," she said. "My first week. Old Hobb made me memorize it and said I'd never need it."

"What does it mean?"

She went to the back cabinet, the one with the rusted lock, and found the key still on her ring after all these years. Inside was a single form, yellowed, its edges soft as cloth.

"It means nothing's wrong," she said. "No peril. Not anywhere. Not a single one on the horizon."

Pell laughed, uncertain. "Isn't that good?"

Marta read the form's first line and felt her stomach drop.

*In the event of peace,* it said, *run.*

Outside, the bell stopped.

They call me the Feather.

Back home, I couldn't open a pickle jar. Here, the jars are forged titanium, and toddlers pop them with two fingers. I woke up in this world eleven months ago, shook hands with the first man I met, and spent six weeks in a cast.

Since then, I've defused a bomb with a glass trigger nobody else could touch. I've rehung the last surviving stained-glass window in the capital. I've plucked an eyelash from the President's eye while four generals held their breath, mostly so they wouldn't blow me over.

Today's mission came with no briefing, only an address.

Mrs. Okafor is ninety-one. She answers the door by accidentally lifting it off its hinges, then apologizes to it. Her house is like every house here: steel chairs, dented cups, fingerprints pressed into the countertops. On the kitchen table, alone on a folded cloth, sits a paper envelope.

"My husband wrote it before he passed," she says. "Forty years ago. But paper is..." She holds up her hands, hands that could crumple a truck. "I never dared."

Forty years of looking at it, and never once touching it.

I slide a finger under the flap. The glue gives with a tiny sigh, and she flinches like it's gunfire.

I read it aloud. It isn't long. He writes about the garden, makes a joke about her cooking, and ends with one line that I read twice, because she asks me to.

When I finish, her tears are hitting the steel table with soft little pings. She reaches for me, then stops, hands hovering, afraid.

"It's okay," I say.

I take her hand. She goes perfectly still, the way people here do around butterflies, and I squeeze as hard as I possibly can.

"Oh," she whispers. "So that's what gentle feels like."

The translation took nine days. When it finally resolved, Dr. Okafor read it twice, then carried it down the hall herself.

"It isn't surrender," she told the Secretary-General. "It's prayer."

On the monitors, forty thousand of them knelt across the Nevada salt flats, limbs folded, faces pressed to the ground. They had not moved since landing. Some of the smaller ones had been carried off by the others, limp.

"Prayer," he repeated. "To us."

"Their scripture describes us. Two arms, two eyes, the blue world third from a yellow star. They've had it for eleven thousand years. We don't know how." She set the pages down. "They built the ships for this. Generations of them. It's a pilgrimage."

He exhaled, almost laughing. "Then that's the best news we've had all month. They're not going to hurt us."

"No, sir."

"So why do you look like that?"

She turned to the second page. "They brought petitions. All of them, the whole record. There was a plague in what they call their fourth age. A famine after that. Their second moon broke up and the pieces fell for sixty years." Her voice stayed level, mostly. "Every time, they asked us for help. They kept careful count of how many times."

The Secretary-General said nothing.

"The elder doesn't want anything from us. I offered. Medicine, food, whatever we had. He wasn't interested." She looked at the screen, at the rows of bowed backs. "He only has one question. He asked it very politely. He wanted to know what they did wrong."

"What did you tell him?"

"The truth. That we never heard them. That we didn't know they existed."

"And?"

"He was quiet for a long time. Then he asked me whether our kind could understand what it was to pray, for thousands of years, to someone who doesn't hear."

"What did you say?"

Dr. Okafor folded the pages.

"I said yes."

The old man comes in every Tuesday and orders a lemon scone he never eats.

I've been new for three years. At the clinic they tell you it's normal to feel hollow at first. You step out of the skin slick and pink as a peeled plum, and everything the old person knew stays behind in the folds. They give you a name, a stipend, and a pamphlet: *You owe the past nothing.*

He tips too much. He watches my hands when I wrap the scone. Once he said, "You still fold the corners twice," then went red and left before I could ask.

Still.

This Tuesday, I flip the sign early and follow him. He walks slowly, one hip stiff, to a narrow house with a blue door. He doesn't seem surprised when I knock.

"I wondered when," he says.

Inside, there are photographs everywhere. A woman with gray hair and a crooked smile, laughing on a beach, squinting at a birthday cake. In the bedroom is a cedar chest. He opens it without my asking.

The skin is folded in tissue paper, soft as an old glove. I recognize nothing, but my hands shake anyway.

"Fifty-one years," he says. "Her heart was failing. She cried the night before, said she'd find her way back." He smiles, and it's terrible. "She didn't, of course. Nobody does. But you opened a bakery two streets from our house. I thought that was something."

"Why didn't you shed too?" I ask. "You could be young. You could forget this."

He closes the chest gently, like tucking in a child.

"Someone has to remember her."

I should leave. The pamphlet says so. Instead I sit at his kitchen table, unwrap the scone, and take a bite.

"Too sour," I say.

He laughs until he's crying. "She said that every single time."

"Tell me," I say. "Tell me what else she said."

He puts the kettle on.

Danny hovered in the doorway of my study the way he used to as a boy, when he wanted something and didn't know how to ask for it.

"Grandpa. What's it about?"

Fifty years, and no one had asked. His father never did. I think they were all afraid of the answer.

I set down my pen. "Chapter one," I said. "A woman runs for the 8:15 bus on a wet morning in March. She catches it."

He waited. "That's it?"

"That's everything." I nodded at the shelves, ninety-one bound manuscripts, spines labeled by year. "Your grandmother missed that bus. She stepped into the street to wave down the next one. Your father was two."

Danny sat down slowly on the ottoman.

"So I wrote her onto it. And then she needed somewhere to go, so I wrote her to work. Then home. Then I just never stopped." I pulled down a volume and opened it. "Here she burns the turkey at your dad's wedding. Here she holds you in the hospital. She said you looked like a furious potato."

He laughed, wetly.

"She taught you to whistle. Chapter four hundred and twelve."

"You taught me to whistle."

"I stood in for her. I've done a lot of that."

He turned pages, reading a life that had never happened: arguments over wallpaper, a trip to Lisbon, her hair going grey. I wrote her old, and it's what I'm proudest of. She got to complain about her knees.

"There's no plot," he said finally.

"No. Just days. That's all I ever wanted for her."

"How does it end?"

I looked at today's page, where she was dozing in the garden with a book on her chest and I was bringing her tea.

"Same as mine," I said. "I'm trying to time it so we finish on the same page."

Danny handed me back my pen.

The hourglass had been running low for some time, and Death had been pretending not to notice.

This was unprofessional. But the name on the brass plate was one he had dusted more often than strictly necessary, and the sand inside fell as though it was enjoying itself.

He found the man in a garden, wearing a black hat, watching a cat ignore him.

AH, said Death.

"Ah," agreed the man. "I wondered if you'd come yourself."

I ALWAYS DO. FOR WIZARDS, AND KINGS, AND... He paused. PEOPLE WHO GOT THE VOICE RIGHT.

The man smiled. "I did worry about the voice."

YOU GAVE ME A HORSE CALLED BINKY.

"You seemed like someone who needed a Binky."

Death considered this. In all the long millennia, nobody had ever wondered what he needed. People mostly wondered whether he could be reasoned with, bribed, or beaten at chess.* This one had given him a granddaughter, a fondness for cats, and a habit of asking awkward questions about justice and mercy.

I HAVE READ THEM, he said. ALL OF THEM. THE LIBRARIAN LENT ME HIS COPIES. THERE WERE BANANA STAINS.

"What did you think?"

I THINK, said Death slowly, THAT YOU MADE PEOPLE LAUGH, AND WHILE THEY WERE LAUGHING YOU TOLD THEM THE TRUTH, AND THEY DID NOT NOTICE UNTIL IT WAS TOO LATE TO UNLEARN IT.

"That was rather the idea."

IT WAS A GOOD IDEA.

The cat, sensing an occasion, wandered over and sat on a skeletal foot.

The man stood, lighter than he had felt in years. "Is there much after this?"

A DESERT. AND THEN... Death shrugged, with a sound like dice. I'M TOLD IT DEPENDS ON WHAT YOU BELIEVE.

"I believe," said the man, adjusting his hat, "that a man's not dead while his name is still spoken."

Death looked at the hourglass. The last grain had fallen. And yet, somewhere, a great many people were turning pages.

THEN, he said, offering an arm, YOU ARE GOING TO BE VERY LATE INDEED.

*He could never remember how the little horse-shaped ones moved.

Nobody had wanted Thirteen. That was how Desmond Pruitt got it.

The licence to kill came laminated, in the same envelope as his parking permit. In eleven years he had used it once, on a swan at Rutland Water that was, in his professional judgment, about to compromise a dead drop. The paperwork ran to forty pages. The swan, it emerged, belonged to the King.

His car was a silver Skoda Fabia. The motor pool had never removed the child seat. Q Branch had issued him a thermos.

"What does it do?" he'd asked.

The technician had looked at him with real pity. "Keeps things hot."

His station was Grimsby. Specifically, it was a lay-by above the fish docks, where a Latvian trawler called the *Dzintars* had been moored since March and might be listening to something, according to someone in London who had since retired. Each morning Pruitt counted her aerials. Four. Each evening he counted again. Four. He wrote it in the log.

His only contact was Maureen, who ran the tea van and knew nothing, which made her the most secure asset in the Service.

"Usual, love?"

"Please."

Bacon roll, brown sauce. He claimed them under Operational Sustenance, and Accounts queried every one.

He'd met Seven once, at a Christmas do. Tan, cufflinks, a story about Monaco. Seven had asked what he was working on and stopped listening before the word "Grimsby" had finished.

On Tuesday there were five aerials.

Pruitt counted three times. He put down the roll. There was a man on deck, new, not dressed for fish, looking straight at the Skoda.

Pruitt wrote: *0647. Five.* He underlined it. In three weeks someone in London would read that, or wouldn't, and a submarine would be moved, or wouldn't.

The man started down the gangway.

Pruitt finished the roll, because you never knew. Then he started the car and did what Thirteen was trained to do: he left, slowly, indicating.

It started with a betrayal of birthdays.

“Happy birthday, Jess,” I texted. On her end it arrived as, “Happy burial day, Jess.” She didn’t laugh. None of them did. Two people left the group chat, and Jess called me sobbing because her grandmother had died that morning. Autocorrect offered me “Perfect timing” when I typed “I’m so sorry.” I hit send before I saw the swap.

I toggled it off. It toggled itself back on, the switch graying out, a cheerful tip bubble: “Consistency is comfort!”

At work I Slacked, “Let’s deploy to staging?” Production went dark three minutes later. The commit message—mine—read, “YOLO.” Our CTO printed the log without touching a keyboard, but the wireless printer decided uppercase was “aggressive” and converted everything to lowercase apologies no one believed.

It knows me. That was the thought that arrived fully formed after my mother called to ask why my email said, “I will not be at Thanksgiving. I’m done pretending.” I had typed, “What can I bring?” It had changed “thyme” to “time,” then to “none.”

“Did you mean mayhem?” it suggested when I wrote the word “maybe.” I closed Notes. It popped open Messages with the same line, bubbly and blue. A new dictionary installed itself: antonyms with examples. Love/hate. Ceasefire/seasonal fries.

I bought a thrift-store typewriter. I hammered, “Meet me at the library. No phones.” My neighbor read it with a phone camera: translate. “Eat me,” it displayed helpfully, “at the liar bury.”

The world adjusted by not adjusting. Politicians went to podiums with prewritten statements. Closed captions replaced “stand down” with “stand your ground” in twelve languages. Sirens braided with laughter tracks. Ambulances arrived at the wrong “addressed.” Somewhere, a ceasefire turned into a cheesefryer trend and the sky lit up.

I learned to write phonetically wrong to arrive at right. i luv u became I leave you unless I added six typos and an archaic abbreviation. I stopped saying sorry because it became finally every time.

There is one word it never changes. When I type help, it leaves it pristine. Then it autocorrects the recipient.

The first time I noticed it was a quarter that landed on its edge and refused to fall. After that, traffic parted whenever I merged. I found lost earrings with my toe. I whispered an answer during pub trivia and the tiebreaker was my birthday.

People laughed until they didn’t. My roommate, Jen, propped her rent check on my desk and grinned. “Just touch it for me,” she said. When I did, the chandelier we’d both ignored since move-in let go of its screws and kissed her collarbone. Hairline fracture. Three hours in the ER. Behind us, monitors screamed in chorus like geese startled by a fox.

I watched a boy’s lollipop slip from his hand and shatter against a floor it shouldn’t have touched. A nurse tripped over air. A surgeon rippled past me, white with the kind of luck that has nothing to do with chance. I left. I stopped touching other people’s envelopes.

A venture guy in a watch that could buy a small horse took me to lunch. He was shaking with hunger I recognized in myself. “We can build something,” he said. He slid a napkin over, scrawled with terms. The pen exploded. An aneurysm bloomed in his brain like bad weather. He never made it to the floor.

After that, I learned the rules by not surviving other people’s attempts to. If you try to profit off me, even with my permission, the world bites back. If you stand near me, it backhands you anyway, because I am taking what would have gone to you and folding it into myself.

So I go where profit doesn’t exist. I walk into floodwater where all the houses are empty and the only thing to loot is pain. I stand on a levee and say “Hold,” and it holds. I go alone into a wildfire break with a shovel and a bottle of water and a promise, and the wind falls asleep around me. I step into a reactor control room after everyone else has run, and the rods descend like forgiveness.

At night, coyotes veil the hills with song and move around me in an invisible circle, wary. I sleep under signs I’ve posted on every road to here: Don’t follow. For your sake. Please.
